== Nature ==
=== Geology ===
Geologically, Astorga is situated in the West Asturian-Leonese Zone, southwest of the Navia-Alto Sil Domain. The most prominent lithological materials in the municipality include Quaternary natural aggregates and [[Miocene]] clays—traditionally used for both industrial and artisanal ceramics—and [[Paleozoic]] quartzites, sandstones, and slates. Over the Miocene alluvial deposits, secondary gold concentrations with low yields are found in both ancient and modern river terraces.<ref name="IGME"/> Stratigraphically, the western part of the municipality features layers from the Los Cabos Series of the Upper [[Cambrian]] and Lower [[Ordovician]], and the Luarca Slates from the Middle Ordovician. Paleozoic outcrops are flanked by Miocene layers, extensively covered by Quaternary sediments that fully overlay the river basins of the Jerga and Tuerto rivers.<ref name="IGME"/><ref name="mapageologico">{{Cite web |url=http://www.igme.es/internet/cartografia/cartografia/datos/magna50/jpg/d1_jpg/Editado_MAGNA50_193.jpg |title=Hoja de Astorga |work=Mapa geológico de España E. 1:50.000 |publisher=Instituto Geológico y Minero de España |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131203005003/http://www.igme.es/internet/cartografia/cartografia/datos/magna50/jpg/d1_jpg/Editado_MAGNA50_193.jpg |archive-date=December 3, 2013}}</ref>

=== Flora ===
The municipality of Astorga lies within the supramediterranean [[Altitudinal zonation|bioclimatic zone]], with its [[climax vegetation]] comprising [[marcescent]] species and [[conifer]]s.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Rivas Martínez |first=Salvador |year=1987 |title=Mapa de series de vegetación de España y memoria |publisher=ICONA |isbn=8485496256 }}</ref><ref name="VEG">{{Cite web |url=http://www.saber.es/web/biblioteca/libros/provincia-leon/html/diversidad-vegetal-leonesa.php |title=La diversidad vegetal leonesa |access-date=February 6, 2012 |author=Penas Merino, Ángel. Fundación Saber.es |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100817230637/http://www.saber.es/web/biblioteca/libros/provincia-leon/html/diversidad-vegetal-leonesa.php |archive-date=August 17, 2010 |url-status=dead}}</ref> These include [[Quercus pyrenaica|oak trees]], which grow in the cooler, wetter western areas on Quaternary deposits and predominantly siliceous soils, and reforested pine forests, mainly around Alto del Cuerno, featuring species such as Scots pine. Holm oaks are present, often scattered but forming a homogeneous, though degraded, stand between [[Castrillo de los Polvazares]] and Murias de Rechivaldo, with stunted trees due to historical use for charcoal and firewood, a practice common across the province.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.maragateria.com/naturaleza/naturaleza.htm |title=Naturaleza |access-date=February 6, 2012 |author=Maragateria.com}}</ref> Lower strata include species such as [[genista]]s, [[Lavandula|lavenders]], and [[Trifolium arvense|hare's-foot clover]]. In areas lacking tree cover, primarily on sunny slopes with poor soil and water scarcity, shrubs such as rosemary, ''[[adenocarpus hispanicus]]'', and rockrose dominate. In the Tuerto River floodplain, aside from poplar plantations, aspens, willows, and alders are found. The rest of the municipal territory consists of wastelands and agricultural fields.

=== Fauna ===
[[File:Parque de La Eragudina.jpg|thumb|Partial view of La Eragudina Park]]
[[File:Muralla, Palacio Gaudí, Catedral de Astorga.jpg|thumb|Melgar Park, with the monumental complex in the background]]
The municipality is home to a rich and varied fauna due to its transitional position between Mediterranean and Eurosiberian ecosystems.<ref name="FAU">{{Cite web |title=La vida animal en la provincia de León |url=http://www.saber.es/web/biblioteca/libros/provincia-leon/html/vida-animal-provincia-leon.php |access-date=June 8, 2013 |author=Juan Manuel Nieto Nafría. University of León |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100918162426/http://www.saber.es/web/biblioteca/libros/provincia-leon/html/vida-animal-provincia-leon.php |archive-date=September 18, 2010 |url-status=dead}}</ref> Regarding [[Ichthyology|fish]], Astorga's waters support only two species: the [[common barbel]] and the [[Pseudochondrostoma duriense|northern straight-mouth nase]], accompanied by mammals such as the otter.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Atlas de vertebrados de la provincia de León. Listado de peces en el municipio de Astorga |url=http://oslo.geodata.es/gia/php/info_municipios.php?tipo=4&id=24008 |access-date=June 8, 2013 |author=Grupo Ibérico de Anillamiento }}</ref> Among amphibians and reptiles, species include the common toad, [[marbled newt]], [[ocellated lizard]], [[Vipera seoanei|Seoane's viper]], and [[Malpolon monspessulanus|Montpellier snake]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Atlas de vertebrados de la provincia de León. Listado de anfibios y reptiles en el municipio de Astorga |url=http://oslo.geodata.es/gia/php/info_municipios.php?tipo=2&id=24008 |access-date=June 8, 2013 |author=Grupo Ibérico de Anillamiento }}</ref> In the municipality's flat areas, birds such as the kestrel and sparrowhawk, and small mammals such as rabbits and Iberian hares, are found. Near population centers, white storks, swallows, common swifts, wood pigeons, various [[Tit (bird)|tits]], rooks, and raptors such as the [[red kite]] are common.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Atlas de vertebrados de la provincia de León. Listado de aves en el municipio de Astorga |url=http://oslo.geodata.es/gia/php/info_municipios.php?tipo=3&id=24008 |access-date=June 8, 2013 |author=Grupo Ibérico de Anillamiento }}</ref> In pastures or wooded areas, species such as the red partridge, roe deer, weasel, fox, wild boar, and occasionally wolves are present.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Atlas de vertebrados de la provincia de León. Listado de mamíferos en el municipio de Astorga |url=http://oslo.geodata.es/gia/php/info_municipios.php?&id=24008 |access-date=June 8, 2013 |author=Grupo Ibérico de Anillamiento }}</ref>

== History ==
[[File:Bellum-Asturicum-Cantabricum.png|thumb|Roman military operations during the [[Cantabrian Wars]]
{{Legend|#EE1E3A|Campaign of {{circa|25 BC}}}}
{{Legend|#52BA65|Campaign of {{circa|26 BC}}}}
{{Legend|#FFCD33|Campaign of [[Julius Caesar]] of {{circa|61 BC}}}}
{{Legend|#C878B2|Campaign of [[Decimus Junius Brutus Callaicus|Decimus Junius Brutus]] of {{circa|137 BC}}}}]]

=== Ancient era ===
{{See also|Asturica Augusta}}
The history of Astorga theoretically dates back to the [[List of the Pre-Roman peoples of the Iberian Peninsula|pre-Roman]] period, as the Greco-Egyptian geographer [[Ptolemy]] referred to Asturica as a city of the [[Astures]] and capital of the Amachians. This has led researchers such as [[Manuel Gómez-Moreno Martínez]] and [[José María Luengo Martínez]] to suggest an indigenous origin.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Gómez Moreno |first=Manuel |year=1905 |title=Catálogo Monumental de la Provincia de León |location=Madrid|publisher=none }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Luengo |first=José María |year=1953 |title=Astorga (León). Exploración de las cloacas romanas |journal=Noticiario Arqueológico Hispánico II }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Luengo |first=José María |year=1956–61 |title=Astorga Romana |journal=Noticiario Arqueológico Hispánico V }}</ref> However, archaeological excavations in the urban area have not yielded materials to confirm such origins.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Mañanes |first=Tomás |year=1983 |title=Astorga romana y su entorno: estudio arqueológico |location=Valladolid |publisher=Universidad de Valladolid. Secretariado de Publicaciones |isbn=84-86192-11-0 }}</ref> Thus, a pre-Roman settlement cannot be scientifically affirmed, despite the presence of several [[Iron Age]] ''[[castra]]'' in the surrounding area, such as La Mesa in Castrillo de los Polvazares.<ref>{{Harvnb|Alonso González|2000|p=23}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |title=Los recortes en investigación paralizan las excavaciones del castro de La Mesa |url=http://www.lacronicadeleon.es/2012/11/21/leon/los-recortes-en-investigacion-paralizan-las-excavaciones-del-castro-de-la-mesa-167235.htm |last=Reinares |first=M.A. |work=La Crónica de León |date=November 21, 2012 |access-date=July 9, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130211093125/http://www.lacronicadeleon.es/2012/11/21/leon/los-recortes-en-investigacion-paralizan-las-excavaciones-del-castro-de-la-mesa-167235.htm |archive-date=February 11, 2013}}</ref>

Based on archaeological evidence, the city's foundation is linked to a detachment of the [[Legio X Gemina]] during the [[Cantabrian Wars]]. This is evidenced by the discovery of two defensive trenches and several foundation ditches for possible wooden structures.<ref name="CAMPA">{{Cite journal |last=González |first=Mari Luz |year=1996 |title=Consideraciones sobre el origen campamental de Asturica Augusta |journal=Actas del Coloquio Internacional: Los Finisterres Atlánticos en la Antigüedad. Época Prerromana y Romana |pages=85–90 |location=Gijón }}</ref> After the campaigns of [[Augustus]] against the [[Astures]] and [[Cantabri]], between {{circa|29 BC}} and {{circa|19 BC}}, the camp was established, and following pacification, it transitioned into a civilian settlement within the [[Hispania Tarraconensis|Tarraconensis province]]. This shift likely occurred in the early 1st century, as evidenced by the hospitality pact with the [[Zoelae]] in 27 AD, indicating stabilized Roman-indigenous relations.<ref>{{Harvnb|Alonso González|2000|p=24}}</ref>

Around the transition between the reigns of [[Claudius]] and [[Vespasian]], the city became the capital of the ''[[Conventus Asturum|Conventus Iuridicus Asturum]]'' and a major recipient of gold from mines such as [[Las Médulas]]. This prosperity led [[Pliny the Elder]], then [[Procurator (ancient Rome)|procurator]] of [[Hispania Citerior]], to describe the city in his ''[[Natural History (Pliny)|Naturalis Historia]]'' as ''vrbs magnifica''.<ref name="VRBS">{{Cite book |last=Pliny the Elder |year=2002 |title=Historia Natural |location=Madrid |publisher=Cátedra |isbn=9788437619583 }}</ref><ref>"Asturica urbe magnifica". [[Pliny the Elder]], ''Naturalis Historia'', Book III, paragraph 28.</ref> With the territorial reorganization in the 3rd century, the city became part of the [[Gallaecia]] province, with [[Bracara Augusta]] (Braga) as its capital. The decline of mining under [[Diocletian]] marked the beginning of the city's decline.

By the mid-3rd century, Astorga likely became an episcopal see, with Basílides as its first bishop around 249.<ref name="DAT"/> The spread of Christianity faced challenges from [[Barbarian invasions into the Roman Empire of the 3rd century|barbarian invasions]] and the rise of [[Priscillianism|Priscillianist]] and [[Manichaeism|Manichean]] doctrines, which were later opposed by [[Hydatius]] and [[Turibius of Astorga|Saint Turibius]].<ref>{{Harvnb|Alonso González|2000|p=27}}</ref>

=== Middle Ages ===
[[File:COA Marquis of Astorga.svg|thumb|In 1465, Henry IV of Castile granted Álvaro Pérez Osorio the title of Marquis of Astorga]]
Following the barbarian invasions, the [[Suebi]] established themselves in the former Gallaecia around 410, and Astorga became part of their kingdom. Conflicts with the Visigoths led to sacks by [[Theodoric II]] in 456<ref>{{Cite book |last=Sayas Abengochea |first=Juan José |title=Historia Antigua de España |volume=II |page=200 |year=2006 |publisher=UNED |isbn=84-362-4398-6}}</ref> and [[Leovigild]] in 569. This resulted in the loss of its status as the capital of the ''conventus'', with the Roman political and administrative system collapsing, and prominence shifting to León. In 714, during the [[Muslim conquest of the Iberian Peninsula]], Astorga was attacked and destroyed by [[Tariq ibn Ziyad|Tariq]] en route north.<ref>{{Harvnb|Alonso González|2000|p=30}}</ref><ref name="COMA">{{Cite journal |last1=Cabero Diéguez |first1=Valentín |last2=López Trigal |first2=Lorenzo |title=La ciudad de Astorga |journal=La provincia de León y sus comarcas |page=240 |publisher=Diario de León |year=1987 |volume=15 |url=http://www.saber.es/web/biblioteca/libros/la-provincia-de-leon-y-sus-comarcas/html/pdf/fas15.pdf |access-date=November 16, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130412052650/http://www.saber.es/web/biblioteca/libros/la-provincia-de-leon-y-sus-comarcas/html/pdf/fas15.pdf |archive-date=April 12, 2013 |url-status=dead}}</ref> The Muslims named it {{lang|ar|إشطرقة}} ({{lang|ar-Latn|Ishṭarqa}}).
After the emergence of the [[Kingdom of Asturias]] in the mid-8th century, King [[Alfonso I of Asturias]] reconquered Astorga among other cities for the Christians. [[Ordoño I of Asturias]], who ascended the throne in 850, tasked Count Gatón with the city's repopulation and reconstruction.

Years later, the five sons of [[Alfonso III of Asturias]] rebelled against him, leading to the division of the crown upon his abdication. [[García I of León]], who received León, established his court in Astorga for four years until his death in 914. After this, [[Ordoño II of León]] moved the capital to León, marking the birth of the [[Kingdom of León]]. In 988, León was sacked by [[Almanzor]], prompting, according to Víctor Gebhardt, a temporary relocation of the court to Astorga.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Gebhardt |first=Víctor |year=1861 |title=Historia general de España y de sus Indias desde los tiempos más remotos hasta nuestros días |volume=III |page=90 |location=Madrid |publisher=Librería Española }}</ref> Astorga itself suffered sieges and plunder by Almanzor's forces in 988, 994, and 996.<ref name="COMA"/>

In 1034, [[Sancho III of Pamplona]] captured Astorga and the rest of León amid disputes with [[Bermudo III of León]]. In 1073, the [[Tenant-in-chief|tenure]] system was established as a form of governance.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Torres Sevilla-Quiñones de León |first=Margarita Cecilia |author-link=Margarita Torres |year=1997 |title=La familia de Diego Ansúrez, conde de Astorga (siglos X-XII) |journal=Astórica: Revista de estudios, documentación, creación y divulgación de temas astorganos |issue=16 |pages=195–204 |issn=0212-6141 }}</ref><ref>{{Harvnb|Alonso González|2000|p=31}}</ref> In the early 12th century, it was occupied by [[Theresa, Countess of Portugal]], who took advantage of the disputes between her sister [[Urraca of León and Castile|Urraca I of León]] and [[Alfonso the Battler|Alfonso I of Aragon]]. In 1143, it became the domain of her son, [[Afonso I of Portugal]].

During the reign of [[Ferdinand III of Castile]], territorial administration shifted from [[Tenencia|''tenencias'']] to lordships. For Astorga, this occurred around 1277, but in 1345, [[Alfonso XI of Castile]] decided the city would be governed by a magistrate and several councilmen.

From 1367 to the end of the century, Astorga faced a crisis due to the plague, conflicts between [[Peter of Castile|Peter I of Castile]] and [[Henry II of Castile]], and economic hardship. During this period, Astorgan merchants maintained trade with various Galician towns, possibly laying the foundation for future [[Arriero|muleteering]].<ref>{{Harvnb|Rodríguez Díez|1981|p=226}}</ref>

On July 16, 1465, through a privilege granted in [[Toro, Zamora|Toro]], [[Henry IV of Castile]] awarded Álvar Pérez Osorio, Count of Trastámara, Lord of Villalobos, and Castroverde, the title of Marquis of Astorga, shifting the city to a feudal status.<ref name="MARQUES">{{Cite journal |last=Martín Fuertes |first=José Antonio |year=1983 |title=El Marquesado de Astorga. Introducción a su historia |journal=Astórica: Revista de estudios, documentación, creación y divulgación de temas astorganos |issue=1 |pages=39–56 |issn=0212-6141}}</ref> The marquisate exerted significant influence over the city's governance, impacting areas controlled by the cathedral chapter.<ref>{{Harvnb|Alonso González|2000|p=36}}</ref>

=== Early modern period ===
The 16th century was marked, in its early years, by the [[Revolt of the Comuneros|Comuneros War]] (1520–1521); Astorga sided with the royalists, as the marquis supported [[Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor|Charles I]].<ref>{{Harvnb|Alonso González|2000|p=38}}</ref> This period saw the establishment of numerous [[confraternity|confraternities]] that aided the poor and pilgrims through hospitals, a practice reinforced by the Camino de Santiago's passage through the city. This tradition of hospitality is preserved in institutions such as the San Juan Bautista and the Cinco Llagas hospitals.<ref>{{Harvnb|Alonso González|2000|p=39}}</ref> The Church's influence was pervasive, not only through moral authority but also because the cathedral chapter owned extensive rural and urban properties.

The arrival of the printing press in 1545, introduced by Agustín de Paz, boosted written production, initially focused on [[Roman Missal|missals]] and ecclesiastical works such as Francisco de Evia's ''Thesaurus Angelorum''. This marked the start of a printing tradition with figures such as Antonio de la Calzada, peaking in the late 19th century and early 20th century, when Astorga had more printing presses than the provincial capital, including those of Antonio Gullón, Juan Alonso, Porfirio López, Nicesio Fidalgo, González Revillo, and Ortiz.<ref>{{Harvnb|Alonso González|2000|p=180}}</ref>

During the 18th century, the city achieved some prosperity, with daily life featuring jousting with canes, bullfights in the Plaza Mayor, [[bowling]]—regulated in 1601—theatrical performances, and sacramental functions.<ref>{{Harvnb|Alonso González|2000|p=40}}</ref> Between the 18th century and 19th century, Astorga's territory was affected by the division of the province into cantons and jurisdictions, later modified during the Peninsular War.

=== Modern era ===
{{See also|Siege of Astorga}}

In the early 19th century, the city's growth stalled due to epidemics and the [[Peninsular War|French occupation]]. Astorga was among the first cities to revolt against the French, with a peasant and laborer uprising on May 2, 1808.<ref name="Alonso González 2000 42"/> In June, the Junta of Armament and Defense was formed. French forces entered on December 31, 1808, and the city changed hands multiple times, with heroic defenses led by General [[José María Santocildes]], until the French surrendered on August 17, 1812, following a strategy by Generals [[Francisco Javier Castaños, 1st Duke of Bailén|Castaños]] and [[Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington|Wellesley]]. General Santocildes documented these events in his ''Historical Summary of the Attacks, Siege, and Surrender of Astorga''.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Santocildes |first=José María |title=Resumen histórico de los ataques, sitio y rendición de Astorga |url=http://saber.es/web/biblioteca/libros/resumen-historico-de-los-ataques-sitio-rendicion-de-astorga/resumen-historico-de-los-ataques-sitio-rendicion-de-astorga.pdf |access-date=June 26, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120203071418/http://www.saber.es/web/biblioteca/libros/resumen-historico-de-los-ataques-sitio-rendicion-de-astorga/resumen-historico-de-los-ataques-sitio-rendicion-de-astorga.pdf |archive-date=February 3, 2012 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

After [[Ferdinand VII of Spain]]'s restoration, he abolished the [[Spanish Constitution of 1812|1812 Constitution]], reverting to [[Absolutism (European history)|absolutism]], a move welcomed by Astorga's ecclesiastical, noble, and bourgeois sectors. The influence of the bishopric and cathedral chapter persisted through the 19th century and 20th century.<ref>{{Harvnb|Alonso González|2000|p=44}}</ref> During [[Joseph Bonaparte]]'s brief rule, a [[History of the territorial organization of Spain|new territorial organization]] was proposed, with Astorga heading the Esla Department.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Melón Ruiz de Gordejuela |first=Amando |title=El mapa prefectural de España (1810) |journal=Estudios geográficos |pages=689–762 |publisher=CSIC |date=1977 |issn=0014-1496}}</ref> This plan failed, and in 1820, during the [[Trienio Liberal]], a new division made Astorga one of the province's eleven districts, but this was annulled in 1823. In 1833, with the [[1833 territorial division of Spain|new territorial reorganization]], Astorga and Maragatería were incorporated into the [[Province of León]].

During [[Isabel II of Spain]]'s reign and after the [[Spanish Constitution of 1845|1845 Constitution]], Astorga was represented by the progressive Santiago Alonso Cordero. In subsequent decades, other representatives included [[Pío Gullón Iglesias]], part of the political alternative to [[Antonio Cánovas del Castillo]], and [[Manuel García Prieto]], who served as prime minister several times, the last in 1922, before [[Miguel Primo de Rivera]]'s coup.<ref>{{Harvnb|Alonso González|2000|p=47}}</ref>

With the outbreak of the [[Spanish Civil War]] on [[Spanish coup of July 1936|July 18, 1936]], after miners' columns passed through toward Asturias, the Civil Guard and military took control of Astorga on July 20, keeping it—along with most of the province—in rebel territory. The [[Spanish transition to democracy|Transition]] and democracy's arrival spurred further development, diversifying the economy through tourism, increased road transport, and revitalization as a regional hub.

== Religion ==
Religion has consistently shaped Astorga's historical development. No evidence of indigenous deities is recorded in Astorgan territory, likely due to its Roman military origin, but the presence of the god Caraedudi is noted in Cuevas—near Celada de la Vega—<ref>[http://www.academia.edu/5801956/Asturica_Augusta._Reflexiones_sobre_su_estatuto_y_su_papel_territorial_finales_del_siglo_I_a._C.-principios_del_siglo_III_d._C._ Refers to the god on p. 107.] Accessed February 27, 2014.</ref><ref>Caraedudi is the dative form ending in *i* of a Celtic-origin god's name. The word derives from "cara," from the Celtic Carus, meaning "stone," commonly seen in Celtiberian toponymy. Cf: José María Blázquez, Religiones primitivas de Hispania, Madrid-Roma, 1962, p. 76.</ref> and a plaque dedicated to Marti Tileno was found in [[Quintana del Marco]].

=== Paganism ===
[[File:Bronze youth chlamys Sous-Parsat CdM Paris.jpg|thumb|Mercury was among the gods worshipped in Astorga]]
;Roman and Greek Gods
With the establishment of the Roman camp, both Roman and Greek gods were adopted in religious practice, with evidence of the following cults in the city:
* [[Mars (mythology)|Mars]], the war god aiding the camp, known in Astorga as Gradivus—also associated with crop growth—and Sagatus, referencing the soldiers' ''sagum'' or campaign cloak.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Guillén |first=José |year=1994 |title=Vrbs Roma Vida y costumbres de los romanos III. Religión y Ejército |page=203 |publisher=Sígueme |isbn=84-301-0801-7}}</ref>
* [[Mercury (mythology)|Mercury]], god of commerce and roads, with a single representation found on a secondary route from Astorga to the [[Las Médulas]] gold mines.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Mañanes |first=Tomás |year=1981 |title=El Bierzo prerromano y romano |pages=313, 314, 342 |location=León |publisher=Centro de Estudios e Investigación "San Isidoro" |isbn=8400049438}}</ref>
* Worship of the Emperor and worship of the Empress, natural for a capital of the [[Conventus Asturum|''Conventus Juridicus'']], housing numerous officials.
* Julia Domna, revered as the mother of the emperor, senate, camp, and homeland, worshipped through the goddesses [[Minerva]] and [[Juno (mythology)|Juno]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Vázquez Hoys |first=A. María |year=1987 |title=Creencias religiosas |journal=Historia General de España y América. Constitución y ruina de la España romana |volume=II |page=419 |location=Madrid |publisher=Rialp}}</ref>
* [[Proserpina]], daughter of [[Ceres (mythology)|Ceres]], known in Astorga as Invicta.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Grimal |first=Pierre |year=1994 |title=Diccionario de mitología griega y romana |page=374 |publisher=Ediciones Paidós Ibérica |isbn=9788449322112}}</ref>
* [[Apollo]], protector of the emperor, associated in Astorga with the Celtic god [[Grannus]], meaning "garnet", "bright as scarlet", or "shining like the sun", with a sanctuary in [[Trier]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bandinelli |year=1984 |title=L'Arte romana |page=98 |location=Roma |publisher=Riuniti |isbn=8835927420}}</ref>
Representations of [[Asclepius]] and his son [[Telesphorus (mythology)|Telesphorus]], linked to medicine and healing, have also been found.

;Oriental gods
Due to its status as a ''conventus'' capital and home to senior imperial officials, dedications to Eastern gods appeared in the late 2nd century and early 3rd century, introduced by the [[Severan dynasty]] and high-ranking Eastern officials such as Ioul or Silvanos Melanion, sometimes inscribed in Greek.
* [[Isis]], depicted with the Greek epithet Myronimo—thousand names—symbolizing her roles as protector of the land, food producer, patron of childbirth, and women's health.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Aymard |first1=André |last2=Auboyer |first2=Jeannine |year=1979 |title=Roma y su imperio |journal=Historia general de las civilizaciones |volume=II |page=410 |location=Barcelona |publisher=Destino |isbn=8423310426}}</ref>
* [[Mithra]], Persian sun god absorbed by Rome, referenced in Astorga by inscriptions such as ''Invicto Deo'' and ''Soli Invicto''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=García Bellido |first=Antonio |year=1956 |title=El culto a Serapis en la península ibérica |journal=Boletín de la Real Academia de Historia |volume=139 |pages=293–355}}</ref>
* [[Serapis]], an Egyptian god often paired with Isis, associated with health and healing, honored with amulets and ex-votos.

=== Christianity and the Episcopal See ===
{{See also|Diocese of Astorga}}

Until Christianity's arrival, religion in Astorga was polytheistic. With Christianity, monotheism emerged, along with churches dedicated to revered saints such as Saint Martin, Saint [[Acisclus]], Saint Christopher, and Saint Martha.

Records confirm that Decencius, Bishop of León, attended the [[Council of Elvira]] between 295 and 314, where 37 Iberian bishops gathered, indicating that León and Astorga jointly formed one of the earliest Christian sees in Hispania.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Quintana |first=Augusto |year=1970 |title=Los primeros siglos del cristianismo en el Convento Jurídico Asturicense |journal=AA. VV., Legio VII Gemina |page=469 |location=León}}</ref> After the [[Edict of Milan]] in 313, León's military character made it heavily influenced by [[Mithraism]], popular among soldiers, and the episcopal see was relocated solely to Astorga. By then, Astorga had lost political influence due to [[Diocletian]]'s provincial reorganization, which stripped it of its ''conventus'' capital status;<ref group="note">This capital status passed to [[Bracara Augusta]].</ref> the transfer of the diocese helped maintain its prominence, now in the religious sphere.<ref group="note">The most significant Christian artifact from this new episcopal see is a sarcophagus decorated with six scenes from the Old and New Testaments, imported from Rome.</ref>

Documents provide evidence of Astorga's bishops from 380, when Simposius attended the first Council of Zaragoza.<ref>{{Cite journal |editor-last=Vives |editor-first=José |editor2-last=Marín Martínez |editor2-first=Tomás |editor3-last=Martínez Díez |editor3-first=Gonzalo |year=1963 |title=Concilios Visigóticos e Hispano-Romanos |journal=España cristiana |volume=1 |page=72 |location=Madrid |publisher=[[Consejo Superior de Investigaciones Científicas]], Instituto Enrique Flórez}}</ref> Astorgan bishops participated in the various Councils of Toledo, starting with Dictinius. Discussions included the maintenance and worship of rural churches, many of which survived as medieval hermitages and sanctuaries, such as the Virgin of Castrotierra hermitage, located at an ancient Iron Age site.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Puertas Tricas |first=Rafael |title=Iglesias Hispánicas (siglo IV al VIII): Testimonios literarios |location=Madrid |year=1975 |pages=314 |isbn=84-369-0387-0|publisher=none}}</ref>

Besides conciliar records, [[Hydatius]]'s ''Chronicle'' documents Astorgan bishops throughout the 5th century. During [[Turibius of Astorga|Saint Turibius's]] episcopate (440–480), invasions by Suebi, Vandals, and Alans, as well as Visigothic attacks led to the destruction of Astorgan churches.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Tranoy |first=Alain |year=1974 |title=Hydace Chronique |pages=158–159 |location=Paris |publisher=ed du Cerf}}</ref> During Turibius's tenure, the [[Manichaeism|Manichean]] heresy emerged, addressed at the Astorgan Council of 456,<ref>E. Flórez, E. S., XVI, 314. Citation from the Catalogue of the Ages of Man.</ref> followed by [[Arianism]] around 585, until [[Reccared I|Reccared]]'s conversion to Christianity in 589 at the [[Third Council of Toledo]], under Bishop [[Talasius]]. Astorgan bishops attended all subsequent [[Councils of Toledo]], up to the XVI Council in 693.<ref group='note'>Three heresies emerged in Astorga's Christian church: Manichaeism, Priscillianism, and Arianism.</ref>

In the Middle Ages, the diocese was restructured. During the repopulation period, Christian life was revitalized, and several churches and monasteries emerged within the city, including those of Saint Christopher, Saint Julian and Saint Basilisa, Saint Acisclus, Saint Salvador, Saint Thomas, Saint Martin, Saint Isidore, and Saint Peter.<ref>{{Harvnb|Rodríguez Díez|1981|pp=581–634}}</ref> Outside the city, the San Dictino monastery was founded. In the 11th century, the Santa María Cathedral, several churches, and the San Juan Bautista hospital were built, along with additional churches, the Santa Clara monastery, and the Santo Tomás Cantuariense hospital outside the city.

Below is a list of Astorga's bishops who attended various councils in Hispania, as documented by the councils' records:
* Polibius attended the first Council of Braga in 561.
* Talasius attended the Third Council of Toledo in 589.
* Concordius attended the Fourth Council of Toledo in 633.
* Oscandus attended the Sixth Council of Toledo in 638.
* Presbyter Paul, representing Bishop Candidatus, attended the Seventh Council of Toledo in 646.
* Bishop Candidatus attended the Eighth Council of Toledo in 653.
* Elpidius attended the Tenth Council of Toledo in 656.
* Isidore attended the Third Council of Braga.
* Abbot Leopardo, representing Bishop Aurelius, attended the Thirteenth Council of Toledo in 683.
* Aurelius attended the Fifteenth Council of Toledo in 688.
* Aurelius attended the Sixteenth Council of Toledo in 693.

Subsequent records of the diocese and its bishops relate to the city's repopulation and the restoration of the bishopric during the [[Reconquista]].<ref>{{Cite book |editor=García Villoslada, Ricardo |title=La iglesia en la España romana y visigoda (siglos I-VIII) |publisher=Biblioteca de Autores Cristianos |location=Madrid |date=1979 |volume=1 |series=Historia de la Iglesia en España |last1=Sotomayor |first1=M |last2=García |first2=T. G. |last3=de Osaba |first3=P. L. |pages=408 ff |isbn=9788422009061 |others=Note from the Catalogue of the Ages of Man}}</ref> The Diocese of Astorga has been under the jurisdiction of the Archdiocese of Oviedo since 1954.

[[File:Nuevos bloques.jpg|thumb|Population growth has been stagnant in recent years. Pictured are newly constructed apartment blocks]]

== Demographics ==
The municipality has a population of 10,308 inhabitants ([[National Statistics Institute (Spain)|INE]] 2024). Unlike cities such as León and Ponferrada, Astorga has not significantly attracted residents from surrounding regions and grew slowly during the 20th century, reaching its peak in 1981, though the 1940 figure was inflated by the presence of soldiers and prisoners from the Civil War.

Since the 1980s, the city has experienced a slight but steady population decline due to aging demographics, fewer births, and emigration to more dynamic centers. In 2011, Astorga ranked 25th among Spain's 100 municipalities with the highest median age, at 46.63 years compared to the national average of 44.1.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.ine.es/jaxi/tabla.do?path=/t20/e244/avance/p03/l0/&file=06002.px&type=pcaxis&L=0 |title=Censos de Población y Viviendas 2011. Resultados Municipales. Municipios con edad media más alta |author=Instituto Nacional de Estadística, España |access-date=July 6, 2014}}</ref>

== Urban planning ==
[[File:Canalización romana.jpg|thumb|The first water channeling system was built in Roman times]]

===The ancient city===
The urban planning of Astorga has historically been shaped by the terrain's topography, with the settlement established in ancient times atop a natural ridge. After the Cantabrian Wars ended and the military camp transitioned into an urban center, the city experienced a period of growth driven by the development of mining activities, which peaked between the 1st century and 3rd century. This led to Astorga becoming the seat of the ''concillium'' (a meeting of delegates from indigenous tribes), the [[Imperial cult (ancient Rome)|imperial cult]], and the ''Conventus Asturicensis''. The city spanned 26 hectares, enclosed by a city wall over two kilometers long. The enclosure's shape was not rectangular due to a narrowing of the ridge at its southern corner, resulting in a triangular layout where the [[Forum (Roman)|forum]] was located. Public buildings were erected, streets—some with porticos—were paved, and a sewer network was constructed, alongside sophisticated domestic architecture. By the 3rd century, Astorga's role as an [[episcopal see]] further defined the city's life in subsequent centuries.<ref>{{Harvnp|Alonso González|2000|p=164}}</ref>

With the [[fall of the Western Roman Empire]], Astorga, like many other urban centers, experienced a period of decline that lasted until the [[Early Middle Ages]], when recovery began. By then, the urban core—still enclosed within its walls—consisted of houses with straw and tile roofs built over the original Roman layout.
[[File:Santuario de Nuestra Señora de Fátima.jpg|thumb|During the medieval period, numerous religious buildings were constructed. Pictured is the former church of San Julián]]

===The medieval city===
In the 9th century, the repopulation policies of Ordoño I led to a population increase over several decades, resulting in the emergence of new neighborhoods and the clearing of nearby lands. During the 12th century and 13th century, new churches began replacing the earlier high-medieval monasteries, which were gradually disappearing. Two key factors shaped the city during the medieval period: the contributions of the Jewish population, which built a [[synagogue]], a cistern, and a cemetery,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Rodríguez Fernández |first=Justiniano |year=1976 |title=Las juderías de la provincia de León |location=León |publisher=Centro de Estudios e Investigación "San Isidoro" |isbn=84-00-04301-4 }}</ref> and the development of the Camino de Santiago, which spurred the construction of hospitals. The urban landscape featured contiguous buildings along narrow streets, plots, orchards, and religious enclosures; by the 12th century, houses typically included a courtyard, wine press, cellar, [[granary]], dovecote, and garden.<ref>{{Harvnp|Alonso González|2000|pp=165-166}}</ref>

The construction of religious buildings continued in subsequent centuries; by the 15th century, there were up to eight churches, several of which later disappeared, such as those of San Dictino and San Feliz. A similar fate befell some monasteries, with older ones such as San Martín and San Francisco vanishing. Meanwhile, various [[chapels funded by guilds]] were built, including San Esteban, San Adrián, San Felipe Neri, and San Pedro, along with numerous hospitals due to the growth of the Camino de Santiago. Additionally, from 1471, the construction of the [[Astorga Cathedral|new cathedral]] began.

===The modern city===
In the late 17th century, Manuel de la Lastra designed the layout of the Plaza Mayor and constructed the Town Hall, where the municipal council meetings, previously held in the atrium of the church of San Bartolomé as was customary in Leonese [[Concejo abierto|open councils]], were henceforth conducted.<ref>{{Harvnp|Alonso González|2000|p=170}}</ref> By the 18th century, the city was organized into four parishes—San Bartolomé, San Miguel, San Julián, and Santa Marta—with the suburbs of San Andrés, Puerta de Rey, and Rectivía located outside the walls. Connections to other parts of the peninsula were limited to cart roads in varying states of repair, and several authors, such as [[Antonio Ponz]] and [[Alexandre de Laborde]], lamented between 1787 and 1807 the poor condition, irregularity, and lack of cleanliness of the city's streets.<ref>{{Harvnp|Alonso González|2000|p=171}}</ref>

[[File:Avenida Ponferrada, Astorga.jpg|thumb|View of Ponferrada Avenue, one of the main thoroughfares in the contemporary city]]

===The contemporary city===
After the end of the War of Independence, which directly impacted Astorga, the city began its recovery through commercial and industrial activity, particularly with the development of the chocolate industry. In the final years of the century, the city, which had previously seen limited expansion, began to grow beyond the walled enclosure: on February 19, 1866, the railway arrived with the opening of the León-Astorga section of the [[León–A Coruña railway|León-La Coruña railway line]], and on July 1, 1898, the Plasencia-Astorga railway line was inaugurated. This dual rail connection spurred growth in the San Andrés and Puerta de Rey neighborhoods, while the link between the [[N-6 road (Spain)|Madrid-La Coruña]] highway and the [[N-120 road (Spain)|León]] road benefited the rest of the city. This development was accompanied by the inauguration of the [[water supply network|water supply system]] in 1889—replacing an earlier project from 1782–1787 called "Viaje de Aguas"—which eliminated the need to fetch water from the Fuente Encalada spring, and the installation of electric lighting in 1897.<ref name="ReferenceA">{{Harvnp|Alonso González|2000|p=172}}</ref>

In the 20th century, specifically in 1924, the Santocildes military barracks were inaugurated. During the second quarter of the century, the urban core expanded northward and westward, though the Civil War slowed this growth. Examples of expansion in subsequent decades include the areas of Santa Clara, Manjarín, Candelas, Cuatro Caminos, and the Pandorado road. In 1996, two green spaces, previously scarce in the urban core, were created with the transformation of La Eragudina into a garden and El Melgar into a recreational area.

Since 1985, a Comprehensive Plan for the Protection of Buildings declared ''[[Bien de Interés Cultural]]'', another for the preservation of facades, and a third for the recovery of unique elements have been in place. These initiatives have led to the rehabilitation of spaces such as the Aljibe, Plaza de la Culebra, and Plaza Romana, as well as the pedestrianization of the so-called Monumental Axis, between Puerta Sol and Plaza Eduardo de Castro.<ref>{{Harvnp|Alonso González|2000|p=190}}</ref>

===Parks and gardens===
[[File:Jardines en Astorga.jpg|thumb|Melgar Park]]
The city features several green spaces, with the Synagogue Garden standing out for its historical significance. In the last decades of the 20th century, the parks of La Eragudina, El Melgar, and El Mayuelo were added.

The Synagogue Garden, previously known as San Francisco, Alfonso XIII, and Generalísimo, is the city's oldest park, established in 1835.<ref>{{Harvnp|Alonso González|2000|p=160}}</ref> The area it occupies was part of the Jewish quarter, where the synagogue was located, hence its name. Three years after the project's inception, the leveling of the significantly sloped terrain was completed. By early 1840, the works were finished, and the garden, one of Spain's first romantic-style gardens according to Roberto Alonso,<ref>{{Cite web |title=El Jardín de Astorga |url=http://www.astorga.com/articulo/jardin.htm |access-date=8 June 2013 |author=Roberto Alonso}}</ref> featured a rockery fountain, hedges, and walkways, later complemented by a rose garden.<ref>{{Cite web |title=El Jardín o Parque de la Sinagoga |url=http://www.astorga.com/articulo/callesyp.htm#JARDIN |access-date=8 June 2013 |author=Martín Martínez}}</ref> From this garden begins what was once the ''[[chemin de ronde]]'' of the city wall, which over time became the city's main promenade.

The Mayuelo Park, located halfway between the urban core and the Sierro hill, occupies a meadow area with several springs, some of which were used for drinking water or laundry. In the mid-1970s, a fountain was built over one of the springs, playground equipment was installed, and trees were planted. In 1993, the Town Council developed a project for the park, which spans over 7,000 square meters. The project included a central tree-lined walkway, children's play areas, and recreational spaces. The fountain was also remodeled by the Workshop School.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Parque del Mayuelo |url=http://www.rectivia.org/p1a1-40.html |access-date=8 June 2013 |author=Rectivía.org}}</ref>

The La Eragudina field, a former recreational area of the marquises of Astorga near the Jerga River, was transformed into a garden in 1996, featuring newly planted tree species such as [[Salix|willows]], ashes, maples, and poplars, along with a fountain and recreational areas.<ref>{{Harvnp|Alonso González|2000|p=177}}</ref> In the same year, the area at the foot of the city wall, known as El Melgar, was also converted into a park, with the surroundings of the Roman Gate, behind the [[apse]] of the cathedral, being landscaped.

Other recreational areas in the city include the Aljibe Park, near the cathedral and named after a medieval water cistern, and the surroundings of Fuente Encalada. This fountain, built in 1674 and remodeled in 1788 in a neoclassical style, now features a landscaped setting.<ref name="ReferenceA"/>

== Economy ==
The city's economic structure is characterized by weak industrial activity, with a strong reliance on the [[tertiary sector]], public administration, and, to a lesser extent, construction. Agriculture remains significant in the municipality's rural areas.

=== Business activity and employment ===
As of March 2013, the municipality had 596 establishments employing 2,280 workers.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.jcyl.es/sie/sas/broker?_PROGRAM=mddbpgm.v2.indexv2.scl&_SERVICE=sasweb&_DEBUG=0&menu=index |title=Número de trabajadores y número de establecimientos. Astorga |publisher=Sistema de Información Estadística. Junta de Castilla y León |access-date=26 June 2013}}</ref> In 2007, of the total employed population in the municipality, 1.3% worked in the primary sector, 14.6% in industry, 14.6% in construction, and the majority, 69.5%, were employed in the service sector, highlighting its importance to the municipal economy.<ref name="CE"/> Unemployment in the 21st century rose from 176 people in May 2005 to 778 in March 2020, with 341 men and 437 women.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.sepe.es/HomeSepe/que-es-el-sepe/estadisticas/datos-estadisticos/municipios.html |title=Paro registrado y contratos por municipios |access-date=9 May 2020 |author=Servicio Público de Empleo Estatal}}</ref>

{{Vertical bar chart|width=600|color1=Green|full_name=Vertical bar chart showing the evolution of the unemployment rate in Astorga between 2006 and 2019<ref name="macro">{{Cite web |url=https://datosmacro.expansion.com/paro/espana/municipios/castilla-leon/leon/astorga |title=Paro por municipios: Astorga - (León) |author=Expansión |access-date=9 May 2020}}</ref>|2006|14.91|2007|16.90|2008|17.81|2009|20.16|2010|20.67|2011|21.54|2012|25.48|2013|25.60|2014|23.90|2015|23.79|2016|21.00|2017|18.78|2018|17.73|2019|17.25|notes=Source: National Statistics Institute of Spain - Graphic elaboration by Wikipedia}}

=== Primary sector ===
[[File:Mercado semanal, Astorga.jpg|thumb|Partial view of the weekly market, where products from Astorga and surrounding regions are sold]]
In 2011, the municipality had an agricultural area of 1,045.8 [[hectare]]s, of which 1,021.5 hectares were arable land, divided between dry farming and irrigated crops located east of the municipality along the Tuerto River. Another 15 hectares were used for vegetable gardens, and 8.3 hectares for fruit trees.<ref name="CE"/> The wine sector was a cornerstone of the city's economy, particularly between the 13th century and 15th century, but by the 17th century, wine had to be imported from [[Rueda, Valladolid|Rueda]] or [[Toro, Zamora|Toro]] due to the gradual disappearance of vineyard land,<ref>{{Harvnp|Rodríguez Díez|1981|p=237}}</ref> leaving only one hectare.<ref name="CE"/> The remaining land is distributed among pastures (2,339.6 hectares), forest species (557.9 hectares), and other non-agricultural spaces (706.2 hectares). Overall, the [[primary sector]] employed 1.3% of workers and accounted for 0.5% of businesses,<ref name="CE"/> reflecting the tertiarization of the municipal economy. Agricultural activity remains present in the various hamlets, while it is nearly nonexistent in the municipal seat.

=== Secondary sector ===
[[File:Poligonoastorga.jpg|thumb|Partial view of the industrial estate next to the [[Autovía A-6|A-6]]]]
In 2007, industry was the second most significant economic activity, employing 29.2% of workers and accounting for 24.5% of businesses.<ref name="CE"/> Most industries are light and generate minimal pollution. The most prominent belong to the [[food industry]], with companies such as Cecinas Pablo, Dulces La Mallorquina, and Alonso, focusing on traditional products such as [[Puff pastry|puff pastries]], [[Mantecadas de Astorga|''mantecadas'']], and [[Cecina de León|''cecina'']]; Astorga is the seat of the [[denomination of origin]] for the latter two. Although now minor, the chocolate industry was significant from the mid-19th century to the first third of the 20th century; in 1916, there were 41 manufacturers, four of which remain active. Their legacy, including wrappers, posters, lithographs, and old machinery, is preserved in the Chocolate Museum.<ref>{{Harvnp|Alonso|2000|p=212}}</ref> The [[textile industry]] was also present, though only one factory survives, along with remnants such as a washhouse.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Alonso González |first=Pablo |year=2008 |title=Arqueología industrial y patrimonio: ¿presente + pasado = futuro? la gestión del patrimonio cultural e industrial de Astorga (II) |journal=Argutorio: Revista de la Asociación Cultural "Monte Irago" |issue=21 (year 9) |pages=48–53 |issn=1575-801X |url=http://dialnet.unirioja.es/servlet/articulo?codigo=2696416 |access-date=17 November 2013}}</ref>

Most industrial activity is concentrated in the industrial estate, promoted by the Town Council and the Chamber of Commerce and Industry. Its development has occurred in four phases: the first (1991) with 65,000 m², the second with nearly 50,000 m², the third (2007) with 79,000 m², and the fourth (2011), still under development.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.proastorga.es/poligono-industrial/ |title=El Polígono |author=Proyección Industrial de Astorga |access-date=28 June 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130612021035/http://www.proastorga.es/poligono-industrial/ |archive-date=12 June 2013}}</ref> In 2011, the city had 2 energy and water companies, 5 chemical companies, 24 metallurgical companies, and 66 manufacturing companies, totaling 97 industrial businesses. The construction sector recorded 100 businesses.<ref name="CAIXA">{{Cite web |url=http://www.anuarieco.lacaixa.comunicacions.com/java/X |title=Anuario Económico de España, 2011 La Caixa (Astorga) |publisher=La Caixa |date=2011 |access-date=27 June 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130714000428/http://www.anuarieco.lacaixa.comunicacions.com/java/X |archive-date=14 July 2013}}</ref>
[[File:Calle Pío Gullón.jpg|thumb|The pedestrianization of part of the historic center has fostered the development of small-scale commerce]]

=== Tertiary sector ===
In 2007, the service sector was prominent, employing 69.5% of workers and comprising 75% of businesses.<ref name="CE"/> The city serves as an economic hub for surrounding regions such as [[Maragatería]] and [[La Cepeda]], resulting in intense commercial activity; in 2012, there were 60 wholesale businesses, and in 2011, 316 retail businesses, including 114 in food retail (16 supermarkets), 188 in non-food retail, and 14 in mixed retail.<ref name="CAIXA"/> In 2012, there were 14 deposit institutions, including five banks and six savings banks.

Cultural tourism plays a significant role in the service sector due to the city's historical and monumental heritage, its festivals, and its position on the Camino de Santiago and the Vía de la Plata.<ref>{{Cite news |title=La Vía de la Plata y la Ruta Romana se consolidan como oferta turística |url=http://www.diariodeleon.es/noticias/provincia/la-via-de-plata-y-ruta-romana-se-consolidan-como-oferta-turistica_763218.html |access-date=29 June 2013 |date=24 January 2013 |newspaper=[[Diario de León]]}}</ref> Nearby, notable villages such as [[Castrillo de los Polvazares]] and [[Santiago Millas]], and iconic Camino de Santiago sites such as [[Foncebadón]], stand out. In March 2013, the municipality had 47 tourism establishments, including three travel agencies, nine rural tourism accommodations (115 beds), 16 hotels (549 beds), and 47 restaurants.<ref name="SIE">{{Cite web |title=Servicio de Información Estadística |url=http://www.jcyl.es/sie/v2/turismov2irAmodulo.html |access-date=29 June 2013 |author=Junta de Castilla y León}}</ref> In 2011, there were 115 cafés and bars.<ref name="CE"/> Since 2004, the city has had a parking area for motorhomes.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Área de Astorga |url=http://www.lapaca.org/areas/ficha_area.php?area_id=29 |access-date=13 July 2013 |author=Plataforma Autocaravanas Autónoma (PACA) |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131230234618/http://www.lapaca.org/areas/ficha_area.php?area_id=29 |archive-date=30 December 2013}}</ref>

== Symbols and titles ==
The municipal [[coat of arms]] is described as follows:<ref name="SIM">{{Cite web |title=Escudo y bandera |url=http://www.aytoastorga.es/municipio/escudo-bandera/ |access-date=8 November 2013 |author=Ayuntamiento de Astorga |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140304034233/http://www.aytoastorga.es/municipio/escudo-bandera/ |archive-date=4 March 2014}}</ref>
{{blockquote|Gules, an oak branch in its natural color. At the crest, a marquess's coronet.}}

The date of its initial use is unknown. A 1320 document features a seal of the Astorga Council depicting a castle with three towers and a tree.<ref>{{Harvnp|Alonso González|2000|p=222}}</ref> By 1635, the current shield was in use, as seen in Pedro Junco's work ''Fundación, nombres y armas de la ciudad de Astorga''. Junco interpreted that the city's ancient name—Roma—led to the term ''robur'', hence the depiction of an [[oak]], with ''[[Quercus robur]]'' being one of the most common species, symbolizing strength, firmness, and fortitude, akin to the attributes of solidity and longevity in [[classical mythology]]. The red field mirrors that of Rome, symbolizing the blood of enemies attempting to conquer the city.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Junco |first=Pedro |title=Fundación, nombres, y armas de la ciudad de Astorga |publisher=Martín de Labàyen |date=1635 |url=http://bvpb.mcu.es/es/consulta/registro.cmd?id=443357 |location=Pamplona |access-date=26 June 2013}}</ref> The flag, rectangular, is described as follows:<ref name="SIM"/>

{{blockquote|Red flag with the shield in the center.}}

Regarding its titles, the city is known as "Very Noble, Loyal, Meritorious, Magnificent, and Augustan." The first three were granted for its role during the War of Independence; centuries earlier, it had been called "Augustan" by Emperor Caesar Augustus and "Magnificent" by Pliny the Elder.<ref>{{Harvnp|Rodríguez Díez|1981|p=463}}</ref>

== Administration and politics ==
[[File:Ayuntamiento de Astorga 2025.jpg|thumb|The town hall in Plaza Mayor]]

=== Public administration ===
;Regional administration

The [[Regional Government of Castile and León]] holds responsibilities for education, managed by the Department of Education, which oversees teachers and educational centers, and healthcare, through Sacyl, which manages the municipality's healthcare services.<ref name="SAL">{{Cite web |url=http://www.saludcastillayleon.es/ciudadanos/es/buscador-recursos |title=Buscador de recursos sanitarios |access-date=15 August 2014 |author=Sacyl |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140719175230/http://www.saludcastillayleon.es/ciudadanos/es/buscador-recursos |archive-date=19 July 2014}}</ref>

;Local administration

Local administration is handled by a democratically managed town council, whose members are elected every four years by universal suffrage. The electoral roll includes all residents registered in Astorga over 18 years old, who are nationals of Spain or other [[member states of the European Union]]. According to the General Electoral Law, which determines the number of eligible councilors based on the municipality's population,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.boe.es/buscar/doc.php?id=BOE-A-1985-11672 |title=Ley Orgánica 5/1985, de 19 de junio, del Régimen Electoral General. Art. 169. |date=1985 |publisher=Jefatura del Estado. BOE no. 147/1985 (España) |access-date=9 June 2013}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.boe.es/boe/dias/2011/01/29/pdfs/BOE-A-2011-1639.pdf |title=Modificación de la Ley Orgánica 5/1985, de 19 de junio, del Régimen Electoral General. |date=2011 |publisher=Jefatura del Estado. BOE no. 25/2011 (España) |access-date=9 June 2013}}</ref> the municipal corporation consists of 17 councilors.

;Judicial administration

Astorga is the head of the judicial district of the same name, the fifth in the province, with two courts of first instance.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Partido judicial de Astorga |url=http://www.cgpe.es/juzgados.aspx?idprovincia=24&numpartido=5 |access-date=9 June 2013 |author=Consejo general de procuradores de España |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130715041912/http://www.cgpe.es/juzgados.aspx?idprovincia=24&numpartido=5 |archive-date=15 July 2013 |url-status=dead}}</ref> The city also has a notary office.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Guía de instituciones oficiales de Astorga |url=http://www.astorga.com/instituciones%20de%20astorga.htm |access-date=9 June 2013 |author=Astorga.com}}</ref>

=== Municipal government ===
In the first democratic elections of 1979, the [[Union of the Democratic Centre (Spain)|Union of the Democratic Centre]] (UCD) came to power under Luis González Pérez, followed in the next term by Recaredo Bautista of the Agrupación Electoral Popular Independiente (AEPI).<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://astorgaredaccion.com/not/582/que_treinta_anos_no_es_nada_hellip_/ |last=Aparicio |first=Abel |title=Que treinta años no es nada |newspaper=AstorgaRedacción |date=18 March 2013 |access-date=26 February 2014}}</ref> In the 1987 elections, Juan José Alonso Perandones ([[PSOE]]) fell just short of an absolute majority, but the four opposition groups united to give the mayoralty to the minority candidacy of Adolfo Alonso Ares.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.la-cronica.net/2009/03/29/comarcas/emel-dia-que-estime-que-acaba-esta-etapa-los-ciudadanos-seran-los-primeros-en-saberloem-30590.htm |last=Oria |first=Laura A. |title=El día que estime que acaba esta etapa, los ciudadanos serán los primeros en saberlo. Entrevista |newspaper=La Crónica de León |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111127114143/http://www.la-cronica.net/2009/03/29/comarcas/emel-dia-que-estime-que-acaba-esta-etapa-los-ciudadanos-seran-los-primeros-en-saberloem-30590.htm |archive-date=27 November 2011 |access-date=9 June 2013}}</ref> However, two years later, with the support of the [[Democratic and Social Centre (Spain)|Democratic and Social Centre]] (CDS) representative Rosa Fernández González, a motion of censure enabled Perandones to become mayor on March 29, 1989, a position he held until 2011, when he announced his retirement from politics.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://leonoticias.com/frontend/leonoticias/El-Corregidor-Que-Nunca-Llego-A-Caesar-vn69076-vst231 |title=El corregidor que nunca llegó a Caesar |newspaper=Leonoticias.com |access-date=14 December 2013 |last=Fuertes |first=Polo |date=29 March 2011}}</ref>

In the 2011 elections, with no coalition agreements reached among the political groups, the mayoralty went to the most-voted list, led by Victorina Alonso Fernández, Perandones' successor in the PSOE.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.elmundo.es/elmundo/2011/06/11/leon/1307825576.html |title=La socialista Victorina Alonso gobernará en minoría en Astorga |newspaper=[[El Mundo (Spain)|El Mundo]] |last=Sutil |first=Álvaro F. |date=11 June 2011 |access-date=9 June 2013}}</ref> In 2015, Arsenio García of the PP was elected mayor in a minority government.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.lanuevacronica.com/el-popular-arsenio-garcia-ya-es-alcalde-de-astorga-en-minoria |title=El popular Arsenio García ya es alcalde de Astorga en minoría |newspaper=La Nueva Crónica |last=Martín |first=S. |date=13 June 2015 |access-date=20 July 2015}}</ref> On July 5, 2019, following a judicial dispute in which the PP contested the validity of a vote initially deemed null, which the High Court of Justice of Castile and León confirmed as invalid,<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.diariodeleon.es/noticias/castillayleon/tsjcyl-considera-papeleta-rasgada-astorga-sufrio-alteracion-voluntaria-intencionada_1345229.html |title=El TSJCyL considera que la papeleta rasgada en Astorga sufrió una "alteración voluntaria e intencionada" |access-date=9 July 2019 |newspaper=Diario de León |date=26 June 2019}}</ref> the PSOE and IU municipal groups formed a coalition government, returning the mayoral staff to Perandones after an eight-year absence from frontline politics.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.diariodeleon.es/noticias/provincia/perandones-volvera-ser-alcalde-astorga-gracias-votos-iu_1346819.html |title=Perandones volverá a ser alcalde de Astorga gracias a los votos de IU |access-date=9 July 2019 |newspaper=Diario de León |date=4 July 2019}}</ref>

== Services ==
=== Communications ===
==== Vehicle fleet ====
In 2011, the municipality had a vehicle fleet of 465.3 cars per 1,000 inhabitants.<ref name="CE" /> According to data from the "Economic Yearbook of Spain 2012" published by [[La Caixa]],<ref name="caixa">{{Cite web |url=http://www.anuarieco.lacaixa.comunicacions.com/java/X?cgi=caixa.le_DEM.pattern&START=YES |title=Anuario económico de España. 2012. Astorga |publisher=La Caixa |access-date=11 June 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130606180024/http://www.anuarieco.lacaixa.comunicacions.com/java/X?cgi=caixa.le_DEM.pattern&START=YES |archive-date=6 June 2013}}</ref> there were 5,491 cars in total. The same data indicates a fleet of 1,250 trucks and vans, with other vehicles totaling 1,150, bringing the total number of motor vehicles to 7,926. The city has a Vehicle Inspection Station located in the industrial estate.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.itevelesa.com/delegaciones-m |title=Delegaciones en la provincia de León |publisher=Grupo Itevelesa |access-date=11 June 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121213184025/http://www.itevelesa.com/delegaciones-m |archive-date=13 December 2012}}</ref>

==== Public transportation ====
;Bus

For passenger transport, the company [[Alsa (bus company)|ALSA]] provides road services between the city and multiple national destinations, such as [[León, Spain|León]], [[Ponferrada]], [[La Coruña]], [[Valladolid]], [[Madrid]], [[Gijón]], or [[Barcelona]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Viajar a Astorga |url=http://www.alsa.es/destinos/astorga.htm |access-date=11 June 2013 |author=ALSA}}</ref> Locally, several companies offer services between Astorga and surrounding regional localities.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Transportes públicos de viajeros |url=http://www.astorga.com/transportes%20publicos%20en%20astorga.htm |access-date=11 June 2013 |author=Astorga.com}}</ref>
;Railway
Since the railway arrived in 1866, the city has had a railway station, located in the Puerta del Rey neighborhood, northeast of the city. Managed by [[Adif]], the station is part of the Palencia-La Coruña line. Astorga's railway connections, operated by [[Renfe Operadora|Renfe]], include:<ref>{{Cite web |title=Viajeros - Horarios |url=http://www.renfe.com/viajeros/ |access-date=11 June 2013 |author=Renfe}}</ref>
{{columns-list|colwidth=22em|
* Astorga-Ponferrada (Alvia)
* Astorga-La Coruña (Alvia, Arco, Trenhotel)
* Astorga-Vigo (Alvia, Arco, Trenhotel)
* Astorga-Ferrol (Trenhotel)
* Astorga-Madrid (Alvia, Trenhotel)
* Astorga-Barcelona (Alvia, Trenhotel)
* Astorga-Bilbao (Arco)
* Astorga-Irún (Arco)
* Astorga-León (Intercity, Regional Express)
}}
Until 1983, Astorga was also the starting point of the Vía de la Plata railway, inaugurated on July 21, 1896, connecting Astorga to Plasencia. For several years, various organizations and companies have demanded its reopening to effectively connect the western peninsula and restore freight transport by rail.<ref>{{Cite news |title=La Fundación Afonso Enriques pide la apertura del tren Vía de la Plata |url=http://www.diariodeleon.es/noticias/noticia.asp?pkid=409552 |date=2 October 2008 |access-date=12 June 2013 |newspaper=[[Diario de León]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |title=Las Cámaras de Comercio de la Vía de la Plata exigen el ferrocarril |url=http://www.diariodeleon.es/noticias/noticia.asp?pkid=408439 |last=Domingo |first=A. |date=26 September 2008 |access-date=12 June 2013 |newspaper=[[Diario de León]]}}</ref><ref name="TREN">{{Cite news |title=El colectivo Tren Vía de la Plata considera viable la reapertura de la línea para viajeros |url=http://www.nortecastilla.es/20081221/zamora/colectivo-tren-plata-considera-20081221.html |date=21 December 2008 |author=Urones, Mª Ángeles |access-date=12 June 2013 |newspaper=[[El Norte de Castilla]]}}</ref>
;Air transport
{{See also|León Airport}}

The León Airport, operational since 1999, is the only airport in the province and the closest to the municipality, located between [[Valverde de la Virgen]] and [[San Andrés del Rabanedo]], 44 kilometers from Astorga.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.aena-aeropuertos.es/csee/Satellite/Aeropuerto-Leon/es/ |title=Aeropuerto de León |publisher=Aena |access-date=12 June 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121023124134/http://www.aena-aeropuertos.es/csee/Satellite/Aeropuerto-Leon/es |archive-date=23 October 2012 |url-status=dead}}</ref> Other nearby options for air transport are the Valladolid and Asturias airports, located 157 and 193 kilometers away, respectively.

=== Education ===
The city's educational infrastructure includes three early childhood and primary education centers, one secondary education institute, and one special education center in the public sector, as well as three private centers offering education from early childhood to secondary school.<ref name="COL">{{Cite web |url=http://www.educa.jcyl.es/educacyl/cm/educacyl/images?locale=es_ES&textOnly=false&idMmedia=210447 |format=PDF |title=Guía del Estudiante |access-date=9 June 2013 |author=[[Junta de Castilla y León]]}}</ref>

The secondary institute offers Compulsory Secondary Education, Baccalaureate, and vocational training programs such as Electricity and Electronics and Cooking and Catering at the basic level, Bakery, Pastry and Confectionery, Administrative Management, Telecommunications Installations, Electrical and Automatic Installations at the intermediate level, and Administration and Finance and Industrial Automation and Robotics at the advanced level.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://iesastorga.centros.educa.jcyl.es/sitio/index.cgi?wid_seccion=13 |title=IES Astorga |access-date=7 May 2020 |author=[[Junta de Castilla y León]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200528233804/http://iesastorga.centros.educa.jcyl.es/sitio/index.cgi?wid_seccion=13 |archive-date=28 May 2020 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

For specialized education, Astorga has an Official Language School offering French, English, and German,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://eoiastorga.centros.educa.jcyl.es/sitio/ |title=E.O.I. Astorga |access-date=9 June 2013 |author=[[Junta de Castilla y León]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130614093008/http://eoiastorga.centros.educa.jcyl.es/sitio/ |archive-date=14 June 2013 |url-status=dead}}</ref> a professional music conservatory, a municipal music school, and an adult education center.
