===Transportation===
The park and landfill are served by the {{NYC bus link|Q22}} and {{NYC bus link|Q52 SBS}} bus routes, which operate on [[Beach Channel Drive]] at the south end of the Edgmere Houses. The Q22 operates across the Rockaway Peninsula between Far Rockaway to the east and [[Roxbury, Queens|Roxbury]] to the west. The Q52, which terminates at Beach 54th Street, travels north via [[Woodhaven and Cross Bay Boulevards]] through [[Broad Channel, Queens|Broad Channel]] to "mainland" Queens. The closest [[New York City Subway]] station is the [[Beach 60th Street (IND Rockaway Line)|Beach 60th Street]] station on the [[IND Rockaway Line]] ({{NYCS trains|Far Rockaway}}), located to the southwest of the park at Beach 59th Street near [[Rockaway Beach Boulevard]].<ref name="MTA-ArverneEdgemereMap-2018"/><ref name="RivelRosenheim2016"/>

==Etymology==
The name Edgemere is derived from an [[Old English|Anglo-Saxon]] term, meaning "edge of the sea".<ref name="NYDaily-EdgemereAir-Jul2003">{{cite news |last1=Woodberry |first1=Warren Jr. |title=OCEAN - & REBIRTH - IN THE EDGEMERE AIR New housing brings a new spirit to area |url=http://www.nydailynews.com/archives/boroughs/ocean-rebirth-edgemere-air-new-housing-brings-new-spirit-area-article-1.514745 |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=[[New York Daily News]] |date=July 13, 2003}}</ref><ref name="JacksonKeller2010">{{cite book |author1=Kenneth T. Jackson |author2=Lisa Keller |author3=Nancy Flood |title=The Encyclopedia of New York City: Second Edition |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lI5ERUmHf3YC&pg=PT1913 |date=December 1, 2010 |publisher=Yale University Press |isbn=978-0-300-18257-6 |page=1913}}</ref> The term Rockaway is derived from a word in the [[Algonquin language|Algonquin]] Native American languages. Several meanings have been given, including "sandy place", "the place of laughing waters", "the place of our own people", or "neck of the land".<ref name="NYC-BrownfieldEdgemere-Ap2016" />{{rp|6}}<ref name="Bellot1918" />{{rp|9}}<ref name="NPS-JamaicaBayHistory-1981" />{{rp|11}} This was the name of the [[Lenape]] tribe, who were a subset of the Canarsee ([[Canarsie, Brooklyn|Canarsie]]) tribe, that occupied much of the area around Jamaica Bay.<ref name="NYCPk-RkwyCommunityPk" /><ref name="NYC-BrownfieldEdgemere-Ap2016"/>{{rp|6}}<ref name="RockawayReview-1948">{{cite journal |title=History of the Rockaways |journal=The Rockaway Review |date=December 1948 |url=http://www.farrockaway.com/farrockawayhistory.pdf |access-date=July 29, 2018}}</ref><ref name="CurbedNY-FarRkwy-Sep2016">{{cite news |last1=Williams |first1=Keith |title=Exploring Far Rockaway, a seaside neighborhood with shifting boundaries: Tracing the history of one of New York City's waterfront communities |url=https://ny.curbed.com/2016/9/2/12756786/queens-far-rockaway-history |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160903181423/http://ny.curbed.com/2016/9/2/12756786/queens-far-rockaway-history |url-status=dead |archive-date=September 3, 2016 |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=[[Curbed New York]] |date=September 2, 2016}}</ref><ref name="Bellot1918"/>{{rp|9}}<ref name="NPS-JamaicaBayHistory-1981">{{cite web |last1=Black |first1=Frederick R. |title=Historic Resources Study: Jamaica Bay, A History; Gateway National Recreation Area |url=http://npshistory.com/publications/gate/jamaica-bay-hrs.pdf |publisher=[[National Park Service]] |access-date=September 13, 2018 |location=[[Washington, D.C.]] |date=1981}}</ref>{{rp|11}}

==History==
===Early history===
[[File:Queens, Vol. 1, Double Page Plate No. 35; Part of Ward 5; Rockaway; (Map bounded by Jamaica Bay, Charmttoir Island, Mc. Caffertys Island, Nortons Creek, Hudson Ave., Columbus Ave., Rochester NYPL1693878.tiff|thumb|right|A 1907 map of Edgemere. At the north end of the site is Little Bay, with various islands within it; this is now the site of the Edgemere Landfill.]]
Prior to the creation of the landfill, the site of Edgemere Park consisted of numerous separate islands within a much larger Little Bay between Dubos Point to the west and Bayswater Point to the east. It was originally known as "Little Bay Marsh". Norton Basin (also called Norton's Creek) originally was connected to the [[Atlantic Ocean]] by a creek called the Wave Crest Inlet, which separated the western peninsula from the mainland.<ref name="NortonBasin-LittleBay-Nov2001">{{cite web |last1=Rhoads |first1=John M. |last2=Yozzo |first2=David J. |last3=Cianciola |first3=Marco M. |last4=Will |first4=Robert J. |title=Norton Basin/Little Bay Restoration Project: Historical and Environmental Background Report: November 2001 |url=http://www1.dec.state.ny.us/docs/regions_pdf/vittor01.pdf |publisher=Barry A. Vittor & Associates, Inc., [[United States Army Corps of Engineers]] |access-date=July 29, 2018 |date=November 2001 |archive-date=October 14, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181014091402/http://www1.dec.state.ny.us/docs/regions_pdf/vittor01.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>{{rp|11–14, 17, 37}}<ref name="Bellot1918"/>{{rp|83, 95−96}} The area around Jamaica Bay including the Rockaways was characterized by marshland.<ref name="NYCPk-RkwyCommunityPk" /><ref name="Bellot1918"/>{{rp|83}} As late as 1872, the neighborhoods of Edgemere and Arverne were populated by cedar trees.<ref name="NortonBasin-LittleBay-Nov2001"/>{{rp|32}}

The area around Jamaica Bay including the Rockaway Peninsula was initially inhabited by the Canarsie and Rockaway Native American groups, who were often referred to erroneously as the [[Indigenous peoples of Long Island|"Metoac" or "Mantinecocks"]].<ref name="NPS-JamaicaBayHistory-1981" />{{rp|7−12}}<ref name="RockawayReview-1948" /><ref name="Bellot1918" />{{rp|9−10}} The Rockaway primarily controlled the eastern and southern shores of Jamaica Bay in present-day Queens and Nassau County, while the Canarsie controlled the northern and western shores in modern-day Brooklyn.<ref name="NYCPk-RkwyCommunityPk" /><ref name="JacksonKeller2010"/><ref name="NPS-JamaicaBayHistory-1981"/>{{rp|7−12}}<ref name="RockawayReview-1948"/><ref name="Bellot1918"/>{{rp|9−10}} In 1685, the Rockaway Peninsula was sold to English [[John Palmer (colonial administrator)|Captain John Palmer]] by two tribal chiefs, [[Tackapausha]] and Paman. Palmer was said to have purchased the land for "31 [[Pound sterling|pounds]], 2 [[Shilling (British coin)|shillings]]".<ref name="RockawayReview-1948" /><ref name="Bellot1918" />{{rp|9−10}} The land was considered to be "barren", consisting of meadow and marsh used for grazing. At the time, the peninsula stretched from the modern [[Rockaway Turnpike]] west to the modern [[Beach 25th Street (IND Rockaway Line)|Wavecrest]] neighborhood, making up the greater [[Far Rockaway, Queens|Far Rockaway]] area of Queens and what is now [[Five Towns]], Nassau County (then called "Rockaway Neck").<ref name="NYCPk-RkwyCommunityPk" /><ref name="NYC-BrownfieldEdgemere-Ap2016"/>{{rp|6}}<ref name="RockawayReview-1948"/><ref name="Bellot1918"/>{{rp|9−10}}<ref name="NYLPC-CornellGraveyard-1970">{{cite web |title=Richard Cornell Graveyard |url=http://www.interment.net/data/us/ny/queens/richard-cornell-graveyard-landmark.pdf |publisher=[[New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission]] |access-date=July 29, 2018 |date=August 18, 1970}}</ref><ref name="CornellGenealogy">{{cite book |last1=Cornell |first1=John |title=Genealogy of the Cornell Family: Being an Account of the Descendants of Thomas Cornell of Portsmouth, R. I. |date=1902 |publisher=Press of T. A. Wright |location=[[New York City|New York]] |url=https://archive.org/details/genealogyofcorne00corn |access-date=July 29, 2018}}</ref>{{rp|146−149}} The peninsula would later be extended west to [[Breezy Point, Queens|Rockaway Point]] by the natural [[Accretion (coastal management)|accretion]] of sand from tidal action.<ref name="RockawayReview-1948"/><ref name="Bellot1918"/>{{rp|10}}<ref name="NPS-JamaicaBayHistory-1981"/>{{rp|35}}<ref name="NPS-Riis-Tilden-Jun1989">{{cite web |title=Development Concept Plan, Environmental Assessment: Jacob Riis Park, Gateway National Recreation Area, New York-New Jersey |url=https://archive.org/details/developjacobriis00nati |website=[[Internet Archive]] |publisher=[[United States Department of the Interior]], [[National Park Service]] |access-date=September 3, 2017 |date=June 1989}}</ref>{{rp|5 (PDF p.11)}}

In 1687 Palmer sold the land to English settler [[Richard Cornell]], whose family would later found [[Cornell University]]. In return, Palmer received land in "Madnan's Neck", now [[Little Neck, Queens]] and [[Great Neck, New York|Great Neck, Nassau County]]. Cornell had previously purchased what would become [[Flushing, Queens]]. Cornell constructed a house overlooking the [[Atlantic Ocean]] known as the "Cornell house" or "Cornell homestead", said to be the first permanent structure in the area.<ref name="NYCPk-RkwyCommunityPk" /><ref name="NYC-BrownfieldEdgemere-Ap2016"/>{{rp|6}}<ref name="RockawayReview-1948"/><ref name="Bellot1918"/>{{rp|9−12}}<ref name="NYLPC-CornellGraveyard-1970"/><ref name="CornellGenealogy"/>{{rp|146−147}} The house was located in the vicinity of Central Avenue (Beach 20th Street), Beach 19th Street, and Empire Avenue in modern Far Rockaway. This is the location of the contemporary [[Hebrew Academy of the Five Towns and Rockaway|Hebrew Institute of Long Island]] at Beach 17th Street and Seagirt Boulevard.<ref name="RockawayReview-1948"/><ref name="NYLPC-CornellGraveyard-1970"/><ref name="NYCPk-CornellBurialGround">{{cite web |title=Cornell Burial Ground |url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/cornell-burial-ground/history |publisher=[[New York City Department of Parks and Recreation]] |access-date=July 29, 2018}}</ref> The family also created a nearby [[Cornell Family Cemetery|burial ground]] on Caffrey Avenue and New Haven Avenue.<ref name="NYLPC-CornellGraveyard-1970"/><ref name="NYCPk-CornellBurialGround"/>

After the partition of the Cornell property in 1809, in 1830 John Leake Norton purchased land  from the Cornell family, consisting of Edgemere and Far Rockaway. Norton formed the Rockaway Association with several prominent New Yorkers, and the association constructed a hotel on the former site of the Cornell house called the [[Marine Pavilion (Queens)|Marine Pavilion]].<ref name="NYC-BrownfieldEdgemere-Ap2016"/>{{rp|6}}<ref name="RockawayReview-1948"/><ref name="CurbedNY-FarRkwy-Sep2016"/><ref name="Bellot1918">{{cite book |author=Alfred Henry Bellot |title=History of the Rockaways from the year 1685 to 1917: being a complete record and review of events of historical importance during that period in the Rockaway Peninsula, comprising the villages of Hewlett, Woodmere, Cedarhurst, Lawrence, Inwood, Far Rockaway, Arverne, Rockaway Beach, Belle Harbor, Neponsit and Rockaway Point |url=https://archive.org/details/cu31924028832941 |page=[https://archive.org/details/cu31924028832941/page/n86 83] |access-date=July 29, 2018 |year=1918 |publisher=Bellot's histories, inc. }}</ref>{{rp|20−21, 83−85}} The pavilion was opened on June 1, 1833.<ref>{{cite news |title=Island Towns; Where People in the Early Fifties Sought Comfort; A Glimpse at Rockaway, Fire Island, Islip, and Other Well Known Places-Famous Sportsmen-Excellent Fishing, Boating and Swimming |url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/50371031/ |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=[[Brooklyn Daily Eagle]] |via=[[Newspapers.com]] |date=August 9, 1890 |page=3}}</ref> Although it burned down on June 25, 1864,<ref name="RockawayReview-1948"/><ref name="Bellot1918"/>{{rp|84}}<ref name="CurbedNY-FarRkwy-Sep2016"/><ref>{{cite news |title=The Fire at Rockaway.; THE MARINE PAVILION AND OTHER BUILDINGS BURNED. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1864/06/29/archives/the-fire-at-rockaway-the-marine-pavilion-and-other-buildings-burned.html |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=June 29, 1864}}</ref> the hotel catalyzed the development of the Rockaways into a resort town.<ref name="NYCPk-RkwyCommunityPk" /><ref name="NYC-BrownfieldEdgemere-Ap2016"/>{{rp|6}}<ref name="Bellot1918"/>{{rp|20−21, 83−85}} The [[Far Rockaway Branch]] Railroad of the [[South Side Railroad of Long Island]] was opened in 1869 between [[Valley Stream station|Valley Stream]] and [[Far Rockaway station (LIRR)|Far Rockaway]], and was extended to the [[Beach 105th Street (IND Rockaway Line)|Seaside House]] in [[Rockaway Park, Queens|Rockaway Park]] in 1872.<ref name="NYC-BrownfieldEdgemere-Ap2016"/>{{rp|6}}<ref name="NortonBasin-LittleBay-Nov2001"/>{{rp|6}}<ref name="Bellot1918"/>{{rp|34−38}}<ref name="RockawayReview-1948"/><ref name="NPS-JamaicaBayHistory-1981"/>{{rp|74}} The [[New York, Woodhaven & Rockaway Railroad]] opened their line from Brooklyn and "mainland" Queens to [[Rockaway Park–Beach 116th Street (IND Rockaway Line)|Rockaway Park]] in 1880.<ref name="Bellot1918"/>{{rp|34−38}}<ref name="NPS-JamaicaBayHistory-1981"/>{{rp|48, 74−76}}<ref>{{cite news |work=[[Brooklyn Daily Eagle]] |location=[[Brooklyn|Brooklyn, NY]] |url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/50504650/ |title=To Rockaway |date=August 23, 1880 |page=4 |via=[[Brooklyn Public Library]]; [[newspapers.com]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |work=[[Brooklyn Daily Eagle]] |location=[[Brooklyn|Brooklyn, NY]] |url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/50504677/ |title=Developing |date=August 26, 1880 |page=1 |via=[[Brooklyn Public Library]]; [[newspapers.com]]}}</ref><ref name=opened>{{cite news |work=[[Brooklyn Daily Eagle]] |location=[[Brooklyn|Brooklyn, NY]] |title=Opened |date=August 26, 1880 |page=4 }}</ref><ref name="route">{{cite news |title=New Route To Rockaway. Steel Rails And Superior Rolling Stock. Extra Trains To Be Run To-day |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1880/08/29/archives/new-route-to-rockaway-steel-rails-and-superior-rolling-stock-extra.html |quote=The New-York, Woodhaven and Rockaway Railroad, which began operations on Thursday last, has already grown into popular savor by reason of the comparative shortness of the route and the superior accommodation |newspaper=[[New York Times]] |date=August 29, 1880 |access-date=November 5, 2012}}</ref> The [[Ocean Electric Railway]] opened a streetcar line via the Far Rockaway Branch tracks in 1897.<ref name="Bellot1918"/>{{rp|34−38}}

Up until the 1880s, the Edgemere and Arverne areas were largely undeveloped and were among the last to be developed on the peninsula.<ref name="NortonBasin-LittleBay-Nov2001"/>{{rp|5−6}}<ref name="NYC-BrownfieldEdgemere-Ap2016"/>{{rp|6}}<ref name="Bellot1918"/>{{rp|98}} Edgemere, originally called "New Venice", was developed by [[Frederick J. Lancaster]] beginning in 1892, with the Hotel Edgemere opening in 1894.<ref name="NYCPk-RkwyCommunityPk" /><ref name="Bellot1918" />{{rp|21, 95−99}}  The Arverne neighborhood was developed by [[Remington Vernam (land developer)|Remington Vernam]]. The Arverne Hotel was erected in 1888. A rail station in the neighborhood at [[Beach 67th Street (IND Rockaway Line)|Gaston Avenue]] was opened in 1888, and a second at [[Beach 60th Street (IND Rockaway Line)|Straiton Avenue]] in 1892.<ref name="NYCPk-RkwyCommunityPk" /><ref name="Bellot1918"/>{{rp|21, 95−99}} The Wave Crest Inlet, also called Wave Crest Lake, was filled in during 1911 in order to further develop the Edgemere neighborhood.<ref name="Bellot1918"/>{{rp|83, 95−96}}

===Creation of the landfill===
In 1916, the New York City Waterfront Company acquired {{convert|359|acre|ha}} of land on the north shore of the Rockaway Peninsula in Arverne and Edgemere, including the area around Little Bay. The land was located north of the former Amstel Canal, now Amstel Boulevard and [[Beach Channel Drive]]. The property was previously owned by [[Remington Vernam (land developer)|Remington Vernam]]. The land, which consisted of salt marshes and beach, was to be filled in order to construct [[bungalow]]s; part of the site was already filled by dirt dredged from Jamaica Bay.<ref>{{cite news |title=Realty on Long Island |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Daily%2520Long%2520Island%2520Farmer%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Daily%2520Long%2520Island%2520Farmer%25201916%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Daily%2520Long%2520Island%2520Farmer%25201916%2520-%25201879.pdf |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=The Daily Long Island Farmer |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=October 9, 1916 |page=1}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Legal Notices: Supreme Court, Queens County |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252015%2FBrooklyn%2520NY%2520Daily%2520Star%2FBrooklyn%2520NY%2520Daily%2520Star%25201916%2FBrooklyn%2520NY%2520Daily%2520Star%25201916%2520-%25201352.pdf |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=Brooklyn Daily Star |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=January 19, 1916 |page=7}}</ref> In 1920, the [[New York City Board of Estimate]] planned to create Amstel Boulevard on the former canal right-of-way between Beach 35th Street and Beach 71st Street, where it would connect with Hammels Avenue and eventually feed in Beach Channel Drive. The route would cut across the New York City Waterfront property. All three roads now make up modern Beach Channel Drive.<ref>{{cite news |title=Gives Details of New Drive; Beach Channel Drive Involves Many Legal Questions Says Louis J. Somerville |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201920%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201920%2520-%25200331.pdf |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=July 29, 1920 |page=1}}</ref>

Garbage landfilling at Edgemere by the [[New York City Department of Sanitation]] began on July 15, 1938. The landfill replaced an incinerator in nearby Arverne.<ref name="Rockawave-Edgemere-Test-Mar1939">{{cite news |title=Let Edgemere be the Test |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201939-1940%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201939-1940%2520-%25200072.pdf |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=March 2, 1939 |page=4}}</ref><ref name="BklynEagle-DumpWar-Jul1938"/> By this time, garbage incineration was considered "obsolete".<ref name="Rockawave-HowardBchDump-Jan1949"/> The property continued to be owned by the New York City Waterfront Company.<ref name="BkylnEagle-Carey-Rice-May1939"/> [[Borrow pit]]s with depths of {{convert|64|ft|m}} and {{convert|51|ft|m}} were dug into the Norton Basin and Little Bay respectively, with the dirt extracted used to create a base for the landfill. Around {{convert|2|e6yd3|e6m3|abbr=off}} of dirt were dredged from underwater for the landfill. The alterations to the basins and landfilling activity changed their biodiversity compared to other water bodies in the area.<ref name="NortonBasin-LittleBay-Nov2001"/>{{rp|1, 12, 17, 32−33, 36−37}} The Edgemere Landfill was one of several landfills created under then-Sanitation Commissioner William F. Carey. In addition to replacing incinerators, the landfill replaced the practice of dumping city garbage in the ocean.<ref name="LIStar-SuperDump-Jan1949"/> This practice was banned by a United States Supreme Court ruling in 1933.<ref name="LIStar-SuperDump-Jan1949"/><ref name="Group1971"/><ref>{{cite news |last1=Bird |first1=David |title=Problem of Ridding City of Garbage Eludes a Solution |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1970/03/24/archives/problem-of-ridding-city-of-garbage-eludes-a-solution-garbage.html |access-date=August 9, 2018 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=March 24, 1970 |page=49}}</ref>

Following complaints from the local community, on July 14, 1938 Andrew J. Kenny threatened to seek an injunction to stop the dumping at Edgemere. Kenny was the president of the Rockaway Chamber of Commerce and the Queens sewer superintendent. That same day, Sanitation Commissioner Carey was confronted by local residents while inspecting the landfill site. One of the complaints was that paint on the side of houses had either peeled or became discolored due to the fumes emitted from the landfill. The fumes were thought to either come from the mud from the bay used to cover the garbage, or the disinfectants used on the waste.<ref name="BklynEagle-DumpWar-Jul1938">{{cite news |title=New Legal War Looms on Dump In Jamaica Bay: Carey Told by Rockaway Residents That Odors Are Hurting Resort |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%25205%2FBrooklyn%2520NY%2520Daily%2520Eagle%2FBrooklyn%2520NY%2520Daily%2520Eagle%25201938%2520Grayscale%2FBrooklyn%2520NY%2520Daily%2520Eagle%25201938%2520Grayscale%2520-%25205767.pdf |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=[[Brooklyn Daily Eagle]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=July 14, 1938 |page=4}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Carey Refuses Plea to End Bay Dumping |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252014%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%25201938%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%25201938%2520-%25200253.pdf |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=Long Island Daily Press |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=July 14, 1938 |page=7}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Action Taken to Restrain Dumping Here; Will Institute Proceedings Against City; East End Residents Jubilant |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201937-1938%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201937-1938%2520-%25200667.pdf |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=July 14, 1938 |page=1}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Action Taken to Restrain Dumping Here; Will Institute Proceedings Against City; East End Residents Jubilant |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201937-1938%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201937-1938%2520-%25200673.pdf |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=July 14, 1938 |page=7}}</ref><ref name="Rockawave-HowardBchDump-Jan1949"/> The next day on July 15, dumping was halted at the landfill. According to Commissioner Carey, the odors at the site were caused by the use of mud to cover the garbage, and clean sand would be used in the future.<ref>{{cite news |title=City Halts Dumping on Shores of Jamaica Bay at Edgemcro |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252014%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%25201938%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%25201938%2520-%25200285.pdf |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=Long Island Daily Press |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=July 15, 1938}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Jamaica Bay Refuse Dumping Is Halted |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252018%2FNew%2520York%2520NY%2520Sun%2FNew%2520York%2520NY%2520Sun%25201938%2FNew%2520York%2520NY%2520Sun%25201938%2520-%25206419.pdf |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=[[The Sun (New York City)]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=July 15, 1938 |page=8}}</ref> Operations resumed on October 10, 1938.<ref>{{cite news |title=It Must Not Happen Here |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201939-1940%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201939-1940%2520-%25200013.pdf |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=January 12, 1939 |page=4}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Dumping of Garbage is Renewed Here; Refuse In Edgemere Marshland Caused Civic Fight in July. |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201937-1938%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201937-1938%2520-%25200771.pdf |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=October 13, 1938 |page=1}}</ref> Meanwhile, residents continued to oppose dumping at Edgemere, citing fires and rat infestations.<ref name="Rockawave-Edgemere-Test-Mar1939"/><ref name="Rockawave-Carey-Edgemere-Feb1939"/> During a tour of the Edgemere Dump on February 11, 1939, Commissioner Carey claimed that it was "four and a half times more expensive" to dispose of waste through incinerators than to bury it in landfills. He also spoke of the benefits of landfilling, including reclaiming marshland and eliminating mosquitoes.<ref name="Rockawave-Carey-Edgemere-Feb1939">{{cite news |title=Grand Jury To Get Garbage Dump Case; Conference Planned |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201939-1940%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201939-1940%2520-%25200053.pdf |access-date=August 30, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=February 16, 1939 |page=1}}</ref>

On March 28, 1939, Sanitation Commissioner William F. Carey and Health Commissioner Dr. John L. Rice were indicted on charges of violating the New York City Penal and Sanitary Codes, specifically of "unlawfully dumping raw garbage and maintaining a public nuisance" and of "dumping under or on top of water, or on land, any refuse in which...offensive and unwholesome material is included."<ref name="BkylnEagle-Carey-Rice-May1939" /><ref name="LIDaily-DumpIndictment-Mar1939-Pg1" /><ref name="LIDaily-DumpIndictment-Mar1939-Pg2" />  The charges were based on the operation of city-run "garbage graveyards" in Queens. The five dumps in question were the Edgemere Dump; the Lefferts Dump at Lefferts Boulevard and [[Sunrise Highway]] ([[Conduit Avenue]]) in [[South Ozone Park, Queens|South Ozone Park]], near the future site of JFK Airport; Bergen Landing; and the future sites of [[Juniper Valley Park]] and [[Baisley Pond Park]], respectively located in [[Middle Village, Queens|Middle Village]] and [[South Jamaica, Queens|South Jamaica]]. The owners of the Edgemere and Lefferts landfills were also named in the indictment.<ref name="BkylnEagle-Carey-Rice-May1939">{{cite news |title=Carey and Rice Indicted for Queens Dumps: Owners of Land Used Also Named In 19-Count Bill |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%25205%2FBrooklyn%2520NY%2520Daily%2520Eagle%2FBrooklyn%2520NY%2520Daily%2520Eagle%25201939%2520Grayscale%2FBrooklyn%2520NY%2520Daily%2520Eagle%25201939%2520Grayscale%2520-%25202600.pdf |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=[[Brooklyn Daily Eagle]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=March 28, 1939 |page=1}}</ref><ref name="LIDaily-DumpIndictment-Mar1939-Pg1">{{cite news |title=Carey and Rice Indicted for Dumping: Early Trial is Promised; Carey and Rice Surrender; Released Without Bail; Text of Dump Indictments |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252014%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%25201939%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%25201939%2520-%25201651.pdf |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=Long Island Daily Press |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=March 28, 1939 |page=1}}</ref><ref name="LIDaily-DumpIndictment-Mar1939-Pg2">{{cite news |title=Carey, Rice Are Released Without Bail; Text of Dump Indictments |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252014%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%25201939%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%25201939%2520-%25201652.pdf |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=Long Island Daily Press |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=March 28, 1939 |page=2}}</ref> Carey and Rice, both cabinet members under Mayor [[Fiorello H. La Guardia]], surrendered to the [[Long Island City Courthouse]] and were released without bail.<ref name="LIDaily-DumpIndictment-Mar1939-Pg1"/>

A change of venue was granted on May 18, 1939 and the trial was moved to the Bronx.<ref name="ElmhurstDaily-DumpingBoard-Jun1939"/><ref>{{cite news |title=Bronx to Try Comm. Carey for Dumping |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201939-1940%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201939-1940%2520-%25200157.pdf |access-date=August 30, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=May 18, 1939 |page=1}}</ref> On May 31, the trial was postponed until October of that year. Around this time, dumping was resumed at the Edgemere Landfill.<ref>{{cite news |title=Carey Trial is Postponed Till October |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201939-1940%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201939-1940%2520-%25200173.pdf |access-date=August 30, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=June 1, 1939 |page=1}}</ref> On June 19, 1939, the indictments were dismissed by Justice [[Isidor Wasservogel]]. As a consolation, a board of four health experts and a sanitary engineer was appointed by U.S. Surgeon General [[Thomas Parran Jr.]] to arbitrate the conflict and to investigate the operations of the five landfills. The board included [[Eugene Lindsay Bishop]] and [[Kenneth F. Maxcy]].<ref name="ElmhurstDaily-DumpingBoard-Jun1939">{{cite news |title=Board to Investigate Dumping |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252024%2FElmhurst%2520NY%2520Daily%2520Register%2FElmhurst%2520NY%2520Daily%2520Register%25201939%2FElmhurst%2520NY%2520Daily%2520Register%25201939%252000298.pdf |access-date=August 30, 2018 |work=The Daily Register |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=June 20, 1939 |page=1}}</ref><ref name="BklynEagle-DumpingBoon-Mar1940"/><ref>{{cite news |title=District Attorney Names Those To Serve As Experts On Dumps |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201939-1940%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201939-1940%2520-%25200219.pdf |access-date=August 30, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=July 6, 1939 |page=1}}</ref><ref name="Rockawave-Carey-Freed-Jun1939">{{cite news |title=Comms. Carey And Rice Are Freed In Dump Indictments: Dumping Charges Are Dropped After Agreement to Let Dr. Thomas Parran, Jr., U.S. Surgeon-General, Appoint a Five-Man Arbitration Commission. |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201939-1940%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201939-1940%2520-%25200203.pdf |access-date=August 30, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=June 22, 1939 |page=1}}</ref> In addition, Carey announced that dumping at Edgemere would end on June 25 and cease until the fall.<ref name="Rockawave-Carey-Freed-Jun1939"/> The charges were dropped by District Attorney [[Charles P. Sullivan]] due to a lack of individuals to testify in the trial.<ref>{{cite news |title=Garbage Dumps Outmoded Way Back In Bible Days |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252014%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%25201939%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%25201939%2520-%25200102.pdf |access-date=August 31, 2018 |work=Long Island Star-Journal |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=August 8, 1939 |page=3}}</ref>

On September 21, 1939, the arbitration board conducted a "secret tour" of the five landfills.<ref>{{cite news |title=Garbage Damp Inspection Ends With A Secret Tour |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252014%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%25201939%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%25201939%2520-%25200762.pdf |access-date=August 31, 2018 |work=Long Island Star-Journal |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=September 22, 1939 |page=1}}</ref> At this time, the Department of Sanitation anticipated resuming landfilling at Edgemere that fall, which was opposed by local residents.<ref>{{cite news |title=East Enders Fear Dumping on Bay Front: Residents In Edgemere Are Uneasy About Future Dumping Here |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201939-1940%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201939-1940%2520-%25200307.pdf |access-date=August 30, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=September 21, 1939}}</ref> In March 1940, the board released its report, which supported continued landfilling at the five Queens landfills including Edgemere as long as "sound sanitary practice is continued", as the landfilling process helped control rat and mosquito populations in marshland.<ref name="BklynEagle-DumpingBoon-Mar1940">{{cite news |title=Health Experts Call Garbage Dumping Boon: Board Sees Rats, Mosquitoes Curbed By Queens Fills |url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/52683734/?terms=%22edgemere%22%2B%22William%2BF.%2BCarey%22%2B%221941%22 |access-date=August 30, 2018 |work=[[Brooklyn Daily Eagle]] |via=[[Brooklyn Public Library]]; [[newspapers.com]] |date=March 16, 1940 |page=15}}</ref> On June 22, 1940, the [[New York City Council]] passed a bill mandating the Department of Sanitation to begin using the available incinerators in the city. The bill was introduced by Councilman [[James A. Burke (New York politician)|James A. Burke]] representing [[Hollis, Queens]]. Burke then proceeded to submit the bill to Mayor Fiorello LaGuardia in an attempt to bypass the Board of Estimate.<ref>{{cite news |title=City Council Passes Curb on Dumping: Burke Bill, Ordering Carey to Use Incinerators, Sent to the Mayor |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252014%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%25201940%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%25201940%2520-%25202371.pdf |access-date=August 30, 2018 |work=Long Island Daily Press |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=June 22, 1940 |page=1}}</ref> Many of the city's incinerators, including the Arverne incinerator, had been closed under Carey's watch.<ref name="LIStar-EndGarbageDump-Jan1946">{{cite news |title=City to End Garbage Dumping |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252014%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%25201946%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%25201946%2520-%25200208.pdf |access-date=August 30, 2018 |work=Long Island Star-Journal |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=January 11, 1946 |page=1}}</ref>

===Rockaway Airport===
On July 16, 1939, the Edgemere Airport (also called Rockaway Airport) was opened on the New York City Waterfront Company land between Beach 46th Street and Beach 54th Street. The airport was operated by [[Lawrence, Nassau County, New York|Lawrence]] resident and commercial pilot Harry Gordon, and was said to be the first privately owned airfield in the Rockaways. Prior to the construction of a hangar, planes for the airport were kept at [[Roosevelt Field (airport)|Roosevelt Field]] in Nassau County.<ref>{{cite news |title=First Privately-Owned Airport Opens In Edgemere Area: Harry Gordon of Lawrence Plans to Erect Six-Plane Hangar |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201939-1940%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201939-1940%2520-%25200235.pdf |access-date=August 4, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=July 20, 1939 |page=1}}</ref> The airport was created for civilian training and leisure flying.<ref name="Rockawave-CoastGuard-Feb1944"/>

Following a lawsuit by Gordon, on December 26, 1939 city Commissioner of Docks John McKenzie was ordered by the [[Manhattan Supreme Court]] to award a permit to the airport.<ref>{{cite news |title=Hospitals Ask Mayor To Curb Noise of Planes |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252018%2FNew%2520York%2520NY%2520Sun%2FNew%2520York%2520NY%2520Sun%25201939%2FNew%2520York%2520NY%2520Sun%25201939%2520a%2520-%25205676.pdf |access-date=August 9, 2018 |work=[[The Sun (New York City)]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=December 13, 1939 |page=3}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Court Orders City to Grant Edgemere Airport License |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252014%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%25201939%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%25201939%2520-%25205595.pdf |access-date=August 4, 2018 |work=Long Island Daily Press |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=December 27, 1939}}</ref> On July 8, 1940 after 15 months of operation, McKenzie issued a letter informing Gordon that the airport would be closed in 30 days due to not meeting facility requirements for airports in the city. Specifically, the airport failed to meet the requirements for {{convert|1800|ft|m|adj=mid|-long}} and {{convert|300|ft|m|adj=mid|-wide}} runways, and for an "unobstructed approach" to the airport.<ref>{{cite news |title=Rules Doom Airport at Edgemere |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252014%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%25201940%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%25201940%2520-%25202861.pdf |access-date=August 4, 2018 |work=Long Island Daily Press |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=July 18, 1940 |page=5}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=The Rockaway Airport: It Deserves a Chance to Make Good |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252014%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%25201940%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%25201940%2520-%25202872.pdf |access-date=August 4, 2018 |work=Long Island Daily Press |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=July 18, 1960 |page=16}}</ref> At this time, work commenced on expanding and developing the airport.<ref>{{cite news |title=Rockaway Airport Work Is Started |url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/52773641/?terms=%22Rockaway%2Bairport%22 |access-date=August 11, 2018 |work=[[Brooklyn Daily Eagle]] |via=[[Brooklyn Public Library]]; [[newspapers.com]] |date=December 8, 1940 |page=10}}</ref> The pilots training at the airport included members of the Women Flyers Of America.<ref>{{cite news |title=Women Flyers Of America Training In Edgemere Field; Ready To Train In Defense |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201939-1940%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201939-1940%2520-%25200768.pdf |access-date=August 9, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=October 10, 1940 |page=1}}</ref> The airport would later become the headquarters of Women's Flyers Association of America.<ref name="Rockawave-Airport-TakenOver-Oct1941"/>

In October 1940, the Rockaway Chamber of Commerce petitioned the federal [[Civil Aeronautics Administration (United States)|Civil Aeronautics Administration]] to create a civilian pilot school at Rockaway Airport.<ref>{{cite news |title=Air School: Rockaway Sends Plea to CAA |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252014%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%25201940%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%25201940%2520-%25204611.pdf |access-date=August 9, 2018 |work=Long Island Daily Press |date=October 12, 1940 |page=10}}</ref> In January 1941, [[Bayside, Queens|Bayside]] resident Charles G. Meyer <!--(son of local real estate developer Cord Meyer; [[Cord Meyer|Cord Meyer Jr.]])-->proposed converting his farm along [[Little Neck Bay]] into a city-operated airfield to train civilian pilots. Several wealthy residents of Bayside protested his plan, including actor and movie producer [[John Golden]]. As an alternative, Golden suggested to Mayor Fiorello LaGuardia that the Edgemere Dump be used for the airfield.<ref>{{cite news |title=Meyer Site for Airport Under Fire: Wealthy Bayside Neighbors Don't Want Amateurs Flying Over Them |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252014%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%25201941%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%25201941%2520a%2520-%25200238.pdf |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=Long Island Daily Press |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=January 13, 1931 |page=1}}</ref> On January 15, 1941, Mayor LaGuardia publicly rejected both the Bayside and Edgemere proposals, due to costs and potential hazards to Bayside residents.<ref>{{cite news |title=Aviation Park Hopes Dashed by La Guardia: Mayor Doesn't Like Bayside or Edgemere Airport Proposals |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252014%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%25201941%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%25201941%2520a%2520-%25200256.pdf |access-date=August 4, 2018 |work=Long Island Daily Press |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=January 15, 1941 |page=1}}</ref> Meyer's farm would later become the [[Bay Terrace, Queens|Bay Terrace]] neighborhood,<ref>{{cite news |last1=Marzlock |first1=Ron |title=Charles G. Meyer's estate on Bell Avenue |url=http://www.qchron.com/qboro/i_have_often_walked/charles-g-meyer-s-estate-on-bell-avenue/article_48a84b85-2b8d-5414-8908-710a031d86b0.html |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=Queens Chronicle |date=August 24, 2017}}</ref> while John Golden's estate would become John Golden Park.<ref>{{cite web |title=John Golden Park: History |url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/john-golden-park/history |publisher=[[New York City Department of Parks and Recreation]] |access-date=July 29, 2018}}</ref>

On July 26, 1941 the Civil Aeronautics Administration approved Rockaway Airport along with Nassau Airport in [[Hicksville, New York|Hicksville, Long Island]] as civilian pilot training facilities. Meanwhile, Idlewild Airport (today's [[JFK Airport]]) was ordered to cease training of pilots.<ref>{{cite news |title=Idlewild Airport Ordered To Stop Training Pilots |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252014%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%25201941%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%25201941%2520-%25203746.pdf |access-date=August 9, 2018 |work=Long Island Daily Press |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=July 26, 1941 |page=2}}</ref> Upon the onset of [[World War II]], in 1941 Gordon offered use of the airport and a supply of planes and pilots to the United States military in order to monitor and patrol the coast of Long Island during the war.<ref>{{cite news |title=Use of Rockaway Airport Offered to the Army |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252014%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%25201941%2FJamaica%2520NY%2520Long%2520Island%2520Daily%2520Press%25201941%2520a%2520-%25201563.pdf |access-date=August 4, 2018 |work=Long Island Daily Press |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=May 1941}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Rockaway Airport Offers Facilities |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%25205%2FBrooklyn%2520NY%2520Daily%2520Eagle%2FBrooklyn%2520NY%2520Daily%2520Eagle%25201941%2520Grayscale%2FBrooklyn%2520NY%2520Daily%2520Eagle%25201941%2520Grayscale%2520-%25209504.pdf |access-date=August 9, 2018 |work=[[Brooklyn Daily Eagle]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=December 12, 1941}}</ref> In October 1941, soldiers from [[Fort Tilden]] in the western Rockaways began using the airport for ten days to conduct [[Strategic bombing during World War II|air raid drills]].<ref name="Rockawave-Airport-TakenOver-Oct1941">{{cite news |title=Beach Airport Is 'Taken Over': Fort Tilden Soldiers to Be 'On Guard' for Next Ten Days |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201941-1942%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201941-1942%2520-%25200346.pdf |access-date=August 5, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=October 9, 1941 |page=5}}</ref> The offer to use the airport was officially accepted by [[Civil Air Patrol]] Major General [[John F. Curry]] in February 1942.<ref>{{cite news |title=Offers Use Of Field and Pilots: Local Airport to Aid In Patrolling Atlantic Coast Waters Off Long Island |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201941-1942%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201941-1942%2520-%25200492.pdf |access-date=August 4, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=February 12, 1942 |page=1}}</ref> Civilian flying, however, was banned by the federal government during World War II and Gordon abandoned the airport at this time.<ref name="Rockawave-CoastGuard-Feb1944"/><ref>{{cite news |title=Interest Reported in Edgemere Airport |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201945-1946%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201945-1946%2520-%25200302.pdf |access-date=August 4, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=September 6, 1945 |page=4}}</ref> In early 1944, the airport was leased by the [[United States Coast Guard]] as a helicopter training base.<ref name="Rockawave-CoastGuard-Feb1944">{{cite news |title=Coast Guard Is To Take Over Local Airport; Leases Edgemere Field For Use as Base for Helicopter Training Purposes |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201943-1944%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201943-1944%2520-%25200511.pdf |access-date=August 4, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=February 17, 1944 |page=1}}</ref>

Following the war, in February 1946 Rockaway Airport was reopened by war veterans Joseph Alta and Perry Fuhr. Alta was an [[United States Army Air Forces|Army Air Force]] pilot in the [[China Burma India Theater]] of the war. Fuhr was a Navy test pilot. Alta had previously operated a flight school at [[Floyd Bennett Field]] in Brooklyn.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Carlton |first1=Roy |title=Sky's the Limit: 146 Days of Flying And Not One Accident! |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252014%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%25201946%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%25201946%2520-%25204252.pdf |access-date=August 9, 2018 |work=Long Island Star-Journal |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=August 31, 1946 |page=2}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Edgemere Airport To Operate Again: Capt. Alta and Associates Busy Getting Field In Readiness for Season |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201945-1946%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201945-1946%2520-%25200538.pdf |access-date=August 5, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=March 21, 1946 |page=8}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Solo Flyers Throw A Party In Celebration At Rockaway Airport |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201945-1946%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201945-1946%2520-%25200636.pdf |access-date=August 5, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=June 20, 1946 |page=1}}</ref> Beginning on January 6, 1947, the airport was used as the receiving point for a helicopter mail service originating at [[LaGuardia Airport]] or [[Newark Airport]], and serving both the Rockaways and [[Five Towns]] in Nassau County.<ref>{{cite news |title=Helicopter Mail Service To Base At Rockaway Airport: Arrangements Completed to Utilize Edgemere Field For Experimental Flights Beginning Jan. 6. ===Park plans and purchase of the property===
[[File:Rockaway Community Pk td 05 - Edgemere Houses.jpg|thumb|left|Rockaway Community Park was planned along with the Edgemere Houses (pictured), which opened in 1960.]]
On January 11, 1946, new Sanitation Commissioner William J. Powell announced that the city would abandon the landfill system favored by his predecessor Carey and instead utilize incinerators, with half of the Borough of Queens' waste to be disposed of via incinerator immediately.<ref name="LIStar-EndGarbageDump-Jan1946"/> On January 17, 1949, the Department of Sanitation opened a "Super Dump" in [[Howard Beach, Queens|Howard Beach]], located along Jamaica Bay stretching west of [[Cross Bay Boulevard]].<ref name="Rockawave-HowardBchDump-Jan1949">{{cite news |title=We Hope They're Right |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201949%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201949%2520-%25200026.pdf |access-date=August 4, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=January 20, 1949 |page=4 |quote=Tho Sanitation Department opened its new super dump at Howard Beach Monday.}}</ref><ref name="LIStar-SuperDump-Jan1949">{{cite news |title=Incinerators Next |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252014%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%25201949%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%25201949%2520b%2520-%25200528.pdf |access-date=August 4, 2018 |work=Long Island Star-Journal |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=January 19, 1949 |page=4}}</ref> The new dump, proposed by Parks Commissioner [[Robert Moses]], was intended to receive most of the garbage from southern Queens and replace smaller landfills in other areas of the borough. The new Super Dump would either reduce the load on or entirely replace the Edgemere Landfill. The Howard Beach dump would operate until the completion of the South Shore Incinerator in [[Spring Creek, Brooklyn]]. Afterwards, the reclaimed land would become part of the planned [[Spring Creek Park]].<ref name="Rockawave-HowardBchDump-Jan1949"/><ref>{{cite news |title=$40,000 For Park Plan; Board of Estimate Furthers Cross Bay Project |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1948/09/30/archives/40000-for-park-plan-board-of-estimate-furthers-cross-bay-project.html |access-date=May 16, 2017 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=September 30, 1948}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=City Approves Super-Dump Plan; Incinerator Proposed for South Shore; 3-Year Moses Program Adopted as Municipal 'Garbage Policy' |access-date=May 16, 2017 |work=Long Island Star-Journal |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=August 20, 1948 |page=1}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=City Officials Promise To Keep Down Odors of New Super-Duper Dump |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252014%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%25201948%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%25201948%2520-%25205764.pdf |access-date=May 16, 2017 |work=Long Island Star-Journal |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=August 17, 1948 |page=1}}</ref><ref name="Rockawave-SCP-Landfill-1951">{{cite news |title=Board of Estimate Adopts Resolution For Filling Spring Creek Park Site |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201951%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201951%2520-%25200219.pdf |access-date=May 16, 2017 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=April 19, 1951 |page=12}}</ref><ref name="LIStar-SuperDump-Aug1948">{{cite news |title=Moses Outlines |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252014%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%25201948%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%25201948%2520-%25205736.pdf |access-date=August 4, 2018 |work=Long Island Star-Journal |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=August 16, 1948 |page=1}}</ref>

In November 1952 and again in January 1953, Parks Commissioner Moses proposed to the [[New York City Board of Estimate]] that the city purchase the Edgemere Landfill, keep it in operation for 15 years, and eventually develop it into a park. At the time, it was estimated that keeping the site in operation would save the city $1 million annually in waste disposal costs.<ref name="LIStar-Dump-Jun61958">{{cite news |title=Dump |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252014%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%25201958%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%25201958%2520-%25204018.pdf |access-date=July 30, 2018 |work=Long Island Star-Journal |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=June 6, 1958 |page=2}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Park Commissioner Moses Assures Steady Development Of Playgrounds |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201953%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201953%2520-%25200021.pdf |access-date=August 12, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=January 3, 1953 |page=8}}</ref>

In 1955, the city began plans for a housing project in Edgemere. The plans included an adjoining park on the site of the Edgemere Landfill, which had been in operation for nearly twenty years at this time.<ref name="Rockawave-SomervillePk-Ap1955"/><ref>{{cite news |title=A Bayfront Park In Edgemere |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201955%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201955%2520-%25200519.pdf |access-date=July 30, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=September 22, 1955}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Plans For Edgemere Houses To Be Ready Early In 1956: May Move Project Boundaries To Avoid Bulkheadin^ In The Area;/ Arvenie-Hanimel Title li Plans May Be Beady Next June; Seaside Plane Still Pending |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201955%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201955%2520-%25200715.pdf |access-date=July 30, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=December 22, 1955 |page=1}}</ref> The [[New York City Board of Estimate]] approved the park project on April 29, 1955.<ref name="Rockawave-SomervillePk-Ap1955"/> On October 4, 1955 the City of New York began condemnation proceedings in order to acquire the Edgmere Landfill site adjacent to the future Edgemere Houses site.<ref name="Rockawave-Edgemere-Condemn-Sep1955"/><ref>{{cite news |title=Looking Backward: What The Wave Said 20 Years Ago This Week |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201972-1975%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201972-1975%2520-%25201492.pdf |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=September 25, 1975 |page=4}}</ref> The park was to be named "Edgemere Park".<ref name="Rockawave-Edgemere-Condemn-Sep1955" /> At the time, the property was still owned by the New York City Waterfront Corporation. Plans for the park included eight tennis courts, along with a boat basin and ice skating rink.<ref name="Rockawave-Edgemere-Condemn-Sep1955">{{cite news |title=City To Condemn Property For Park |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201955%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201955%2520-%25200511.pdf |access-date=July 30, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=September 22, 1955 |page=1}}</ref> By this time, the site occupied {{convert|264|acre|ha}}. Many of the small islands that once existed in Little Bay were now joined together and connected to the main Rockaway peninsula by landfilling. However, much of the future park site was still underwater.<ref name="Rockawave-SomervillePk-Ap1955">{{cite news |title=Somerville Park Area Is Approved: City Designates 264 Acres Along Bayfront For Recreation Development |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201955%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201955%2520-%25200225.pdf |access-date=July 30, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=April 28, 1955 |page=8}}</ref><ref name="Rockawave-Edgemere-Condemn-Sep1955"/><ref>{{cite news |title=Edgemere Will Have New Park: Waterfront Property To Be Used By The City For Recreational Purposes |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201955%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201955%2520-%25200497.pdf |access-date=July 30, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=September 15, 1955 |page=1}}</ref> It was referred to as "the largest remaining undeveloped area in the Rockaways".<ref>{{cite news |title=Local Benefits From Edgemere Houses |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201955%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201955%2520-%25200101.pdf |access-date=July 30, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=February 24, 1955}}</ref> Moses developed several public housing projects on the Rockaway peninsula during this time, all of which included an adjoining park.<ref name="KaplanKaplan2003"/>

Construction on the other adjoining infrastructure for the Edgemere Housing Project, Public School 105 and Rockaway Beach Hospital (the future [[Peninsula Hospital Center|Peninsula Hospital]]), began in 1957.<ref>{{cite news |title=NEW HOSPITAL SPEEDED; Ground to Be Broken in June at Rockaway Beach |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1956/02/26/archives/new-hospital-speeded-ground-to-be-broken-in-june-at-rockaway-beach.html |access-date=August 11, 2018 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=February 26, 1956}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Creating Rockaway's Most Modern Section |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201957%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201957%2520-%25200065.pdf |access-date=August 11, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=February 7, 1957}}</ref> The landfill site was purchased by the city via condemnation on December 12, 1957, costing $1,496,564.<ref name="Rockawave-Crisona-Edgemere-Jun121958">{{cite news |title=Crisona, Wagner Split on Confidential Report Covering Edgemere Park Sale |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201958%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201958%2520-%25200248.pdf |access-date=July 30, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=June 12, 1958 |page=1}}</ref> The purchase of the property by the city was criticized in 1958 by Queens Borough President [[James J. Crisona]], with Crisona believing that the city paid too much for the property. The city paid $1.5 million for the site following an evaluation by city real estate appraiser James C. Sheridan. However, the city tax rolls assessed the site at $150,000, exactly one tenth of its purchase price. Crisona noted that Sheridan's appraisal was based on the land's potential for industrial development, but claimed that it could not be developed for 20 to 30 years due to its status as a landfill. He also compared the price of Edgemere Park to that of other properties in the area, which were appraised at much lower prices. Crisona criticized Sheridan, Corporation Council [[Peter Campbell Brown]], and Mayor [[Robert F. Wagner Jr.]] for their roles in the purchase. Sheridan proceeded to file a $1 million [[defamation]] suit against Crisona, while Sheridan's $22,000 commission for the job was withheld by City Controller [[Lawrence E. Gerosa]]<ref name="Rockawave-Crisona-Edgemere-Jun121958"/><ref>{{cite news |title=Re-Opening of Edgemere Park Land Purchase Seems Doomed |access-date=July 30, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=June 19, 1958 |page=5}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Crisona to Air Land Deal Charges: Sheridan Files
