|access-date=July 30, 2018 |work=Long Island Star-Journal |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=July 24, 1958 |page=2}}</ref>

===Initial park development===
By July 1958, the Rockaway Airport was closed and demolished to make way for the housing project.<ref>{{cite news |title=The Beachcomber |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201958%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201958%2520-%25200340.pdf |access-date=August 9, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=July 24, 1958}}</ref><ref name="Stoff2004">{{cite book |author=Joshua Stoff |title=Long Island Airports |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ukaOiywl1b4C&pg=PA100 |access-date=August 5, 2018 |year=2004 |publisher=Arcadia Publishing |isbn=978-0-7385-3676-7 |page=100}}</ref> On October 16, 1958, ground was broken on the Edgemere Houses project, with Robert Moses, Borough President James Crisona, and Governor [[W. Averell Harriman]] in attendance. During the ceremony, Moses spoke about his plans for the adjoining Edgemere Park. The first portion of the park would be a {{convert|300|ft|m|adj=mid|-wide}} "buffer between the Edgemere State Housing Project and the operations of the Department of Sanitation". The plans for the remainder of the park, which would be the "largest park on the Rockaway peninsula," included an 18-hole golf course and a marina.<ref name="KaplanKaplan2003">{{cite book |author1=Lawrence Kaplan |author2=Professor Lawrence Kaplan |author3=Carol P. Kaplan |title=Between Ocean and City: The Transformation of Rockaway, New York |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vkR7XDsAXOoC&pg=PA81 |access-date=August 10, 2018 |year=2003 |publisher=Columbia University Press |isbn=978-0-231-12848-3 |pages=81, 100–105, 111}}</ref><ref name="Rockawave-Edgemere-Moses-Oct1958">{{cite news |title=Complete Text Of Robert Moses' Remarks At Edgemere Ground Breaking Ceremony |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201958%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201958%2520-%25200501.pdf |access-date=July 30, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=October 16, 1958 |page=4}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Edgemere Houses Ceremony Today: Harriman, Crisona, Reid Are Among Notables At Ground-Breaking |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201958%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201958%2520-%25200476.pdf |access-date=July 30, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=October 9, 1958 |page=1}}</ref> Moses planned to create several parks on wetlands by filling the land with municipal waste before developing the land into parkland. These included the future Edgemere Park and Spring Creek Park, as well as sites in [[Marine Park, Brooklyn]]; <!--[[Pelham Bay Park|Pelham Bay]]-->[[Ferry Point Park|Ferry Point, Bronx]]; [[Fresh Kills Landfill|Fresh Kills, Staten Island]]; and [[Kissena Corridor Park]] in Queens.<ref name="30YrsOfProgress">{{cite book |title=30 Years of Progress: 1934–1965 |date=June 9, 1964 |publisher=[[New York City Department of Parks and Recreation]] |url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/sub_about/parks_history/library/pdf/thirty_years_of_progress.pdf |access-date=March 31, 2017}}</ref>{{rp|8}}<ref name="LIStar-KissenaCor-Dump-May1951">{{cite news |title=FitzGerald Says: Corridor Park Garbage Dump Unnecessary; 146th St. Can Be Taken Off Map to Leave Present Grade, He Contends |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252014%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%25201951%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%25201951%2520-%25204077.pdf |access-date=May 28, 2018 |work=Long Island Star-Journal |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=May 22, 1951 |page=1}}</ref><ref name="LIStar-SpCrkPk-Landfill-Jan1962">{{cite news |last1=Sullivan |first1=Michael |title=Garbage Dump Today, Park Tomorrow |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/viewer/?file=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252014%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%25201962%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%25201962%2520-%25200097.pdf&highlightsFile=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2Fhighlighter%2Fhits%2F699d2438844616a78a288d95f9229668#page=1 |access-date=January 7, 2017 |work=Long Island Star-Journal |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=January 4, 1962}}</ref>

In December 1959, the Board of Estimate allocated $144,650 to add an additional 160,000 cubic yards of sand to the Edgemere Landfill, which would extend the site up to {{convert|2000|ft|m}} north into Jamaica Bay. The Board also planned to lay out Almeda Avenue between Conch Place (Conch Basin) and Beach 58th Street (Sommerville Basin), and to lay out Beach 51st Street, Beach 54th Street and Beach 58th Street in the area north of Beach Channel Drive. These streets would eventually serve the new housing project and park.<ref>{{cite news |title=Edgemere Park To Get More Landfill |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201959%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201959%2520-%25200577.pdf |access-date=August 7, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=December 10, 1959 |page=1}}</ref> In July 1960, the Board of Estimate approved of plans to begin developing {{convert|12|acre|ha}} of Edgemere Park on the north side of Almeda Avenue across from the Edgemere Houses. The park would include baseball fields and eight clay tennis courts along with landscaping and paths.<ref>{{cite news |title=O.K. Recreation Program AI Edgemere |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201960%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201960%2520-%25200320.pdf |access-date=July 30, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=August 4, 1960 |page=1}}</ref> Conch Playground, then known as P.S. 105 Playground, was opened in August 1960.<ref name="NYCPks-ConchPlayground"/> On October 17, 1960, Parks Commissioner [[Newbold Morris]] (successor to Robert Moses) announced plans for improvements to Edgemere Park, including baseball fields, tennis courts, and a park trail.<ref>{{cite news |title=Plan Improvements For Rockaway Area: Commissioner Morris Announces Plans To Beautify Beach Front |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201960%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201960%2520-%25200436.pdf |access-date=July 30, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=October 20, 1960 |page=1}}</ref> The first building of the Edgemere Houses was opened on November 27, 1960.<ref>{{cite news |title=HA to Open New Project: In Edgemere |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252014%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%25201960%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%25201960%2520a%2520-%25200418.pdf |access-date=July 30, 2018 |work=Long Island Star-Journal |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=November 26, 1960 |page=6}}</ref> By 1962, plans remained to develop a marina at Edgemere Park.<ref name="Rockawave-EdgemereMarina-1962">{{cite news |title=Rockaway's Marina Still On Paper |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201962%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201962%2520-%25200497.pdf |access-date=July 31, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |date=December 6, 1962}}</ref> The next year, tennis courts were completed at Edgemere Park, with a playground planned.<ref>{{cite news |title=Parks to Get $3 Million |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252014%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%25201963%2FLong%2520Island%2520City%2520NY%2520Star%2520Journal%25201963%2520-%25200353.pdf |access-date=July 30, 2018 |work=Long Island Star-Journal |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=April 8, 1963 |page=14}}</ref>

In 1965, it was claimed that the Edgemere Landfill contained more [[American herring gull]]s feeding and residing at the landfill than [[Cape Ann]], Massachusetts, a known nesting region for the herring gulls, along with "all of [[Nova Scotia]] and [[Maine]]".<ref name="NortonBasin-LittleBay-Nov2001" />{{rp|37}}<ref name="Group1971" /> At the time, it was estimated that 20 to 30 thousand herring gulls resided in [[Jamaica Bay Wildlife Refuge|the area around Jamaica Bay]], attracted by the Edgemere Landfill and the Pennsylvania and Fountain Avenue Landfills in Brooklyn.<ref name="NortonBasin-LittleBay-Nov2001"/>{{rp|37}}<ref name="Group1971">{{cite book |author=Jamaica Bay Environmental Study Group |title=Jamaica Bay and Kennedy Airport: a Multidisciplinary Environmental Study: A Report |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cJgrAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA70 |access-date=August 9, 2018 |date=January 1, 1971 |publisher=National Academies |pages=49−59, 70, 82, 87 |isbn=9780309018715 |id=NAP:15660}}</ref> That year, the Department of Sanitation opened the landfill for public use on a trial basis, accepting large items such as appliances, furniture, plumbing, and automobiles.<ref>{{cite news |title=The Wave Editorials - and Special Features; The Beachcomber |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201965%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201965%2520-%25200344.pdf |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=August 26, 1965}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Continue The Experiment Longer |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201965%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201965%2520-%25200409.pdf |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=October 7, 1965}}</ref> In July 1966 in response to complaints from residents, the Parks Department began pesticide spraying at Edgemere Park in order to combat mosquitoes, rats, and [[phragmites]]. To eliminate the phragmites, the chemical [[Dalapon]] was used. It was suggested that physically uprooting the phragmites would be a better solution, but the equipment necessary to harvest the plants could not be used in the park as much of it still consisted of marshland. The rats, meanwhile, were said to have been brought by the dumping of trash at the landfill.<ref name="Rockawave-Edgemere-Pests-Jul1966"/><ref name="Rockawave-Edgemere-Pests-Jul1966-Pg6">{{cite news |access-date=August 30, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=July 14, 1966 |page=6}}</ref> That month, $29,250 was allocated for additional landfilling on the Edgemere Park land in order to create a playground and sports fields.<ref>{{cite news |title=Edgemere Park Landfill Planned |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201966%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201966%2520-%25200311.pdf |access-date=August 30, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=July 21, 1966 |page=2}}</ref> During the fall of 1966, Edgemere Park was used as a practice field for the [[Far Rockaway High School]] football team, as their own home field was not usable during the season.<ref>{{cite news |title=Congratulations To Our Seahorses |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201966%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201966%2520-%25200504.pdf |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=April 26, 1973 |page=6}}</ref><ref name="Rockawave-RkComPk-Jun1973">{{cite news |title=Dedication Brings Hope That Park Is Due For New Work |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201972-1975%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201972-1975%2520-%25200652.pdf |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=June 21, 1973 |page=1}}</ref> While portions of the park including basketball courts and beach land were available for use at the time, most of the site had yet to be developed. Jamaica Bay Council president Jerome Hipscher desired for the park to be developed into "a miniature [[Central Park]]".<ref name="Rockawave-RkComPk-Jun1973"/> It was also proposed to integrate the park with the new [[Gateway National Recreation Area]] created by the [[National Park Service]].<ref name="Rockawave-NewPark-May1973"/>

===Toxic waste dumping and calls to close the landfill===
[[File:Departing JFK.JPG|thumb|left|The south end of Runway 4L at JFK Airport extending into Jamaica Bay, with the Rockaways in the distance.]]
In September 1973, the Edgemere Landfill was described as "the highest land area on the entire Rockaway Peninsula. It is a hugh mound of sand-covered garbage and waste material which has obliterated the marshy shoreline where marine life thrived for many years."<ref>{{cite news |title=Edgemere Bay-front A "Sleeper?" |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201972-1975%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201972-1975%2520-%25200767.pdf |access-date=July 30, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=September 27, 1973 |page=4}}</ref> On August 29, 1974 the bodies of three boys from the Edgemere Houses were found on the beach surrounding the Edgemere Landfill. Their deaths were suspected to have been caused by drowning or a lightning strike.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Kaufman |first1=Michael T. |title=3 Young Brothers' Bodies Found Off Queens Beach |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1974/08/30/archives/3-young-brothers-bodies-found-off-queens-beach-detective-theorizes.html |access-date=September 14, 2018 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=August 30, 1974}}</ref> In late 1975, the city began experimenting with methods to discourage birds from feeding off the Edgemere Landfill, in order to prevent them from interfering with planes at [[John F. Kennedy International Airport]]. The experiments included poisoning the supply of [[food waste]] at the site, shredding food waste accepted by the landfill into small pieces, narrowing the area in which garbage was dumped, and installing a horizontal-wire grid over the landfill to discourage birds from landing on it. This was in addition to the existing shotgun patrols at the airport who would discharge firearms or set off fireworks to scare the birds away. The shredding method had already been tested on landfills in the Midwest and in [[Charleston, South Carolina]]. The initiatives were motivated by an [[Overseas National Airways Flight 032|incident in November 1975]], when an [[Overseas National Airways|ONA]] [[DC-10]] aircraft crashed upon takeoff after [[bird strike|colliding with seagulls]], which were sucked into the right-wing engine destroying it.<ref name="NYTimes-JFK-Birds-Dec1975">{{cite news |last1=Witkin |first1=Richard |title=Kennedy Steps Up Drive On Birds on the Runways |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1975/12/14/archives/kennedy-steps-up-drive-on-birds-on-the-runways-kennedy-steps-up.html |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=December 14, 1975 |page=1}}</ref><ref name="NYTimes-JFK-BirdPeril-Mar1976"/><ref>{{cite news |last1=Carr |first1=Stanley |title=Notes: At JFK Airport, A Very Stubborn Flock |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1975/11/23/archives/notes-at-jfk-airport-a-very-stubborn-flock-notes-about-travel-notes.html |access-date=September 14, 2018 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=November 23, 1975}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Solutions To Bird Problem Flock To Kennedy Airport |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201976%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201976%2520-%25200156.pdf |access-date=September 16, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=May 16, 1976 |page=15}}</ref>

Following the crash, on March 8, 1976, the [[National Transportation Safety Board]] recommended closing the landfill due to potential dangers for aircraft from the airport.<ref name="NYTimes-JFK-BirdPeril-Mar1976">{{cite news |last1=Witkin |first1=Richard |title=Proposals Made to End Kennedy Airport Bird Peril |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1976/03/09/archives/proposals-made-to-end-kennedy-airport-bird-peril.html |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=March 9, 1976 |page=36}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=City Mum On Proposal To Shut Edgemere Dump |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201976%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201976%2520-%25200092.pdf |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=March 18, 1976 |page=15}}</ref><ref name="NYDaily-JFK-Feds-Nov1979"/> On May 18, 1976 the Sanitation Department informed officials from [[Queens Community Board 14]] and the Gateway National Recreation Area that the Edgemere Landfill would remain in operation until 1985. At the time, the DSNY refuted the assertion that the dump contributed to the bird hazard of JFK Airport. Mosquitoes and foul odors were also blamed on the landfill.<ref>{{cite news |title=Will Dump Garbage Until '85: Planners Seek Countours To Make Dump A Park |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201976%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201976%2520-%25200169.pdf |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=May 20, 1976 |page=1}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Will Dump Garbage Until '85: Planners Seek Countours To Make Dump A Park |url=http://fultonhistory.com/Newspapers%2021/Rockaway%20Beach%20NY%20%20Wave%20Of%20Long%20Island/Rockaway%20Beach%20NY%20%20Wave%20Of%20Long%20Island%20%201976/Rockaway%20Beach%20NY%20%20Wave%20Of%20Long%20Island%20%201976%20-%200173.pdf |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=May 20, 1976 |page=8}}</ref> In 1977 the Parks Department and Department of Sanitation garnered controversy over the closure of the Edgemere Landfill on weekends between Saturday afternoon and Monday morning. As opposed to traveling to the Fountain Avenue Landfill in Brooklyn, Parks Department garbage trucks collecting waste from [[Rockaway Beach and Boardwalk|Rockaway Beach]] would deposit their loads onto a parking lot at Beach 64th Street and Larkin Avenue in Arverne (now part of the [[Arverne by the Sea]] development) and wait until Monday to deposit the trash in Edgemere.<ref>{{cite news |title=Double Trouble |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201977%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201977%2520-%25200664.pdf |access-date=September 16, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=May 11, 1977}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Gonna Build A Mountain |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspapers%252021%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201977%2FRockaway%2520Beach%2520NY%2520%2520Wave%2520Of%2520Long%2520Island%2520%25201977%2520-%25200813.pdf |access-date=September 16, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=June 8, 1977 |page=1}}</ref> In November 1979 following 11 bird strike incidents at JFK Airport in a period of six weeks, the [[Federal Aviation Administration]] began collecting evidence in preparation to sue the city in order to close the Edgemere, Pennsylvania Avenue and Fountain Avenue Landfills. FAA Regional Director Murray Smith had previously met with Mayor [[Ed Koch]] on October 5 of that year to discuss the correlation of the bird hazard with the presence of the landfills.<ref name="NYDaily-JFK-Feds-Nov1979">{{cite news |last1=Edmonds |first1=Richard |title=Feds may sue the city over bird hazards at JFK |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/24553033/feds_may_sue_the_city_over_bird_hazards/ |access-date=September 5, 2018 |work=[[New York Daily News]] |via=[[Newspapers.com]] |date=November 15, 1979}}</ref>

During the 1970s, the landfill was said to have received hazardous waste on a daily basis. Meanwhile, waste oil was added to the garbage at Edgemere and other landfills in order to control dust.<ref name="USGS-Nitrogen-2007">{{cite web |last1=Benotti |first1=Mark J. |last2=Abbene |first2=Michele |last3=Terracciano |first3=Stephen A. |title=Nitrogen Loading in Jamaica Bay, Long Island, New York: Predevelopment to 2005 |url=https://pubs.usgs.gov/sir/2007/5051/SIR2007-5051.pdf |publisher=[[United States Geological Survey]], [[National Park Service]] |access-date=July 31, 2018 |date=2007 |pages=8−9}}</ref><ref name="LLC1983">{{cite journal |last1=Holzer |first1=Harold |title=The Enemy Below |journal=[[New York (magazine)|New York]] |date=February 7, 1983 |volume=16 |issue=6 |pages=42–46 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nMoBAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA44 |access-date=July 31, 2018 |issn=0028-7369}}</ref><ref name="CityLimits-NoForeWarning-2001">{{cite news |last1=Ulam |first1=Alex |title=No Fore Warning |url=https://citylimits.org/2001/09/01/no-fore-warning/ |access-date=September 4, 2018 |work=[[City Limits (New York magazine)]] |date=September 1, 2001}}</ref> Between March and October 1979, 5,000 to 6,000 gallons of oil and petroleum byproducts were deposited in the Edgemere, Pennsylvania and Fountain Avenue Landfills, with most of the waste going to Fountain Avenue.<ref name="LLC1983" />

In 1981 it was discovered that, beginning {{circa}} 1972–1974, DSNY supervisors were paid $100 per truck to allow the dumping of liquid toxic waste at five of the city's landfills including the Edgemere Landfill, and into the sewer system. The other sites were the Pennsylvania Avenue and Fountain Avenue Landfills in Brooklyn; the [[Tallapoosa Point]] Landfill at [[Pelham Bay Park]] in the Bronx; and the Brookfield Avenue Landfill across from Fresh Kills in Staten Island. The waste was dumped into trenches dug into the landfills. The waste had originated from plants owned by [[Ford Motor Company]], [[Exxon]], [[Chrysler]], [[Ingersoll Rand]], [[Alcan Aluminum]], and others, including the Ford stamping plant in [[Economy of Buffalo, New York|Buffalo, New York]]. In March 1982 Kenneth Mansfield, a plant manager and truck driver for an oil refining and disposal company operating<!-- the Mahler companies; Quanta--> in the metropolitan area, pled guilty to federal charges of conspiracy concerning the dumping.<ref name="LLC1983" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Moore |first1=Yvette |title=Starrett City Tenants Want to Know More About Toxic Dumping |journal=[[City Limits (New York magazine)]] |date=May 1982 |volume=12 |issue=5 |pages=18–19 |url=https://www.scribd.com/document/79599022/City-Limits-Magazine-May-1982-Issue |access-date=September 3, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Lubasch |first1=Arnold H. |title=Guilt Admitted In Toxic Dumping at City Landfills |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1982/03/28/nyregion/guilt-admitted-in-toxic-dumping-at-city-landfills.html |access-date=September 3, 2018 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=March 28, 1982}}</ref><ref name="NYTimes-PaidToClean-May1982">{{cite news |last1=Blumenthal |first1=Ralph |title=Accused Polluter was Paid to Clean Up Sites |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1982/05/07/nyregion/accused-polluter-was-paid-to-clean-up-sites.html |access-date=September 3, 2018 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=May 7, 1982}}</ref><ref name="NYTimes-ToxicEntrepreneur-1982"/><ref name="NYTimes-14Corps-Mar1985">{{cite news |last1=Purnick |first1=Joyce |title=14 Corporations Sued by the City on Toxic Waste |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1985/03/14/nyregion/14-corporations-sued-by-the-city-on-toxic-waste.html |access-date=September 11, 2018 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=March 14, 1985}}</ref><ref name="SuperfundReport-Aug1992"/> Mansfield and company owner Russell W. Mahler later pleaded guilty in [[United States District Court for the District of New Jersey|New Jersey District Court]] for dumping oil and chemical wastes into the [[Hudson River]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Blumenthal |first1=Ralph |title=2 Plead Guilty to Dumping Chemicals Into Hudson |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1982/11/04/nyregion/2-plead-guilty-to-dumping-chemicals-into-hudson.html |access-date=September 3, 2018 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=November 4, 1982}}</ref> Mahler also pled guilty to disposing of waste oil in the abandoned Butler Mine Tunnel in [[Butler Township, Luzerne County, Pennsylvania|Butler Township, Pennsylvania]], which in 1979 overflowed into the [[Susquehanna River]]. He was sentenced to one year in prison for the crime. The mine would later become a Superfund site.<ref name="NYTimes-ToxicEntrepreneur-1982">{{cite news |last1=Chavez |first1=Lydia |title=Toxic Waste Entrepreneur |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1982/05/27/business/toxic-waste-entrepreneur.html |access-date=September 3, 2018 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=May 27, 1982}}</ref><ref name="SuperfundReport-Aug1992"/> Mahler's firm had also received contracts to clean up some of the sites that it had previously contaminated with oil, including one in [[College Point, Queens|College Point]].<ref name="NYTimes-PaidToClean-May1982"/><ref name="NYTimes-ToxicEntrepreneur-1982"/> In 1982, New York City spent $2.5 million to clean up the company's [[Long Island City]] plant, located near the [[Greenpoint Avenue Bridge]] just north of [[Newtown Creek]].<ref name="LLC1983"/><ref name="NYTimes-DebateCleanup-Feb1984">{{cite news |last1=Lemoyne |first1=James |title=State and City Debate Cleanup of Toxic Waste |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1984/02/29/nyregion/state-and-city-debate-cleanup-of-toxic-waste.html |access-date=September 11, 2018 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=February 29, 1984}}</ref> In 1985, the city filed suit under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (a.k.a. the Federal Superfund Act) against the 14 companies who originally generated the toxic waste later dumped in the city landfills.<!--City of New York v. Exxon Corp., 744 F. Supp. 474 (S.D.N.Y. 1990)--><ref name="NYTimes-14Corps-Mar1985"/><ref name="SuperfundReport-Aug1992">{{cite web |title=Inside EPA Superfund Report August 12, 1992 |url=https://semspub.epa.gov/work/05/200938.pdf |publisher=[[United States Environmental Protection Agency]] |access-date=September 11, 2018 |pages=23–25}}</ref>

In February 1983, nearly 3,000 55-gallon metal drums of waste were discovered inside the Edgemere Landfill.<ref name="NortonBasin-LittleBay-Nov2001"/>{{rp|39}}<ref name="NYTimes-Edgemere-WasteDrums-Mar1983"/><ref name="NYDaily-Edgemere-Drums-Jul1983">{{cite news |last1=Dallas |first1=Gus |title=Watchful eye at the dumps |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/24553037/watchful_eye_at_the_dumps/ |access-date=September 5, 2018 |work=[[New York Daily News]] |via=[[Newspapers.com]] |date=July 31, 1983 |page=B7}}</ref> The drums were discovered in the "neck" area of the peninsula just south of the main landfill,<ref name="NortonBasin-LittleBay-Nov2001"/>{{rp|36}} when a tractor spreading dirt struck the drums by accident.<ref name="NYDaily-Landfill-Dec1987"/><ref name="NYTimes-Edgemere-WasteDrums-Mar1983"/> While most of the drums were empty, many contained lead-based paint and resin.<ref name="NYTimes-Edgemere-WasteDrums-Mar1983"/><ref name="NYDaily-Edgemere-Drums-Jul1983"/> The drums were said to have been buried beginning in 1968, around 15 years prior, when there were fewer regulations concerning the disposal of chemicals.<ref name="NYTimes-Edgemere-WasteDrums-Mar1983"/><ref name="NYDaily-Edgemere-Drums-Jul1983"/> Following the discovery, the [[New York City Department of Environmental Protection]] began testing the air, soil, and ground water of the local area for runoff from the drums.<ref name="LLC1983"/><ref name="NYTimes-Edgemere-WasteDrums-Mar1983">{{cite news |last1=Dunlap |first1=David W. |title=Buried Waste Drums Found in Queens |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1983/03/09/nyregion/buried-waste-drums-found-in-queens.html |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=March 9, 1983}}</ref> That month, the landfill was designated a [[Superfund]] site.<ref name="NYC-BrownfieldEdgemere-Ap2016"/>{{rp|50}}<ref>{{cite news |title=State Lists 100 Dump Sites for Hazardous Waste Tests |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1983/02/19/nyregion/state-lists-100-dump-sites-for-hazardous-waste-tests.html |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=February 18, 1983 |last=Barbanel |first=Josh}}</ref>

On May 18, 1983, the Toxics Project of the [[New York Public Interest Research Group]] released a report documenting the dumping of chemical toxic waste at city landfills from 1964 to 1979. The year-long study covered the Edgemere Landfill in Queens, the Pennsylvania and Fountain Landfills in Brooklyn, the Tallapoosa/Pelham Bay Landfill in the Bronx, and the Fresh Kills and Brookfield Avenue Landfills in Staten Island, based on unreleased DSNY internal records. It concluded that "hundreds of tons" of chemical wastes had been deposited at the landfills with the permission of the Sanitation Department, which had been legal until 1979, along with the illegal dumping of "millions of pounds" of toxic wastes such as waste oil.<ref name="Poust 1983" /><ref name="Blumenthal 1983" /> It also confirmed the use of oil at the landfills to control dust, which occurred weekly for six months in each year. This oil was contaminated waste product. The study further concluded that the landfills were not designed to contain chemical wastes, and violated state and federal regulations.<ref name="Poust 1983">{{cite news |last1=Poust |first1=Mary Ann |title=Report: Pelham Bay landfill contaminated with 'waste oils' |url=http://fultonhistory.com/highlighter/highlight-for-xml?altUrl=http%3A%2F%2Ffultonhistory.com%2FNewspaper%252010%2FYonkers%2520NY%2520Herald%2520Statesman%2FYonkers%2520NY%2520Herald%2520Statesman%25201983%2520Grayscale%2FYonkers%2520NY%2520Herald%2520Statesman%25201983%2520a%2520Grayscale%2520-%25200185.pdf |access-date=September 16, 2018 |work=[[Yonkers Herald Statesman]] |agency=[[Fultonhistory.com]] |date=May 19, 1983 |page=3}}</ref><ref name="Blumenthal 1983">{{cite news |last1=Blumenthal |first1=Ralph |title=Toxic Dumping in City Landfills Cited in a Study |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1983/05/19/nyregion/toxic-dumping-in-city-landfills-cited-in-a-study.html |access-date=September 16, 2018 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=May 19, 1983 |page=B3}}</ref>

In 1984, the Edgemere Landfill was listed by the [[New York State Department of Environmental Conservation]] (NYSDEC) among 895 hazardous-waste sites in the state and among 144 that required top priority to be cleaned up.<ref>{{cite news |title=State Lists Hazardous-Waste Sites |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1984/01/29/nyregion/state-lists-hazardous-waste-sites.html |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=January 28, 1984}}</ref> That year, the city began negotiations with the state to close the Edgemere and Fountain Avenue Landfills.<ref name="NYTimes-DebateCleanup-Feb1984"/>

In 1985, it was anticipated that the Edgemere Landfill would close the next year.<ref name="NYTimes-LaughingGulls-May1990">{{cite news |last1=Fried |first1=Joseph P. |title=While Laughing Gulls Flourish, Airport Officials Fret |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1990/05/01/nyregion/while-laughing-gulls-flourish-airport-officials-fret.html |access-date=September 5, 2018 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=May 1, 1990}}</ref><ref name="CityLimits-GarbageDilemma-1985"/> By December, however, the Department of Sanitation began negotiating with the NYSDEC to obtain a permit in order to keep the landfill open.<ref>{{cite news |title=Looking Backward: What The Wave Said |url=https://www.rockawave.com/articles/looking-backward-403/ |access-date=September 16, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |date=December 16, 2005 |quote=20 Years Ago… New York City’s Department of Sanitation will not close the Edgemere landfill by the end of this year, as many people in this area had been hoping. It is negotiating with the State Department of Environmental Conservation for a permit to operate this landfill.}}</ref> In February 1986, the Department of Sanitation announced that the Edgemere Landfill would operate for an additional 21 years until 2007, pending the approval of the NYSDEC. The DSNY argued that the landfill only took in 550 tons of garbage daily, compared to the 22,000 tons accepted by Fresh Kills. They stated that only waste from the Rockaways would be dumped at the landfill. The move to keep the landfill open was opposed by Queens Borough President [[Claire Shulman]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Rockaway dump stays open |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/24553060/rockaway_dump_stays_open/ |access-date=September 5, 2018 |work=[[New York Daily News]] |via=[[Newspapers.com]] |date=February 9, 1986}}</ref>

===Closing and capping of the landfill===
In July 1987, the city reached an agreement with the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation to close the landfill by 1991, unless a permit could be awarded to the landfill. Under the agreement, landfill operations could continue until July 1991 while the state conducted an investigation of the site. Dumping in the area where the waste drums were discovered, however, was banned.<ref name="NYTimes-Edgemere-Close-Jul1987">{{cite news |last1=Miller |first1=Lori B. |title=Landfill in Queens to Close by 1991 Under Agreement |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1987/07/09/nyregion/landfill-in-queens-to-close-by-1991-under-agreement.html |access-date=July 29, 2018 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=July 9, 1987}}</ref><ref name="NYDaily-Hallelujahs-Nov1997">{{cite news |last1=Shin |first1=Paul H.B. |title=Dump Nearly Redeemed Hallelujahs as Park by Bay Arises |url=http://www.nydailynews.com/archives/boroughs/dump-redeemed-hallelujahs-park-bay-arises-article-1.779585 |access-date=July 28, 2018 |work=[[New York Daily News]] |date=November 13, 1997}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=Environment Reporter |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OZ5CAQAAIAAJ |access-date=September 16, 2018 |year=1987 |publisher=Bureau of National Affairs |page=838}}</ref> By this time, the landfill's daily intake of garbage was increased to around 1,000 tons of garbage. By comparison, Fresh Kills Landfill received 23,500 tons daily.<ref name="NYDaily-Landfill-Dec1987"/><ref name="NYTimes-Edgemere-Close-Jul1987"/><ref name="NYDaily-Hallelujahs-Nov1997"/> With the eventual closure of Edgemere and Fresh Kills imminent, the city planned to replace the landfills with several "[[resource recovery]] facilities" in the future. This included [[Waste-to-energy plant|waste-to-energy incinerators]], one of which would be located at the [[Brooklyn Navy Yard]], which would generate electricity from burning garbage. In addition, gas recovery plants to extract methane would be created at several inactive landfills including Fresh Kills and Pelham Bay.<ref name="NYCostal-Aug1982"/><ref name="NYTimes-Edgemere-Close-Jul1987"/><ref name="CityLimits-GarbageDilemma-1985">{{cite journal |last1=Hershkowitz |first1=Allen |title=New York's Garbage Disposal Dilemma |journal=[[City Limits (New York magazine)]] |date=November 1985 |volume=10 |issue=9 |pages=24–25 |url=https://www.scribd.com/document/79617183/City-Limits-Magazine-November-1985-Issue |access-date=September 4, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Hevesi |first1=Dennis |title=State Approves the Brooklyn Navy Yard Incinerator |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1993/09/12/nyregion/state-approves-the-brooklyn-navy-yard-incinerator.html |access-date=September 4, 2018 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=September 12, 1993}}</ref><ref name="LLC1990"/> In December 1987, local community groups and politicians filed suit to have the landfill shut down, citing the fact that the landfill was operating without a permit. At the time, it was referred to as the "most toxic landfill in the world" due to the historical dumping of oil and chemicals.<ref name="NYDaily-Landfill-Dec1987" /> It was also stated that 167,000 gallons of toxic liquid seeped from the landfill on a daily basis. It was compared to the [[Love Canal]] landfill, another Superfund site located in [[Niagara Falls, New York|Niagara Falls]].<ref name="NYDaily-Landfill-Dec1987"/><ref name="NYDaily-EdgemereAir-Jul2003"/> In 1989, Edgemere handled over 1,500 tons of city garbage on a daily basis, making up 7.6 percent of the city's waste. In comparison, 4.4 percent of the city's waste <!--(845 tons per day) -->was burned in city-owned incinerators, 8.1 percent was disposed of in apartment incinerators, and 73.4 percent (14,000 tons per day) was taken to Fresh Kills Landfill in Staten Island.<ref name="GoldsteinIzeman1990">{{cite book |author1=Eric A. Goldstein |author2=Mark A. Izeman |author3=Natural Resources Defense Council |title=The New York Environment Book |url=https://archive.org/details/newyorkenvironme0000gold |url-access=registration |access-date=September 3, 2018 |year=1990 |publisher=Island Press |isbn=978-1-55963-018-4 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/newyorkenvironme0000gold/page/5 5], 12}}</ref>

<!--section break?-->
In March 1990, the city and state began removing 7,000 drums of toxic waste from the Edgemere Landfill.<ref name="NYDaily-EdgemereAir-Jul2003"/><ref name="NYDaily-Hallelujahs-Nov1997"/><ref name="DSNY-2000Report"/><ref name="LLC1990">{{cite journal |title=How Bad Is New York's Environment?; Garbage: Running out of room to dump it, the city bunts for solutions |journal=[[New York (magazine)|New York]] |date=April 16, 1990 |volume=23 |issue=15 |pages=30–36 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=wqJY4DcHuiYC&pg=PA30 |access-date=September 14, 2018 |issn=0028-7369}}</ref> That year, the Department of Sanitation's Bureau of Waste Prevention, Reuse and Recycling (BWPRR) began a pilot [[compost]]ing program at the Edgemere Landfill, handling 1,000 tons of leaves. Another composting facility would be opened that year at Fresh Kills.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Flammer |first1=Rich |title=Composting Comes Back to the Big Apple |journal=BioCycle |date=September 2005 |volume=46 |issue=9 |page=29 |url=https://www.biocycle.net/2005/09/22/composting-comes-back-to-the-big-apple/ |access-date=September 7, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Composting in New York City: A Complete Program History |url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/dsny/docs/about_2001-composting-in-nyc_0815.pdf |publisher=[[New York City Department of Sanitation]] Bureau of Waste Prevention, Reuse and Recycling |access-date=September 7, 2018 |date=August 2001}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Managing Food Waste in New York City: A Development Framework for Organic Waste Facilities |url=http://mpaenvironment.ei.columbia.edu/files/2014/06/Food-Waste-Workshop-Final-Report.pdf |publisher=[[School of International and Public Affairs, Columbia University]], [[Global Green USA]] |access-date=September 7, 2018 |date=2014 }}{{Dead link|date=September 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

The Edgemere Landfill was closed on schedule in July 1991.<ref name="NYTimes-EdgemereClose-Jul1991"/> This left Fresh Kills Landfill as the city's only landfill, joined by six municipal incinerators and the city's growing recycling program.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Polan |first1=Steven M. |title=Garbage Gridlock: New Yorkers produce 26,000 tons of garbage each day, and our landfill space is quickly running out. Where will we put our trash? |journal=[[City Journal (New York City)]] |date=Autumn 1992 |url=https://www.city-journal.org/html/garbage-gridlock-12673.html |access-date=September 7, 2018}}</ref> <!--Upon the closure of Edgemere,-->By this time, the president of the Bayswater Civic Association had nicknamed the landfill "Mount Edgemere".<ref name="NYTimes-EdgemereClose-Jul1991"/> This was similar to the "Mount Corona" nickname given to a {{convert|90|ft|m|adj=on}} mound of ash in the former Corona Ash Dumps, now the site of [[Flushing Meadows–Corona Park]].<ref name="FMCPStrategic-AppHistory">{{cite web |title=Flushing Meadows Corona Park Strategic Framework Plan; Appendix: The History of Flushing Meadows Corona Park |url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/sub_your_park/vt_flushing_meadows/presentation/07appendix.pdf |publisher=[[New York City Department of Parks and Recreation]]}}</ref><ref name="Steinberg2015">{{cite book |author=Ted Steinberg |title=Gotham Unbound: The Ecological History of Greater New York |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=arkrCgAAQBAJ&pg=PA211 |date=July 21, 2015 |publisher=[[Simon and Schuster]] |isbn=978-1-4767-4128-4 |pages=209–225}}</ref><ref name="NYCPk-TomorrowsWorld">{{cite web |title=Tomorrow's World: The New York World's Fairs and Flushing Meadows Corona Park |url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/pagefiles/73/tomorrows-world-publication.pdf |publisher=[[New York City Department of Parks and Recreation]] |access-date=March 27, 2017 |date=June 26, 2015}}</ref> Following its closure, the New York City Department of Environmental Protection assumed responsibility for the cleanup of the site and other former landfills. 75 percent of cleanup costs would be covered by the New York State Superfund program.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Sugarman |first1=Raphael |title=Stemming Pelham Bay toxins |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/24553071/stemming_pelham_bay_toxins/ |access-date=October 14, 2018 |work=[[New York Daily News]] |via=[[Newspapers.com]] |date=November 29, 1994}}</ref> The closure of the Edgemere Landfill, and the previous decommissioning of the Pennsylvania Avenue and Fountain Avenue Landfills, helped to reduce the bird strike hazard at JFK Airport.<ref name="JFKBirdHazard-2012-Ch1">{{cite web |title=Bird Hazard Reduction Program: John F. Kennedy International Airport; Supplement to the Environmental Impact Statement; Chapter 1: Purpose and Need for Action |url=https://www.aphis.usda.gov/regulations/pdfs/nepa/Final%20JFK%20SEIS%20Chapter%201.pdf |publisher=[[Wildlife Services|USDA Wildlife Services]], [[Fish and Wildlife Service]], [[National Park Service]], [[Federal Aviation Administration]], [[Government of New York City|City of New York]], [[Port Authority of New York and New Jersey]] |access-date=September 5, 2018 |date=April 2012 |archive-date=January 31, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170131040032/https://www.aphis.usda.gov/regulations/pdfs/nepa/Final%20JFK%20SEIS%20Chapter%201.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In summer 1992 the [[New York City Department of City Planning]] released the New York City Comprehensive Waterfront Plan, which sought to improve and expand the waterfront parkland within the city including the area around Jamaica Bay.<ref name="RPA-JamaicaBayTrail-Dec2014" />{{rp|5}}<ref name="NYCWaterfrontPlan-1992">{{cite web |title=New York City Comprehensive Waterfront Plan: Reclaiming the City's Edge |url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/about/publications/cwp.pdf |publisher=[[New York City Department of City Planning]] |access-date=August 25, 2018 |date=Summer 1992}}</ref>{{rp|i−xi}} The plan urged the DSNY and Department of Environmental Protection to develop a containment plan for the Edgemere Landfill, which should include "innovative bio-technology approaches".<ref name="NYCWaterfrontPlan-1992"/>{{rp|39 (PDF p. 57)}} It also sought to create additional parkland in Edgemere, and preserve the wetlands along the Sommerville and Conch Basins.<ref name="NYCWaterfrontPlan-1992" />{{rp|39−40, 224−225 (PDF p. 57−58, 242−243)}} In July 1992, a $30.4 million settlement with over 100 corporations and public entities was reached in the 1985 Superfund lawsuit over dumping at Edgemere Landfill and four other city landfills. It was the fourth settlement reached under that suit.<ref>{{cite news |title=Update |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1992/08/02/nyregion/update.html |access-date=September 14, 2018 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=August 2, 1992}}</ref>

Capping of the Edgemere Landfill began in September 1995, which would permanently seal the site.<ref name="NYSDEC-Edgemere-Search"/><ref name="NYDaily-Hallelujahs-Nov1997"/> The landfill was covered with a 6-inch base of topsoil, an impermeable [[geomembrane]] used to contain gasses emitted from the landfill, a layer of clay, and a second layer of topsoil. The uppermost layer of soil contained [[Spartina]] grass.<ref name="NYDaily-Hallelujahs-Nov1997"/><ref name="DSNY-2000Report"/> The landfill was graded with a 4 percent slope to allow optimal storm runoff.<ref name="NYDaily-Hallelujahs-Nov1997"/> {{convert|700,000|yd3}} of topsoil for the capping project were brought to the site by barges, as officials from Queens Community Board 14 requested the use of the barges instead of trucks.<ref name="NYDaily-Hallelujahs-Nov1997"/><ref name="Freshkills-NYCLandfillsPastPresent"/> A pier was constructed in the Sommerville Basin to accept the topsoil; this was later converted into the fishing piers.<ref name="DSNY-2000Report" /><ref name="NYDaily-Hallelujahs-Nov1997"/> Rock-covered channels were created circumscribing the landfill to prevent erosion.<ref name="NYDaily-Hallelujahs-Nov1997"/> A gas extraction and [[gas flare|flaring]] system was constructed in order to collect the gas emitted from the landfill, which would then be used as fuel or sold.<ref name="NYDaily-Hallelujahs-Nov1997"/><ref name="DSNY-2000Report">{{cite web |title=D.S.N.Y. Annual Report 2000 |url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/dsny/docs/about_2000_Annual_Report_0915.pdf |publisher=[[New York City Department of Sanitation]] |access-date=July 28, 2018 |page=15 |date=2000}}</ref> The flaring system was used to control odor, the first such system for a landfill in the city.<ref name="Freshkills-NYCLandfillsPastPresent">{{cite web |title=New York City Landfills Past and Present |url=http://freshkillspark.org/wp-content/uploads/2011/12/marty-bellew-lecture-112911_lowrez.pdf |website=[[Freshkills Park|freshkillspark.org]] |access-date=November 19, 2015 |date=2011}}</ref> It had been estimated in 1991 that the methane produced by the landfill could provide heat for over 100,000 homes.<ref>{{cite news |title=LOOKING BACKWARD: What The Wave Said 20 Years Ago This Week |url=https://www.rockawave.com/articles/looking-backward-what-the-wave-said-20-years-ago-this-week-39/ |access-date=July 28, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |date=July 7, 2001}}</ref> In the neck area of the site where the drums were discovered, a groundwater [[Environmental remediation#Pump and treat|"pump and treat"]] well system was installed to decontaminate the area.<ref name="DSNY-2010Report"/><ref name="NYSDEC-Edgemere-Search"/> The capping project was completed in 1997 at the cost of $40 million. Afterwards, a 15-year monitoring period began to regulate the gasses emitted by the landfill.<ref name="DSNY-2010Report"/><ref name="NYDaily-Hallelujahs-Nov1997"/>

===2000s===
By March 2000, the NYSDEC declassified the landfill as a Class 2 Site ("significant threat to the public health or environment") and reclassified it as a Class 4 site ("site properly closed-requires continued management"). It was expected at this time that the site would need 10 to 15 years of monitoring and management to fully close the site.<ref name="DSNY-2000Report"/> The landfill was declared "cleaned of all toxins" by the DEC in 2003. At the time it was one of two Superfund Sites in the Rockaways, along with a former [[Long Island Lighting Company]] [[coal gasification]] plant at Beach 108th Street in [[Rockaway Park, Queens|Rockaway Park]].<ref name="NYC-BrownfieldEdgemere-Ap2016"/>{{rp|50}}<ref>{{cite news |last1=Lander |first1=Mara |title=Report on Superfund Sites Raises Health Issues |url=https://www.rockawave.com/articles/report-on-superfund-sites-raises-health-issues/ |access-date=July 28, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |date=June 27, 2003 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140818065748/http://www.rockawave.com/news/2003-06-27/Community/051.html |archive-date=August 18, 2014 |url-status=live}}</ref>

In May 2007, the Parks Department designated Rockaway Community Park, Bayswater Park, and Beach Channel West park in [[Belle Harbor, Queens|Belle Harbor]] as parks with off-leash areas for dogs.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Rosenberg |first1=Miriam |title=Dogs Bark For Joy As Parks Announces Off-Leash Rules |url=https://www.rockawave.com/articles/dogs-bark-for-joy-as-parks-announces-off-leash-rules/ |access-date=September 13, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |date=May 18, 2007}}</ref> In 2009, Queens Community Board 14 district manager Jonathan Gaska proposed using the Edgemere Landfill as a [[solar panel]] field. The proposal was suggested to the [[Long Island Power Authority]] (LIPA), which provides electricity to the Rockaways. It was supported by New York State Assemblywoman [[Audrey Pheffer]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Rosenberg |first1=Noah |title=Proposal to use Rockaway landfill for solar power |url=https://qns.com/story/2009/06/10/proposal-to-use-rockaway-landfill-for-solar-power/ |access-date=July 31, 2018 |work=Queens Courier |date=June 10, 2009}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Brosh |first1=Brendan |title=Will Landfill Light up Lives? Proposal would put solar panel field near JFK in Rockaways |url=http://www.nydailynews.com/new-york/queens/landfill-light-lives-proposal-put-solar-panel-field-jfk-rockaways-article-1.374735 |access-date=July 31, 2018 |work=[[New York Daily News]] |date=June 1, 2009}}</ref>

On October 19, 2013, twenty thousand trees and five thousand shrubs were planted at Rockaway Community Park by volunteers as part of the Park's Department's MillionTreesNYC program, the largest planting event in the program's history. The trees would act as a buffer for a future storm, and were planted in response to [[Hurricane Sandy]] in 2012. The project was supported by the NY/NJ Super Bowl Host Committee for [[Super Bowl XLVIII]], which was to be played in February 2014, along with the [[National Football League]] themselves and [[Verizon]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=McFadden |first1=Katie |title=Tree Mendous: 20 Thousand Trees To Take Root |url=https://www.rockawave.com/articles/tree-mendous/ |access-date=July 31, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |date=October 18, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Trees Please |url=https://www.rockawave.com/articles/trees-please-2/ |access-date=July 31, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |date=October 25, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=NYC Parks Joins NY/NJ Super Bowl Host Committee And NFL To Plant 20,000 Trees Rockaways |url=http://m.qgazette.com/news/2013-10-23/Front_Page/NYC_Parks_Joins_NYNJ_Super_Bowl_Host_Committee_And.html#.W4c30egzqUk |access-date=August 30, 2018 |work=Queens Gazette |date=October 23, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181014130116/http://m.qgazette.com/news/2013-10-23/Front_Page/NYC_Parks_Joins_NYNJ_Super_Bowl_Host_Committee_And.html#.W4c30egzqUk |archive-date=October 14, 2018 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The project replaced invasive species with trees native to coastal environments.<ref name="RkwyPksConceptual-Final"/>{{rp|32}} In 2016, interns with the Rockaway Waterfront Alliance discovered a population of [[diamondback terrapin]] turtles in the former landfill.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Asimov |first1=Judah |title=A Summer with Environmentor |url=https://www.rockawave.com/articles/a-summer-with-environmentor/ |access-date=July 28, 2018 |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |date=September 2, 2016}}</ref>

===Rockaway Parks Conceptual Plan===
<!-- and future development-->
{{multiple image
 | align            = right
 | direction        = horizontal
 | background color = 
 | width            = 200
 | image1           = Rockaway Community Pk td 15.jpg
 | caption1         = 
 | alt1             = Baseball field
 | image2           = Rockaway Community Pk td (2018-12-13) 39 - Tennis Courts.jpg<!--Rockaway Community Pk td 16.jpg-->
 | caption2         = 
 | alt2             = Tennis courts
 | image3           = Rockaway Community Pk td 19.jpg
 | caption3         = 
 | alt3             = Entrance court
 | width2           = <!-- displayed width of image; overridden by "width" above -->
 | footer_align     = left
 | footer           = Empty recreational facilities within Rockaway Community Park. The park is underutilized due to the presence of mosquitoes.

In May 2014, the New York City Department of Parks and Recreation released the Rockaway Parks Conceptual Plan, which proposed several upgrades to parks on and around the peninsula following Hurricane Sandy in 2012. The plan included a major renovation of Rockaway Community Park.<ref name="RkwyPksConceptual-Final"/>{{rp|32}}<ref name="RkwyPksConceptual-Board-Mar2014"/><ref name="RkwyPksConceptual-Summary-2014">{{cite web |title=Rockaway Parks Conceptual Plan Executive Summary: Spring 2014 |url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/pagefiles/71/Conceptual-Plan-Summary_3.pdf |publisher=[[New York City Department of Parks and Recreation]] |access-date=August 12, 2018 |date=2014}}</ref><ref name="NYCPk-RkwyResiliency-Dec2016"/> The existing recreational facilities along Almeda Avenue would be upgraded, with a "Gaming Area" featuring [[ping pong]] and [[shuffleboard]] to be added. The Gaming Area would replace the existing handball courts in the center of the park, while new handball courts would be erected on the adjacent small playground. Additional handball courts would be erected on a portion of the current tennis courts at the far east end of the park. The open grass areas at the far south end of the park would be converted into picnic and barbecuing areas.<ref name="RkwyPksConceptual-Final"/>{{rp|32−34}}<ref name="RkwyPksConceptual-Board-Mar2014"/><ref name="RkwyPksConceptual-Summary-2014"/> The three natural areas on the outskirts of the park would be developed, with a continuous pathway to be established circumscribing the park. The portion of the pathway on the Sommerville Basin in the west natural area would be paved, and extend south to Beach Channel Drive to improve access to the park. North of Almeda Avenue, a wetland [[boardwalk]] would be created on the Sommerville Basin. An additional fishing pier would be built on the Sommerville Basin near Almeda Avenue, while a kayak launch point would be installed on the Conch Basin at the east end of the park. The wetlands and upland forest in this area would be restored.<ref name="RkwyPksConceptual-Final"/>{{rp|32−34}}<ref name="RkwyPksConceptual-Board-Mar2014"/><ref name="RkwyPksConceptual-Summary-2014"/> The triangular east natural area would be developed into a [[skatepark]], with an additional picnic area to be established.<ref name="RkwyPksConceptual-Final"/>{{rp|32−34}}<ref name="RkwyPksConceptual-Board-Mar2014"/><ref name="RkwyPksConceptual-Summary-2014"/> In addition, the Conch Playground would be developed as part of Rockaway Community Park. An artificial turf field would be constructed, while the existing playground would be renovated.<ref name="RkwyPksConceptual-Final"/>{{rp|32−34}}<ref name="RkwyPksConceptual-Board-Mar2014"/><ref name="RkwyPksConceptual-Summary-2014"/> Numerous additional mosquito magnets would be installed around the park.<ref name="RkwyPksConceptual-Final"/>{{rp|32−34}}<ref name="RkwyPksConceptual-Board-Mar2014"/>

As part of the Conceptual Plan, a Bayside Nature Trail would be established through the Rockaway Peninsula, running east along the Jamaica Bay Shore from the Rockaway Freeway Dog Run underneath [[Hammels Wye]] at Beach 84th Street, to the [[Jamaica Bay Park]] in Far Rockaway at the Queens-Nassau County border. The trail would cross Rockaway Community Park via the new pathways on the west and east ends of the park, and the existing pathway in the northern natural area, with a second pathway to be established parallel to Almeda Avenue.<ref name="RkwyPksConceptual-Final"/>{{rp|17−19, 32−34}}<ref name="RkwyPksConceptual-Board-Mar2014"/><ref name="RkwyPksConceptual-Summary-2014"/>

In December 2014, the [[Regional Plan Association]] proposed a Jamaica Bay Water Trail around Jamaica Bay, expanding the existing [[water trail]] network within the city.<ref name="RPA-JamaicaBayTrail-Dec2014">{{cite web |title=Paddling The Bay: Advancing the Jamaica Bay Water Trail |url=http://library.rpa.org/pdf/RPA-NPS-Jamaica-Bay-Water-Trail-Report.pdf |publisher=[[Regional Plan Association]] |access-date=August 25, 2018 |date=December 2014 |archive-date=September 8, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150908135602/http://library.rpa.org/pdf/RPA-NPS-Jamaica-Bay-Water-Trail-Report.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Licata |first1=Salvatore |title=New water trails may come to Jamaica Bay |url=https://qns.com/story/2015/03/18/new-water-trails-may-come-to-jamaica-bay/ |access-date=August 25, 2018 |work=Queens Courier |date=March 18, 2015}}</ref> Rockaway Community Park would be part of the Rockaway Bayside Trail, running along the northern Jamaica Bay shore of the Rockaway Peninsula from Breezy Point east to [[North Woodmere, New York|North Woodmere Park]] and Idlewild Park across from JFK Airport. A primary launch point and kayak rental site for the trail would be located at the base of the park in the Conch Basin, with additional access points at Marina 59 in the Sommerville Basin to the west, and at Bayswater Park in the Norton Basin to the east. Both Marina 59 and Bayswater Park are preexisting access points.<ref name="RPA-JamaicaBayTrail-Dec2014"/>{{rp|11−15, 19}}

On April 25, 2016 during a meeting of [[Queens Community Board 14]], [[Anbaric Development Partners]] proposed to create a [[microgrid]] and cable electrical system, with an underwater [[high-voltage direct current]] cable running from New Jersey to Long Island. The microgrid system would involve installing solar panels on the Edgemere Landfill, at the parking lot of [[Jacob Riis Park]] in western Rockaway, and at [[Green Acres Mall]] in [[South Valley Stream, New York|South Valley Stream, Nassau County]]. The solar panels would then feed into the cable system.<ref>{{cite news |last1=McFadden |first1=Katie |title=CB 14 Economic Committee Recap. Boardwalk Vendors, Downtown Far Rock & Microgrids |url=http://rockawaytimes.com/index.php/columns/812-cb-14-economic-committee-recap-boardwalk-vendors-downtown-far-rock-microgrids |access-date=September 7, 2018 |work=Rockaway Times |date=April 28, 2016 |archive-date=October 14, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181014112952/http://rockawaytimes.com/index.php/columns/812-cb-14-economic-committee-recap-boardwalk-vendors-downtown-far-rock-microgrids |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Economic Development Committee Meeting: April 25, 2016 |url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/queenscb14/pdf/minutes/april_25_16.pdf |website=[[Government of New York City|nyc.gov]] |publisher=[[Queens Community Board 14]] |access-date=September 7, 2018 |date=April 25, 2016}}</ref>

On October 29, 2017, Mayor [[Bill de Blasio]] announced $145 million in resiliency projects in the Rockaways following Hurricane Sandy, building upon the Rockaway Parks Conceptual Plan and the Resilient Edgemere Community Plan. The plan proposes to raise the shoreline or [[berm]] around the Edgemere Landfill and restore the native wetland plants around the landfill to act as a barrier against [[storm surge]]. The funding for the various projects would come from surplus [[FEMA]] funds from previous resiliency projects.<ref name="NYCPk-RkwyResiliency-Dec2016">{{cite web |title=Rockaway Resiliency Projects & FEMA Funding; PS/MS 42 Robert Vernam School; |url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/pagefiles/110/Rockaway-Resiliency-Projects__5854562518868.pdf#page=15 |publisher=[[New York City Department of Parks and Recreation]], New York City Office of Recovery & Resiliency |access-date=August 30, 2018 |date=December 12, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Mayor Announces Major Investments to Protect the Rockaways from Future Storms: $145 million in new and upgraded parks and facilities will help protect the Rockaways from coastal storms and flooding |url=https://www1.nyc.gov/office-of-the-mayor/news/694-17/mayor-major-investments-protect-rockaways-future-storms#/0 |access-date=August 30, 2018 |work=[[Government of New York City]] |date=October 29, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Toussaint |first1=Kristin |title=City to invest $145 million to protect the Rockaways from future storms: Mayor Bill de Blasio announced the resilience plans on the fifth anniversary of Hurricane Sandy. |url=https://www.metro.us/news/local-news/new-york/145-million-investment-protect-the-rockaways-future-storms |access-date=August 30, 2018 |work=[[Metro New York]] |date=October 30, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Mancini |first1=Ralph |title=Better Late Than Never: Mayor announces funding for Rockaway park projects at Arverne Y |url=https://www.rockawave.com/articles/better-late-than-never-2/ |work=[[Wave of Long Island]] |date=November 2, 2017}}</ref>
