======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Marine pollution
======================================================================

{{short description|Harmful effects to oceans caused by discarded substances or emitted energy}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=August 2026}}

[[File:Obvious water pollution.jpeg|thumb|While marine pollution can be obvious, as with the [[marine debris]] shown above, it is often the pollutants that cannot be seen that cause most harm.]]
'''Marine pollution''' occurs when substances used or spread by humans, such as [[industrial waste|industrial]], [[agricultural pollution|agricultural]], and [[municipal solid waste|residential]] [[waste]]; [[particle (ecology)|particles]]; [[noise]] or light; excess [[carbon dioxide]]; or [[invasive organism]]s enter the [[ocean]] and cause harmful effects there. The majority of this waste (80%) comes from land-based activity, although [[Marine Transportation|marine transportation]] significantly contributes as well.<ref name=":03">{{Cite book|title=World seas: an Environmental Evaluation|date=2019|isbn=978-0-12-805204-4|editor-first=Charles|editor-last=Sheppard|edition=Second|volume=III, Ecological Issues and Environmental Impacts|location=London |publisher=Academic Press |oclc=1052566532}}</ref> It is a combination of chemicals and trash, most of which comes from land sources and is washed or blown into the ocean. This pollution results in damage to the [[Natural environment|environment]], to the health of all organisms, and to economic structures worldwide.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Marine Pollution |url=https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/marine-pollution/ |access-date=2023-06-19 |publisher=Education {{!}} National Geographic Society |language=en}}</ref> Since most inputs come from land, via rivers, [[sewage]], or the [[atmosphere]], it means that [[Continental shelf|continental shelves]] are more vulnerable to pollution. [[Air pollution]] is also a contributing factor, as it carries iron, carbonic acid, [[nitrogen]], silicon, sulfur, [[pesticides]], and dust particles into the ocean.<ref>{{Cite journal |author=Duce, Robert |author2=Galloway, J. |author3=Liss, P. |date=2009|title=The Impacts of Atmospheric Deposition to the Ocean on Marine Ecosystems and Climate |journal=WMO Bulletin |volume=58 |issue=1 |publisher=World Meteorological Organization |url=https://public-old.wmo.int/en/bulletin/impacts-atmospheric-deposition-ocean-marine-ecosystems-and-climate|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231218175210/https://public-old.wmo.int/en/bulletin/impacts-atmospheric-deposition-ocean-marine-ecosystems-and-climate|archive-date=18 December 2023|access-date=22 September 2020}}</ref> The pollution often comes from [[nonpoint source pollution|nonpoint source]]s such as agricultural [[surface runoff|runoff]], wind-blown [[debris]], and dust. These nonpoint sources are largely due to runoff that enters the ocean through rivers, but wind-blown debris and dust can also play a role, as these pollutants can settle into waterways and oceans.<ref>{{cite web |title=What is the biggest source of pollution in the ocean? |url=https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/pollution.html |access-date=2022-09-21 |website=National Ocean Service (US) |publisher=National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration |location=Silver Spring, MD}}</ref> Pathways of pollution include direct discharge, land runoff, [[Environmental effects of shipping|ship pollution]], [[bilge pollution]], [[dredging]] (which can create [[dredge plume]]s), atmospheric pollution and, potentially, [[deep sea mining]].

Different types of marine pollution can be grouped as pollution from [[marine debris]], [[Plastic soup|plastic pollution]], including [[microplastics]], [[ocean acidification]], [[nutrient pollution]], toxins, and underwater noise. Plastic pollution in the ocean is a type of marine pollution by [[Plastic pollution|plastics]], ranging in size from large original materials such as bottles and bags, down to [[microplastics]] formed from the fragmentation of plastic materials. Marine debris is mainly discarded human rubbish that floats on or is suspended in the ocean. Plastic pollution is harmful to [[marine life]].

Another concern is the runoff of [[nutrient]]s (nitrogen and phosphorus) from [[Intensive farming|intensive agriculture]], and the disposal of untreated or partially treated [[sewage]] to rivers and subsequently oceans. These [[nitrogen]] and [[phosphorus]] nutrients (which are also contained in [[fertilizer]]s) stimulate [[phytoplankton]] and [[macroalgal]] growth, which can lead to harmful [[algal bloom]]s ([[eutrophication]]) that can be harmful to humans as well as marine creatures. Excessive algal growth can also smother sensitive [[coral reef]]s and lead to [[Biodiversity loss|loss of biodiversity]] and coral health. A second major concern is that the degradation of [[algal bloom]]s can lead to consumption of [[oxygen]] in coastal waters, a situation that may worsen with [[climate change]] as warming reduces vertical mixing of the water column.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1=Breitburg|first1=Denise|last2=Levin|first2=Lisa A.|last3=Oschlies|first3=Andreas|last4=Grégoire|first4=Marilaure|last5=Chavez|first5=Francisco P.|last6=Conley|first6=Daniel J.|last7=Garçon|first7=Véronique|last8=Gilbert|first8=Denis|last9=Gutiérrez|first9=Dimitri|last10=Isensee|first10=Kirsten|last11=Jacinto|first11=Gil S.|date=2018-01-05|title=Declining oxygen in the global ocean and coastal waters|journal=Science|language=en|volume=359|issue=6371|article-number=eaam7240|doi=10.1126/science.aam7240|pmid=29301986|bibcode=2018Sci...359M7240B|issn=0036-8075|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Many potentially toxic chemicals adhere to tiny particles which are then taken up by [[plankton]] and [[benthos|benthic animals]], most of which are either [[deposit feeder]]s or [[filter feeder]]s. In this way, the toxins are [[biomagnification|concentrated upward]] within ocean [[food chain]]s. When pesticides are incorporated into the [[marine ecosystem]], they quickly become absorbed into marine [[food web]]s. Once in the food webs, these pesticides can cause [[mutation]]s, as well as diseases, which can be harmful to humans as well as the entire food web. [[Toxic metal]]s can also be introduced into marine food webs. These can cause changes to tissue matter, biochemistry, behavior, reproduction, and suppress growth in marine life. Also, many [[compound feed|animal feeds]] have a high [[fish meal]] or [[fish hydrolysate]] content. In this way, [[Toxin|marine toxins]] can be transferred to land animals and appear later in meat and dairy products.

==Pathways of pollution==
{{Pollution sidebar|Water}}
{{See also|Water pollution}}There are many ways to categorize and examine the inputs of pollution into marine ecosystems. There are three main types of inputs of pollution into the ocean: direct discharge of waste into the oceans, runoff into the waters due to rain, and pollutants released from the atmosphere.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.offshore-environment.com/anthropogenicimpact.html |title=Anthropogenic impact in the sea and marine pollution |last=Patin, S.A. |website=offshore-environment.com |access-date=1 February 2018}}</ref>

One common path of entry by [[contaminant]]s to the sea are rivers. The evaporation of water from oceans exceeds precipitation. The balance is restored by rain over the continents entering rivers and then being returned to the sea. The [[Hudson River]] in [[New York State]] and the [[Raritan River]] in [[New Jersey]], which empty at the northern and southern ends of [[Staten Island]], are a source of [[mercury (element)|mercury]] contamination of [[zooplankton]] ([[copepod]]s) in the open ocean. The highest concentration in the filter-feeding [[copepod]]s is not at the mouths of these rivers but {{convert|70|mi|km}} south, nearer [[Atlantic City, New Jersey|Atlantic City]], because water flows close to the coast. It takes a few days before toxins are taken up by the [[plankton]].<ref name=Gerlach/> Ohio River and Tennessee River both join Mississippi River ultimately drains organic contaminants from several northern states into the Gulf of Mexico.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1016/j.marpolbul.2024.116833 | title=Assessment of toxicity potential of freely dissolved PAHs using passive sampler in Kentucky Lake and Ohio River | date=2024 | last1=Kim | first1=Na Yeong | last2=Loganathan | first2=Bommanna G. | last3=Kim | first3=Gi Beum | journal=Marine Pollution Bulletin | volume=207 | article-number=116833 | pmid=39159572 | bibcode=2024MarPB.20716833K }}</ref>

Pollution is often classed as [[point source]] or [[nonpoint source pollution]]. Point source pollution occurs when there is a single, identifiable, localized source of the pollution. An example is directly discharging sewage and industrial waste into the ocean. Pollution such as this occurs particularly in [[Developing country|developing nations]].{{citation needed|date=August 2021}} Nonpoint source pollution occurs when the pollution is from ill-defined and diffuse sources. These can be difficult to regulate. Agricultural [[surface runoff|runoff]] and wind blown [[debris]] are prime examples.

===Direct discharge===
[[File:Rio tinto river CarolStoker NASA Ames Research Center.jpg|thumb|[[Acid mine drainage]] in the Rio Tinto River]]
{{See also|Sewerage|Industrial waste|Environmental impact of mining}}

Pollutants enter rivers and the sea directly from urban [[sewerage]] and [[industrial waste]] discharges, sometimes in the form of [[hazardous waste|hazardous]] and [[toxic waste]]s, or in the form of plastics.{{citation needed|date=April 2023}}

In a study published by ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'', Jambeck ''et al.'' (2015) estimated that the 10 largest emitters of oceanic plastic pollution worldwide are, from the most to the least, China, Indonesia, Philippines, Vietnam, Sri Lanka, Thailand, Egypt, Malaysia, Nigeria, and Bangladesh.<ref name=Science2015>{{cite journal |last1=Jambeck |first1=J. R. |last2=Geyer |first2=R. |last3=Wilcox |first3=C. |last4=Siegler |first4=T. R. |last5=Perryman |first5=M. |last6=Andrady |first6=A. |last7=Narayan |first7=R. |last8=Law |first8=K. L. |title=Plastic waste inputs from land into the ocean |journal=Science |date=12 February 2015 |volume=347 |issue=6223 |pages=768–771 |doi=10.1126/science.1260352 |pmid=25678662 |bibcode=2015Sci...347..768J |s2cid=206562155 }}</ref>

Inland [[mining]] for copper, gold, etc., is another source of marine pollution. Most of the pollution is simply soil, which ends up in rivers flowing to the sea. However, some minerals discharged in the course of the mining can cause problems, such as [[copper]], a common industrial pollutant, which can interfere with the [[biological life cycle|life history]] and development of coral polyps.<ref>{{cite web |last=Young |first=Emma |title=Copper decimates coral reef spawning |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn4391-copper-decimates-coral-reef-spawning |date=2003-11-18 |publisher=New Scientist |location=London}}</ref> Mining has a poor environmental track record. For example, according to the [[United States Environmental Protection Agency]], mining has contaminated portions of the headwaters of over 40% of watersheds in the western continental US.<ref>{{cite web |title=Liquid Assets 2000: Americans Pay for Dirty Water |url=http://www.epa.gov/water/liquidassets/dirtywater.html |access-date=23 January 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080515191140/http://www.epa.gov/water/liquidassets/dirtywater.html |archive-date=15 May 2008 |publisher=U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)}}</ref> Much of this pollution ends up in the sea.{{citation needed|date=April 2023}}

===Land runoff===
{{Main|Surface runoff}}
{{See also|Urban runoff|Stormwater|Nutrient pollution}}
[[Surface runoff]] from farming, as well as [[urban runoff]] and runoff from the construction of roads, buildings, ports, channels, and harbours, can carry soil and [[particle (ecology)|particles]] laden with carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and minerals. This nutrient-rich water can cause fleshy algae and [[phytoplankton]] to thrive in coastal areas; known as [[algal bloom]]s, which have the potential to create [[hypoxia (environmental)|hypoxic]] conditions by using all available oxygen. In the coast of southwest Florida, harmful [[algal bloom]]s have existed for over 100 years.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |jstor=j.ctt5hj4c2.10 |date=2009|publisher=Rutgers University Press|isbn=978-0-8135-4548-6|editor-last=Weis|editor-first=Judith S.|series=A Natural and Unnatural History|pages=117–149|editor-last2=Butler|editor-first2=Carol A.|last1=Weis|first1=Judith S.|last2=Butler|first2=Carol A.|title=Salt Marshes|chapter=Pollution}}</ref> These algal blooms have been a cause of species of fish, turtles, dolphins, and shrimp to die and cause harmful effects on humans who swim in the water.<ref name=":0" />

Polluted runoff from roads and highways can be a significant source of water pollution in coastal areas. About 75% of the toxic chemicals that flow into [[Puget Sound]] are carried by [[stormwater]] that runs off paved roads and driveways, rooftops, yards and other developed land.<ref>{{cite web|publisher=Washington State Department of Ecology |title=Control of Toxic Chemicals in Puget Sound, Phase 2: Development of Simple Numerical Models |date=2008|url=http://www.ecy.wa.gov/Programs/wq/pstoxics/index.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170302010119/http://www.ecy.wa.gov/programs/wq/pstoxics/index.html|archive-date=2 March 2017}}</ref> In California, there are many rainstorms that runoff into the ocean. These rainstorms occur from October to March, and these runoff waters contain petroleum, heavy metals, pollutants from emissions, etc.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Holt |first1=Benjamin |last2=Trinh |first2=Rebecca |last3=Gierach |first3=Michelle M. |title=Stormwater runoff plumes in the Southern California Bight: A comparison study with SAR and MODIS imagery |journal=Marine Pollution Bulletin |date=May 2017 |volume=118 |issue=1–2 |pages=141–154 |doi=10.1016/j.marpolbul.2017.02.040 |pmid=28238485 |bibcode=2017MarPB.118..141H }}</ref>

In China, there is a large coastal population that pollutes the ocean through land runoff. This includes sewage discharge and pollution from [[urbanization]] and land use. In 2001, more than 66,795&nbsp;mi<sup>2</sup> of the Chinese coastal ocean waters were rated less than Class I of the Sea Water Quality Standard of China.<ref name=":02">{{Cite journal|last1=Daoji|first1=Li|last2=Daler|first2=Dag|date=2004|title=Ocean Pollution from Land-Based Sources: East China Sea, China|jstor=4315461|journal=Ambio|volume=33|issue=1/2|pages=107–113|doi=10.1579/0044-7447-33.1.107|pmid=15083656 |bibcode=2004Ambio..33..107D |s2cid=12289116}}</ref> Much of this pollution came from Ag, Cu, Cd, Pb, As, DDT, PCBs, etc., which occurred from contamination through land runoff.<ref name=":02" />

===Ship pollution===
{{Main|Environmental impact of shipping}}
{{See also|Ballast water discharge and the environment}}
[[File:Ship pumping ballast water.jpg|thumb|A cargo ship pumps ballast water over the side]]

Ships can pollute waterways and oceans in many ways including through their ballast, bilge, and fuel tanks. [[Oil spill]]s can have devastating effects. In addition to being toxic to marine life, [[polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon]]s (PAHs), found in [[crude oil]], are very difficult to clean up, and last for years in the [[sediment]] and marine environment.<ref name="Panetta">{{Cite book |author=Panetta, L.E. (Chair) |year=2003 |title=America's living oceans: charting a course for sea change |url=https://nauticalcharts.noaa.gov/hsrp/admin/nov2004/oceans_report.pdf |publisher=Pew Oceans Commission |page=64}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Van Landuyt |first1=Josefien |last2=Kundu |first2=Kankana |last3=Van Haelst |first3=Sven |last4=Neyts |first4=Marijke |last5=Parmentier |first5=Koen |last6=De Rijcke |first6=Maarten |last7=Boon |first7=Nico |date=2022-10-18 |title=80 years later: Marine sediments still influenced by an old war ship |journal=Frontiers in Marine Science |volume=9 |article-number=1017136 |doi=10.3389/fmars.2022.1017136 |issn=2296-7745|doi-access=free |bibcode=2022FrMaS...917136V |hdl=1854/LU-01GKS4PJA2JJ06GXN0FQHFMB4D |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Additionally, [[bilge pollution]] can be toxic to the surrounding environment when [[bilge water]] is released from a ship's [[bilge]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bilge dumping: Illegal pollution you've never heard of – DW – 04/28/2022 |url=https://www.dw.com/en/bilge-dumping-how-cargo-carriers-cut-corners-and-contaminate-the-oceans/audio-61622516 |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=dw.com |language=en}}</ref>

Oil spills are one of the most emotive of marine pollution events. However, while a tanker wreck may result in extensive newspaper headlines, much of the oil in the world's seas comes from other smaller sources, such as tankers discharging ballast water from oil tanks used on return ships, leaking pipelines or engine oil disposed of down sewers.<ref>{{cite book |author=Farmer, Andrew |year=1997 |title=Managing Environmental Pollution |publisher=Psychology Press |isbn=978-0-415-14515-2 }}{{page needed|date=January 2018}}</ref>

Discharge of cargo residues from [[bulk carrier]]s can pollute ports, waterways, and oceans. In many instances vessels intentionally discharge illegal wastes despite foreign and domestic regulation prohibiting such actions. An absence of national standards provides an incentive for some [[cruise liner]]s to dump waste in places where the penalties are inadequate.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Schulkin |first1=Andrew |title=Safe harbors: Crafting an international solution to cruise ship pollution |journal=Georgetown International Environmental Law Review |url=https://www.proquest.com/openview/408bf9d53e951415fbc9bbef80bfce9c/1 |volume=15 |issue=1 |year=2002 |pages=105–132 }}</ref> It has been estimated that [[container ship]]s lose over 10,000 [[containerization|containers]] at sea each year (usually during storms).<ref>{{cite web |url=http://news.nationalgeographic.com/news/2001/06/0619_seacargo.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010703073644/http://news.nationalgeographic.com/news/2001/06/0619_seacargo.html |archive-date=3 July 2001 |title=Lost Sea Cargo: Beach Bounty or Junk? |access-date=8 April 2008 |date=19 June 2001 |author=Podsadam, Janice |publisher=National Geographic News}}</ref> Ships also create [[noise pollution]] that disturbs natural wildlife, and water from [[sailing ballast|ballast]] tanks can spread harmful [[algae]] and other [[invasive species]].<ref name="Meinesz">Meinesz, A. (2003) [https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/nova/algae/impact.html Deep Sea Invasion: The Impact of Invasive Species] PBS: NOVA. Retrieved 26 November 2009</ref>

[[Ballast water]] taken up at sea and released in port is a major source of unwanted exotic marine life. The [[invasive species|invasive]] freshwater zebra mussels, native to the Black, Caspian, and Azov seas, were probably transported to the Great Lakes via ballast water from a transoceanic vessel.<ref>[http://www.wsg.washington.edu/mas/pdfs/leastwanted.pdf Aquatic invasive species. A Guide to Least-Wanted Aquatic Organisms of the Pacific Northwest] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080725040002/http://www.wsg.washington.edu/mas/pdfs/leastwanted.pdf |date=25 July 2008}}. 2001. University of Washington</ref> Meinesz believes that one of the worst cases of a single invasive species causing harm to an ecosystem can be attributed to a seemingly harmless [[jellyfish]]. ''[[Mnemiopsis leidyi]]'', a species of comb jellyfish that spread so it now inhabits estuaries in many parts of the world, was first introduced in 1982, and thought to have been transported to the [[Black Sea]] in a ship's ballast water. The population of the jellyfish grew exponentially and, by 1988, it was wreaking havoc upon the local [[fishing industry]]. "The [[anchovy]] catch fell from 204,000 tons in 1984 to 200 tons in 1993; [[sprat]] from 24,600 tons in 1984 to 12,000 tons in 1993; horse [[mackerel]] from 4,000 tons in 1984 to zero in 1993."<ref name="Meinesz"/> Now that the jellyfish have exhausted the [[zooplankton]], including fish larvae, their numbers have fallen dramatically, yet they continue to maintain a stranglehold on the [[ecosystem]].

[[Invasive species]] can take over once occupied areas, facilitate the spread of new diseases, introduce new [[genetics|genetic]] material, alter underwater seascapes, and jeopardize the ability of [[native species]] to obtain food. Invasive species are responsible for about $138&nbsp;billion annually in lost revenue and management costs in the US alone.<ref name=pimental>{{cite journal |last1=Pimentel |first1=David |last2=Zuniga |first2=Rodolfo |last3=Morrison |first3=Doug |title=Update on the environmental and economic costs associated with alien-invasive species in the United States |journal=Ecological Economics |date=February 2005 |volume=52 |issue=3 |pages=273–288 |doi=10.1016/j.ecolecon.2004.10.002 |bibcode=2005EcoEc..52..273P }}</ref>

===Atmospheric pollution===
[[File:Barbadosdustgraph.gif|thumb|upright=1.75|A graph linking atmospheric dust to various coral deaths across the [[Caribbean Sea]] and [[Florida]].<ref>[https://coastal.er.usgs.gov/african_dust/barbados.html Coral Mortality and African Dust: Barbados Dust Record: 1965–1996] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090806184410/http://coastal.er.usgs.gov/african_dust/barbados.html |date=6 August 2009 }} [[US Geological Survey]]. Retrieved 10 December 2009</ref>]]

Another pathway of pollution occurs through the atmosphere. The ocean has long been affected by the passage of chemicals from the atmosphere (e.g. nutrient source; pH influence).<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-11-12 |title=The Impacts of Atmospheric Deposition to the Ocean on Marine Ecosystems and Climate |url=https://public-old.wmo.int/en/bulletin/impacts-atmospheric-deposition-ocean-marine-ecosystems-and-climate |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231218175210/https://public-old.wmo.int/en/bulletin/impacts-atmospheric-deposition-ocean-marine-ecosystems-and-climate |archive-date=18 December 2023 |access-date=2022-08-11 |website=public.wmo.int |language=en}}</ref> Wind-blown dust and debris, including [[plastic bag]]s, are blown seaward from [[landfill]]s and other areas. Dust from the [[Sahara]] moving around the southern periphery of the [[subtropical ridge]] moves into the Caribbean and [[Florida]] during the warm season as the ridge builds and moves northward through the subtropical Atlantic. Dust can also be attributed to a global transport from the [[Gobi]] and [[Taklamakan]] deserts across [[Korea]], Japan, and the Northern [[Pacific]] to the [[Hawaiian Islands]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Duce |first1=RA |last2=Unni |first2=CK |last3=Ray |first3=BJ |last4=Prospero |first4=JM |last5=Merrill |first5=JT |title=Long-Range Atmospheric Transport of Soil Dust from Asia to the Tropical North Pacific: Temporal Variability |journal=Science |date=26 September 1980 |volume=209 |issue=4464 |pages=1522–1524 |doi=10.1126/science.209.4464.1522 |pmid=17745962 |s2cid=30337924 |bibcode=1980Sci...209.1522D |s2cid-access=free }}</ref>

Since 1970, dust outbreaks have worsened due to periods of drought in Africa. There is a large variability in dust transport to the Caribbean and Florida from year to year;<ref>Usinfo.state.gov. [http://www.gcrio.org/OnLnDoc/pdf/african_dust.pdf Study Says African Dust Affects Climate in U.S., Caribbean.] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070620013708/http://www.gcrio.org/OnLnDoc/pdf/african_dust.pdf |date=20 June 2007}}. Retrieved 10 June 2007</ref> however, the flux is greater during positive phases of the [[North Atlantic Oscillation]].<ref>{{cite journal |doi= 10.1038/320735a0 |title= Impact of the North African drought and El Niño on mineral dust in the Barbados trade winds |journal= Nature |volume= 320 |issue= 6064 |pages= 735–738 |year= 1986 |last1= Prospero |first1= J. M. |last2= Nees |first2= R. T. |bibcode= 1986Natur.320..735P|s2cid= 33094175 }}</ref> The USGS links dust events to a decline in the health of coral reefs across the Caribbean and Florida, primarily since the 1970s.<ref>[[U. S. Geological Survey]]. [https://coastal.er.usgs.gov/african_dust/ Coral Mortality and African Dust.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120502091350/http://coastal.er.usgs.gov/african_dust/ |date=2 May 2012 }}. Retrieved 10 June 2007</ref>

[[Effects of global warming on oceans|Climate change is raising ocean temperatures]]<ref>[http://www.ipcc.ch/pdf/assessment-report/ar4/wg1/ar4-wg1-chapter5.pdf Observations: Oceanic Climate Change and Sea Level] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170513164252/http://www.ipcc.ch/pdf/assessment-report/ar4/wg1/ar4-wg1-chapter5.pdf |date=13 May 2017 }} In: ''Climate Change 2007: The Physical Science Basis''. Contribution of Working Group I to the Fourth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. (15MB)</ref> and raising levels of [[carbon dioxide in Earth's atmosphere|carbon dioxide in the atmosphere]]. These rising levels of carbon dioxide are [[ocean acidification|acidifying the oceans]].<ref>Doney, S. C. (2006) "[http://www.precaution.org/lib/06/ocean_acidification_from_c02_060301.pdf The Dangers of Ocean Acidification] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304042304/http://www.precaution.org/lib/06/ocean_acidification_from_c02_060301.pdf |date=4 March 2016 }}" ''Scientific American'', March 2006</ref> This, in turn, is altering [[aquatic ecosystem]]s and modifying fish distributions,<ref>Cheung, W.W.L., et al. (2009) "[http://www.seaaroundus.org/ClimateChange/images/Pew%20OSS%20Final%20climate%20change%20and%20fisheries.pdf Redistribution of Fish Catch by Climate Change. A Summary of a New Scientific Analysis] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110726113553/http://www.seaaroundus.org/ClimateChange/images/Pew%20OSS%20Final%20climate%20change%20and%20fisheries.pdf |date=26 July 2011}}" Pew Ocean Science Series</ref> with impacts on the [[sustainability of fisheries]] and the livelihoods of the communities that depend on them. Healthy ocean ecosystems are also important for the mitigation of climate change.<ref>[http://www.climatefish.org/index_en.htm PACFA] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091215221120/http://www.climatefish.org/index_en.htm |date=15 December 2009 }} (2009) [http://www.fao.org/climatechange/17789-1-0.pdf Fisheries and Aquaculture in a Changing Climate]</ref>

===Deep sea mining===
{{excerpt|Deep sea mining#Environmental impacts|paragraphs=1|file=no}}Some of the potential toxic metals include copper, zinc, cadmium, lead as well as rare earth elements such as [[lanthanum]] and [[yttrium]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hauton |first1=Chris |last2=Brown |first2=Alastair |last3=Thatje |first3=Sven |last4=Mestre |first4=Nélia C. |last5=Bebianno |first5=Maria J. |last6=Martins |first6=Inês |last7=Bettencourt |first7=Raul |last8=Canals |first8=Miquel |last9=Sanchez-Vidal |first9=Anna |last10=Shillito |first10=Bruce |last11=Ravaux |first11=Juliette |date=2017-11-16 |title=Identifying Toxic Impacts of Metals Potentially Released during Deep-Sea Mining—A Synthesis of the Challenges to Quantifying Risk |journal=Frontiers in Marine Science |volume=4 |article-number=368 |doi=10.3389/fmars.2017.00368 |issn=2296-7745|doi-access=free |bibcode=2017FrMaS...4..368H |hdl=2445/138040 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Following the release of toxins there is an increase of noise, light, sediment le dan plumes and elements that have the potential to impact the [[ecosystem]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lopes |first1=Carina L. |last2=Bastos |first2=Luísa |last3=Caetano |first3=Miguel |last4=Martins |first4=Irene |last5=Santos |first5=Miguel M. |last6=Iglesias |first6=Isabel |date=2019-02-10 |title=Development of physical modelling tools in support of risk scenarios: A new framework focused on deep-sea mining |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S004896971833852X |journal=Science of the Total Environment |language=en |volume=650 |issue=Pt 2 |pages=2294–2306 |doi=10.1016/j.scitotenv.2018.09.351 |pmid=30292122 |bibcode=2019ScTEn.650.2294L |s2cid=52945921 |issn=0048-9697|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Deep sea minerals (DSM) can be extremely beneficial, it can cause wealth, raising living standards as well as economic opportunities for both current and future generations.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Ovesen |first1=Vidar |last2=Hackett |first2=Ron |last3=Burns |first3=Lee |last4=Mullins |first4=Peter |last5=Roger |first5=Scott |date=2018-09-01 |title=Managing deep sea mining revenues for the public good – ensuring transparency and distribution equity |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0308597X17301264 |journal=Marine Policy |language=en |volume=95 |pages=332–336 |doi=10.1016/j.marpol.2017.02.010 |bibcode=2018MarPo..95..332O |s2cid=111380724 |issn=0308-597X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In addition, if the wealth is poorly managed it can have the potential to cause great economic and social damage. The instability of price and production levels of minerals can cause an external [[Shock (economics)|economic shock]] leading to a significant backlash on the [[domestic economy]].<ref name=":1" />

===Nutrient pollution===
{{Main|Eutrophication}}
{{See also|Nutrient pollution}}
[[File:Aguas del lago de Maracaibo contaminadas por Lemna 03.JPG|thumb|right|A polluted lagoon]]
[[File:Scheme eutrophication-en.svg|thumb|The effect of eutrophication on marine [[benthos|benthic life]]]]

[[Eutrophication]] is an increase in chemical [[nutrient]]s, typically compounds containing [[nitrogen]] or [[phosphorus]], in an [[ecosystem]]. It can result in an increase in the ecosystem's [[primary productivity]] (excessive plant growth and decay), and further effects including lack of oxygen and severe reductions in water quality, fish, and other animal populations. [[Nutrient pollution]], a form of [[water pollution]], refers to contamination by excessive inputs of nutrients. It is a primary cause of eutrophication of surface waters, in which excess nutrients, usually [[nitrate]]s or [[phosphate]]s, stimulate algae growth. Such blooms are naturally occurring but may be increasing as a result of anthropogenic inputs or alternatively may be something that is now more closely monitored and so more frequently reported.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hallegraeff|first1=Gustaaf M.|last2=Anderson|first2=Donald M.|last3=Belin|first3=Catherine|last4=Bottein|first4=Marie-Yasmine Dechraoui|last5=Bresnan|first5=Eileen|last6=Chinain|first6=Mireille|last7=Enevoldsen|first7=Henrik|last8=Iwataki|first8=Mitsunori|last9=Karlson|first9=Bengt|last10=McKenzie|first10=Cynthia H.|last11=Sunesen|first11=Inés|date=2021|title=Perceived global increase in algal blooms is attributable to intensified monitoring and emerging bloom impacts|journal=Communications Earth & Environment|language=en|volume=2|issue=1|page=117|doi=10.1038/s43247-021-00178-8|pmid=37359131 |pmc=10289804 |bibcode=2021ComEE...2..117H|issn=2662-4435|s2cid=235364600|doi-access=free}}</ref>

The biggest culprit are rivers that empty into the ocean, and with it the many chemicals used as [[fertilizer]]s in agriculture as well as waste from [[livestock]] and [[human]]s. An excess of oxygen-depleting chemicals in the water can lead to [[hypoxia (environmental)|hypoxia]] and the creation of a [[dead zone (ecology)|dead zone]].<ref name=Gerlach>Gerlach, S. A. (1975) ''Marine Pollution'', Springer, Berlin</ref>

[[Estuary|Estuaries]] tend to be naturally eutrophic because land-derived nutrients are concentrated where [[surface runoff|runoff]] enters the marine environment in a confined channel. The [[World Resources Institute]] has identified 375 hypoxic coastal zones around the world, concentrated in coastal areas in Western Europe, the Eastern and Southern coasts of the US, and East Asia, particularly in Japan.<ref>
Selman, Mindy (2007) ''Eutrophication: An Overview of Status, Trends, Policies, and Strategies.'' World Resources Institute</ref> In the ocean, there are frequent [[red tide]] algae blooms<ref>{{cite web
|url=http://www.tulane.edu/~bfleury/envirobio/enviroweb/DeadZone.htm
|title=The Gulf of Mexico Dead Zone and Red Tides
|access-date=27 December 2006
|archive-date=7 May 2015
|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150507132040/http://www.tulane.edu/~bfleury/envirobio/enviroweb/DeadZone.htm
|url-status=dead
}}</ref> that kill fish and marine mammals and cause respiratory problems in humans and some domestic animals when the blooms reach close to shore.

In addition to [[land runoff]], atmospheric [[human impact on the environment|anthropogenic]] [[nitrogen fixation|fixed nitrogen]] can enter the open ocean. A study in 2008 found that this could account for around one third of the ocean's external (non-recycled) nitrogen supply and up to three per cent of the annual new marine biological production.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Duce |first1=R. A. |last2=LaRoche |first2=J. |last3=Altieri |first3=K. |last4=Arrigo |first4=K. R. |last5=Baker |first5=A. R. |last6=Capone |first6=D. G. |last7=Cornell |first7=S. |last8=Dentener |first8=F. |last9=Galloway |first9=J. |last10=Ganeshram |first10=R. S. |last11=Geider |first11=R. J. |last12=Jickells |first12=T. |last13=Kuypers |first13=M. M. |last14=Langlois |first14=R. |last15=Liss |first15=P. S. |last16=Liu |first16=S. M. |last17=Middelburg |first17=J. J. |last18=Moore |first18=C. M. |last19=Nickovic |first19=S. |last20=Oschlies |first20=A. |last21=Pedersen |first21=T. |last22=Prospero |first22=J. |last23=Schlitzer |first23=R. |last24=Seitzinger |first24=S. |last25=Sorensen |first25=L. L. |last26=Uematsu |first26=M. |last27=Ulloa |first27=O. |last28=Voss |first28=M. |last29=Ward |first29=B. |last30=Zamora |first30=L. |title=Impacts of Atmospheric Anthropogenic Nitrogen on the Open Ocean |journal=Science |date=16 May 2008 |volume=320 |issue=5878 |pages=893–897 |doi=10.1126/science.1150369 |pmid=18487184 |s2cid=11204131 |bibcode=2008Sci...320..893D |s2cid-access=free |hdl=21.11116/0000-0001-CD7A-0 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> It has been suggested that accumulating reactive nitrogen in the environment may have consequences as serious as putting carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.<ref>[http://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2008-05/uov-at051208.php ''Addressing the nitrogen cascade''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160823023230/http://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2008-05/uov-at051208.php |date=23 August 2016 }} Eureka Alert, 2008</ref>

One proposed solution to eutrophication in estuaries is to restore shellfish populations, such as oysters. [[Oyster]] reefs remove nitrogen from the water column and filter out suspended solids, subsequently reducing the likelihood or extent of [[harmful algal bloom]]s or anoxic conditions.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Kroeger |first1=Timm |date=May 2012 |title=Dollars and Sense: Economic Benefits and Impacts from two Oyster Reef Restoration Projects in the Northern Gulf of Mexico |url=https://www.conservationgateway.org/Files/Pages/dollars-and-sense-economi.aspx |website=The Nature Conservancy }}</ref> Filter feeding activity is considered beneficial to water quality<ref>Burkholder, JoAnn M. and Shumway, Sandra E. (2011). "Bivalve shellfish aquaculture and eutrophication". In: ''Shellfish Aquaculture and the Environment''. Ed. Sandra E. Shumway. John Wiley & Sons</ref> by controlling phytoplankton density and sequestering nutrients, which can be removed from the system through shellfish harvest, buried in the sediments, or lost through [[denitrification]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kaspar |first1=H. F. |last2=Gillespie |first2=P. A. |last3=Boyer |first3=I. C. |last4=MacKenzie |first4=A. L. |title=Effects of mussel aquaculture on the nitrogen cycle and benthic communities in Kenepuru Sound, Marlborough Sounds, New Zealand |journal=Marine Biology |date=1985 |volume=85 |issue=2 |pages=127–136 |doi=10.1007/BF00397431 |bibcode=1985MarBi..85..127K |s2cid=83551118 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Newell |first1=Roger I. E. |last2=Cornwell |first2=Jeffrey C. |last3=Owens |first3=Michael S. |title=Influence of simulated bivalve biodeposition and microphytobenthos on sediment nitrogen dynamics: A laboratory study |journal=Limnology and Oceanography |date=September 2002 |volume=47 |issue=5 |pages=1367–1379 |doi=10.4319/lo.2002.47.5.1367 |s2cid=6589732 |bibcode=2002LimOc..47.1367N |doi-access=free }}</ref> Foundational work toward the idea of improving marine water quality through shellfish cultivation to was conducted by Odd Lindahl et al., using [[mussel]]s in Sweden.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lindahl |first1=Odd |last2=Hart |first2=Rob |last3=Hernroth |first3=Bodil |last4=Kollberg |first4=Sven |last5=Loo |first5=Lars-Ove |last6=Olrog |first6=Lars |last7=Rehnstam-Holm |first7=Ann-Sofi |last8=Svensson |first8=Jonny |last9=Svensson |first9=Susanne |last10=Syversen |first10=Ulf |title=Improving Marine Water Quality by Mussel Farming: A Profitable Solution for Swedish Society |journal=Ambio: A Journal of the Human Environment |date=March 2005 |volume=34 |issue=2 |pages=131–138 |doi=10.1579/0044-7447-34.2.131 |pmid=15865310 |bibcode=2005Ambio..34..131L |s2cid=25371433 }}</ref>

===Industrial pollution and toxic chemicals===
{{See also|Mercury in fish}}
Apart from plastics, there are particular problems with other toxic pollutants that either do not break down or only very slowly in the marine environment. Examples of [[persistent organic pollutant|persistent toxicant]]s are [[PCBs]], [[DDT]], [[tributyltin|TBT]], [[pesticide]]s, [[furan]]s, [[polychlorinated dibenzodioxins|dioxins]], [[phenols]], [[radioactive waste]], and [[Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances|PFAS]]. [[Heavy metal (chemistry)|Heavy metals]] are metallic chemical elements that have a relatively high density and are toxic or poisonous at low concentrations. Examples are [[mercury (element)|mercury]], [[lead]], [[copper]] and [[cadmium]]. Some [[toxicant]]s can accumulate in the tissues of many species of aquatic life in a process called [[bioaccumulation]]. They are also known to accumulate in [[benthic zone|benthic environments]], such as [[estuary|estuaries]] and [[bay mud]]s: a geological record of human activities of the last century.

DDT is a very toxic chemical that was used as a pesticide in mass quantities<ref>{{Cite web |date=July 1975 |title=DDT Regulatory History: A Brief Survey (to 1975) |url=https://www.epa.gov/archive/epa/aboutepa/ddt-regulatory-history-brief-survey-1975.html#:~:text=During%20the%2030%20years%20prior,pounds%20in%20the%20early%201970s. |access-date=2023-11-10 |website=United States Environmental Protection Agency}}</ref> throughout the United States and is known to be neurotoxic, a reproductive toxin, an [[endocrine disruptor]], and a carcinogen.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Harada |first1=Takanori |last2=Takeda |first2=Makio |last3=Kojima |first3=Sayuri |last4=Tomiyama |first4=Naruto |date=2016-01-31 |title=Toxicity and Carcinogenicity of Dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT) |journal=Toxicological Research |language=en |volume=32 |issue=1 |pages=21–33 |doi=10.5487/TR.2016.32.1.021 |issn=1976-8257 |pmc=4780236 |pmid=26977256|bibcode=2016ToxRe..32...21H }}</ref> DDT is a major focus of the book ''[[Silent Spring]]'' published by [[Rachel Carson]] in 1962. This is often attributed to launching the [[Environmental movement|modern environmental movement]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Legacy of Rachel Carsons Silent Spring National Historic Chemical Landmark |url=https://www.acs.org/education/whatischemistry/landmarks/rachel-carson-silent-spring.html |access-date=2023-11-10 |publisher=American Chemical Society |language=en}}</ref> and setting the stage for the creation of the [[United States Environmental Protection Agency|EPA]] in 1970.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-04-22 |title=How Rachel Carson's 'Silent Spring' Awakened the World to Environmental Peril |url=https://www.history.com/news/rachel-carson-silent-spring-impact-environmental-movement |access-date=2023-11-10 |website=HISTORY |language=en}}</ref> DDT was banned in the U.S. two years later in 1972.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-09-02 |title=Dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT) Factsheet {{!}} National Biomonitoring Program {{!}} CDC |url=https://www.cdc.gov/biomonitoring/DDT_FactSheet.html |access-date=2023-11-10 |website=cdc.gov |language=en-us}}</ref> Unfortunately, large quantities had already entered the ocean through runoff and had been dumped directly into the ocean.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-09-26 |title=Chemical Dumpsite Offshore Southern California |url=https://scripps.ucsd.edu/ddtcoastaldumpsite |access-date=2023-11-10 |website=scripps.ucsd.edu |language=en}}</ref> This toxin impacts marine ecosystems by accumulating from [[Plankton|lower trophic levels]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Xinhong |last2=Wang |first2=Wen-Xiong |date=2005-08-01 |title=Uptake, absorption efficiency and elimination of DDT in marine phytoplankton, copepods and fish |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0269749105000655 |journal=Environmental Pollution |volume=136 |issue=3 |pages=453–464 |doi=10.1016/j.envpol.2005.01.004 |pmid=15862399 |bibcode=2005EPoll.136..453W |issn=0269-7491|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and up the food chain into higher trophic levels such as from arctic cod into seals,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Muir |first1=Derek C. G. |last2=Norstrom |first2=Ross J. |last3=Simon |first3=Mary. |date=September 1988 |title=Organochlorine contaminants in arctic marine food chains: accumulation of specific polychlorinated biphenyls and chlordane-related compounds |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/es00174a012 |journal=Environmental Science & Technology |language=en |volume=22 |issue=9 |pages=1071–1079 |doi=10.1021/es00174a012 |pmid=22148662 |bibcode=1988EnST...22.1071M |issn=0013-936X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> from fish then eaten by dolphins,<ref>{{Cite journal |title=Distribution and Total Burdens of Chlorinated Hydrocarbons in Bodies of Striped Dolphins (''Stenella coeruleoalba'') |journal=Agricultural and Biological Chemistry |volume=45 |issue=11 |date=1 November 1981 |pages=2569–2578 |doi=10.1271/bbb1961.45.2569 |last1=Tanabe |first1=Shinsuke |last2=Tatsukawa |first2=Ryo |last3=Tanaka |first3=Hiroyuki |last4=Maruyama |first4=Kohji |last5=Miyazaki |first5=Nobuyuki |last6=Fujiyama |first6=Toraya |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Tanabe |first1=Shinsuke |last2=Tanaka |first2=Hiroyuki |last3=Tatsukawa |first3=Ryo |date=1984-11-01 |title=Polychlorobiphenyls, ΣDDT, and hexachlorocyclohexane isomers in the western North Pacific ecosystem |journal=Archives of Environmental Contamination and Toxicology |language=en |volume=13 |issue=6 |pages=731–738 |doi=10.1007/BF01055937 |bibcode=1984ArECT..13..731T |s2cid=85012745 |issn=1432-0703}}</ref> and from cod and eels into seals.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ruus |first1=A |last2=Ugland |first2=K. I |last3=Espeland |first3=O |last4=Skaare |first4=J. U |date=1999-08-01 |title=Organochlorine contaminants in a local marine food chain from Jarfjord, Northern Norway |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0141113699000379 |journal=Marine Environmental Research |volume=48 |issue=2 |pages=131–146 |doi=10.1016/S0141-1136(99)00037-9 |bibcode=1999MarER..48..131R |issn=0141-1136|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Shortly after Rachel Carson's publication of ''Silent Spring,'' PCBs were identified as another persistent, toxic chemical that has been released in extensive quantities to the environment. PCBs are a very well-studied class of chemicals that are manufactured from oil.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last1=Montano |first1=Luigi |last2=Pironti |first2=Concetta |last3=Pinto |first3=Gabriella |last4=Ricciardi |first4=Maria |last5=Buono |first5=Amalia |last6=Brogna |first6=Carlo |last7=Venier |first7=Marta |last8=Piscopo |first8=Marina |last9=Amoresano |first9=Angela |last10=Motta |first10=Oriana |date=2022-07-01 |title=Polychlorinated Biphenyls (PCBs) in the Environment: Occupational and Exposure Events, Effects on Human Health and Fertility |journal=Toxics |language=en |volume=10 |issue=7 |page=365 |doi=10.3390/toxics10070365 |issn=2305-6304 |pmc=9323099 |pmid=35878270 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2022Toxic..10..365M }}</ref> These chemicals are banned in the United States under the [[Toxic Substances Control Act of 1976|Toxic Substance Control Act]],<ref>{{Cite web |date=8 August 2023 |title=Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA) and Federal Facilities |url=https://www.epa.gov/enforcement/toxic-substances-control-act-tsca-and-federal-facilities#:~:text=Six%20chemical%20substances%20receive%20special,to%20promulgate%20PCB%20disposal%20regulations. |access-date=2023-11-10 |website=United States Environmental Protection Agency}}</ref> but are still found in the soil, air, sediments, and biota.<ref name=":3" /> PCBs are known to accumulate in the fatty tissues of animals. In particular, PCBs build up and are stored in the [[blubber]] of marine mammals including dolphins and killer whales.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last1=Jepson |first1=Paul D. |last2=Deaville |first2=Rob |last3=Barber |first3=Jonathan L. |last4=Aguilar |first4=Àlex |last5=Borrell |first5=Asunción |last6=Murphy |first6=Sinéad |last7=Barry |first7=Jon |last8=Brownlow |first8=Andrew |last9=Barnett |first9=James |last10=Berrow |first10=Simon |last11=Cunningham |first11=Andrew A. |last12=Davison |first12=Nicholas J. |last13=ten Doeschate |first13=Mariel |last14=Esteban |first14=Ruth |last15=Ferreira |first15=Marisa |date=2016-01-14 |title=PCB pollution continues to impact populations of orcas and other dolphins in European waters |journal=Scientific Reports |language=en |volume=6 |issue=1 |article-number=18573 |doi=10.1038/srep18573  |doi-access=free|issn=2045-2322 |pmc=4725908 |pmid=26766430|bibcode=2016NatSR...618573J }}</ref> These chemicals cause reproductive issues for many species.<ref name=":4" /> In mud crabs, PCBs have been discovered to be immunotoxic by reducing resistance to bacterial disease, reducing antioxidant enzyme activity, and damaging DNA responsible for immune system functions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Xiao |first1=Chongyang |last2=Zhang |first2=Yunfei |last3=Zhu |first3=Fei |date=2021-12-15 |title=Immunotoxicity of polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) to the marine crustacean species, Scylla paramamosain |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S026974912101811X |journal=Environmental Pollution |volume=291 |article-number=118229 |doi=10.1016/j.envpol.2021.118229 |pmid=34582922 |bibcode=2021EPoll.29118229X |s2cid=238218223 |issn=0269-7491|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

PFAS are an important emerging class of man-made persistent toxicants that contain extremely strong [[Carbon–fluorine bond|carbon-fluorine bonds]] which make these chemicals extremely difficult to break down. They have [[Amphiphile|unique properties]] that make them useful for manufacturing a wide variety of products such as [[firefighting foam]]s, clothing, carpets, and fast food wrappers.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Mahmoudnia |first=Ali |date=2023-01-18 |title=The role of PFAS in unsettling ocean carbon sequestration |journal=Environmental Monitoring and Assessment |language=en |volume=195 |issue=2 |article-number=310 |doi=10.1007/s10661-023-10912-8 |issn=1573-2959 |pmc=9848026 |pmid=36652110|bibcode=2023EMnAs.195..310M }}</ref> These useful properties in manufacturing unfortunately translate to problematic properties in the environment and organisms from plants to people. Because PFAS are not broken down in the environment, they have been circulated through the air and water to essentially all regions of the atmosphere, land, and ocean.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Panieri |first1=Emiliano |last2=Baralic |first2=Katarina |last3=Djukic-Cosic |first3=Danijela |last4=Buha Djordjevic |first4=Aleksandra |last5=Saso |first5=Luciano |date=February 2022 |title=PFAS Molecules: A Major Concern for the Human Health and the Environment |journal=Toxics |language=en |volume=10 |issue=2 |page=44 |doi=10.3390/toxics10020044 |issn=2305-6304 |pmc=8878656 |pmid=35202231 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2022Toxic..10...44P }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Muir |first1=Derek |last2=Miaz |first2=Luc T. |date=2021-07-20 |title=Spatial and Temporal Trends of Perfluoroalkyl Substances in Global Ocean and Coastal Waters |journal=Environmental Science & Technology |language=en |volume=55 |issue=14 |pages=9527–9537 |doi=10.1021/acs.est.0c08035 |pmid=33646763 |bibcode=2021EnST...55.9527M |s2cid=232090620 |issn=0013-936X|doi-access=free }}</ref> These chemicals have many negative effects on marine life, such as significantly inhibited growth of [[phytoplankton]] over time<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Niu |first1=Zhiguang |last2=Na |first2=Jing |last3=Xu |first3=Wei'an |last4=Wu |first4=Nan |last5=Zhang |first5=Ying |date=2019-09-01 |title=The effect of environmentally relevant emerging per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances on the growth and antioxidant response in marine Chlorella sp. |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0269749118357920 |journal=Environmental Pollution |volume=252 |issue=Pt A |pages=103–109 |doi=10.1016/j.envpol.2019.05.103 |pmid=31146223 |bibcode=2019EPoll.252..103N |s2cid=171092231 |issn=0269-7491|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and accumulation in seals, polar bears,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Boisvert |first1=Gabriel |last2=Sonne |first2=Christian |last3=Rigét |first3=Frank F. |last4=Dietz |first4=Rune |last5=Letcher |first5=Robert J. |date=2019-09-01 |title=Bioaccumulation and biomagnification of perfluoroalkyl acids and precursors in East Greenland polar bears and their ringed seal prey |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0269749119319438 |journal=Environmental Pollution |volume=252 |issue=Pt B |pages=1335–1343 |doi=10.1016/j.envpol.2019.06.035 |pmid=31252131 |bibcode=2019EPoll.252.1335B |s2cid=195764669 |issn=0269-7491|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and dolphins.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Stockin |first1=K. A. |last2=Yi |first2=S. |last3=Northcott |first3=G. L. |last4=Betty |first4=E. L. |last5=Machovsky-Capuska |first5=G. E. |last6=Jones |first6=B. |last7=Perrott |first7=M. R. |last8=Law |first8=R. J. |last9=Rumsby |first9=A. |last10=Thelen |first10=M. A. |last11=Graham |first11=L. |last12=Palmer |first12=E. I. |last13=Tremblay |first13=L. A. |date=2021-12-01 |title=Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), trace elements and life history parameters of mass-stranded common dolphins (Delphinus delphis) in New Zealand |journal=Marine Pollution Bulletin |volume=173 |issue=Pt A |article-number=112896 |doi=10.1016/j.marpolbul.2021.112896 |pmid=34601248 |bibcode=2021MarPB.17312896S |s2cid=238258920 |issn=0025-326X|doi-access=free |hdl=2292/58033 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Current research is underway investigating the full extent of the harm to marine ecosystems caused by PFAS.

;Specific examples:
* Chinese and Russian industrial pollution such as [[phenols]] and heavy metals in the [[Amur River]] have devastated fish stocks and damaged its [[estuary]] soil.<ref>[http://www.npolar.no/ansipra/english/Indexpages/Ethnic_groups.html#19 "Indigenous Peoples of the Russian North, Siberia and Far East: Nivkh" ] by Arctic Network for the Support of the Indigenous Peoples of the Russian Arctic</ref>
* Acute and chronic [[pollution]] events have been shown to impact southern California [[kelp forest]]s, though the intensity of the impact seems to depend on both the nature of the contaminants and duration of exposure.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Grigg, R.W. |author2=Kiwala, R.S. |year=1970|title= Some ecological effects of discharged wastes on marine life|journal= California Department of Fish and Game|volume= 56|pages= 145–155}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |doi= 10.1109/OCEANS.1989.586780 |chapter= Contaminants in Sediments Near a Major Marine Outfall: History, Effects, and Future |title= Proceedings OCEANS |volume= 2 |pages= 481–484 |year= 1989 |last1= Stull |first1= J. K.|s2cid= 111153399 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |doi= 10.1007/978-94-011-1998-6_33 |chapter= History of kelp beds (''Macrocystis'') in Orange and San Diego Counties, California |title= Fourteenth International Seaweed Symposium |page= 277 |year= 1993 |last1= North |first1= W. J. |last2= James |first2= D. E. |last3= Jones |first3= L. G. |isbn= 978-94-010-4882-8}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi= 10.1016/0141-1136(94)00008-D |title= Effects of a large sewage spill on a kelp forest community: Catastrophe or disturbance? |journal= Marine Environmental Research |volume= 40 |issue= 2 |pages= 181–224 |year= 1995 |last1= Tegner |first1= M. J. |last2= Dayton |first2= P. K. |last3= Edwards |first3= P. B. |last4= Riser |first4= K. L. |last5= Chadwick |first5= D. B. |last6= Dean |first6= T. A. |last7= Deysher |first7= L.|bibcode= 1995MarER..40..181T |url= https://zenodo.org/record/1258321 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Carpenter |first1=S. R. |last2=Caraco |first2=N. F. |last3=Correll |first3=D. L. |last4=Howarth |first4=R. W. |last5=Sharpley |first5=A. N. |last6=Smith |first6=V. H. |title=Nonpoint Pollution of Surface Waters with Phosphorus and Nitrogen |journal=Ecological Applications |date=August 1998 |volume=8 |issue=3 |pages=559–568 |doi=10.1890/1051-0761(1998)008[0559:NPOSWW]2.0.CO;2 |hdl=1808/16724 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>
* Due to their high position in the [[food chain]] and the subsequent [[bioaccumulation|accumulation]] of [[heavy metals]] from their diet, [[mercury (element)|mercury]] levels can be high in larger species such as bluefin and [[albacore]]. As a result, in March 2004 the United States [[Food and Drug Administration|FDA]] issued guidelines recommending that pregnant women, nursing mothers and children limit their intake of tuna and other types of predatory fish.<ref>{{cite web |title=Advice about Eating Fish For Women Who Are or Might Become Pregnant, Breastfeeding Mothers, and Young Children |url=https://www.fda.gov/food/consumers/advice-about-eating-fish |website=FDA |date=24 February 2020 }}</ref>
* Some shellfish and crabs can survive polluted environments, accumulating heavy metals or toxins in their tissues. For example, [[mitten crab]]s have a remarkable ability to survive in highly modified [[aquatic habitat]]s, including polluted waters.<ref Name=issg.org>{{cite web |url=http://www.issg.org/database/species/ecology.asp?si=38&fr=1&sts= |title=Ecology of ''Eriocheir sinensis'' |author=Gollasch, Stephen |date=3 March 2006}}</ref> The farming and harvesting of such species needs careful management if they are to be used as a food.<ref name=mbcmc>{{cite journal |last1=Hui |first1=Clifford A. |last2=Rudnick |first2=Deborah |last3=Williams |first3=Erin |title=Mercury burdens in Chinese mitten crabs (Eriocheir sinensis) in three tributaries of southern San Francisco Bay, California, USA |journal=Environmental Pollution |date=February 2005 |volume=133 |issue=3 |pages=481–487 |doi=10.1016/j.envpol.2004.06.019 |pmid=15519723 |bibcode=2005EPoll.133..481H }}</ref><ref name=uctip>{{cite journal |last1=Silvestre |first1=F |last2=Trausch |first2=G |last3=Péqueux |first3=A |last4=Devos |first4=P |title=Uptake of cadmium through isolated perfused gills of the Chinese mitten crab, Eriocheir sinensis |journal=Comparative Biochemistry and Physiology Part A: Molecular & Integrative Physiology |date=January 2004 |volume=137 |issue=1 |pages=189–196 |doi=10.1016/s1095-6433(03)00290-3 |pmid=14720604 |bibcode=2004CmpBP.137..189S }}</ref>
* Surface runoff of pesticides can alter the gender of fish species genetically, transforming male into female fish.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Saey |first1=Tina Hesman |date=12 August 2002 |title=DDT treatment turns male fish into mothers |url=https://www.sciencenews.org/article/ddt-treatment-turns-male-fish-mothers |work=Science News |url-access=subscription }}</ref>
* Heavy metals enter the environment through [[oil spill]]s – such as the [[Prestige oil spill]] on the [[Galicia (Spain)|Galician]] coast and Gulf of Mexico which unleashed an estimated 3.19 million barrels of oil<ref>{{cite web |title=Gulf Oil Spill |url=https://ocean.si.edu/conservation/pollution/gulf-oil-spill |website=Smithsonian Ocean |date=30 April 2018 }}</ref> – or from other natural or [[pollution|anthropogenic sources]].
* In 2005, the [['Ndrangheta]], an Italian mafia syndicate, was accused of [[toxic waste dumping by the 'Ndrangheta|sinking at least 30 ships loaded with toxic waste, much of it radioactive]]. This has led to widespread investigations into [[Ocean disposal of radioactive waste|radioactive waste disposal]] rackets.<ref name=esp050805>Bocca, Riccardo (5 August 2005) [http://www.archivio900.it/it/articoli/art.aspx?r=relauto&id=5978 Parla un boss: Così lo Stato pagava la 'ndrangheta per smaltire i rifiuti tossici]. ''L'Espresso''</ref>
* Since the end of World War II, various nations, including the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom, the United States, and Germany, have disposed of chemical weapons in the [[Baltic Sea]], raising concerns of environmental contamination.<ref>{{cite news |title=Chemical Weapon Time Bomb Ticks in the Baltic Sea |url=https://www.dw.com/en/chemical-weapon-time-bomb-ticks-in-the-baltic-sea/a-3102728 |work=DW |date=1 February 2008 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://helcom.fi/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/BSEP114.pdf |title=Activities 2007 Overview |series=Baltic Sea Environment Proceedings No. 112. |publisher=[[HELCOM|Helsinki Commission]] }}</ref>
* The [[Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster]] in 2011 caused radioactive toxins from the damaged power plant to leak into the air and ocean. There are still many isotopes in the ocean, which directly affects the benthic food web and also affects the whole food chain. The concentration of 137Cs in the bottom sediment that was contaminated by water with high concentrations in April–May 2011 remains quite high and is showing signs of very slow decrease with time.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bezhenar |first1=Roman |last2=Jung |first2=Kyung Tae |last3=Maderich |first3=Vladimir |last4=Willemsen |first4=Stefan |last5=de With |first5=Govert |last6=Qiao |first6=Fangli |title=Transfer of radiocaesium from contaminated bottom sediments to marine organisms through benthic food chains in post-Fukushima and post-Chernobyl periods |journal=Biogeosciences |date=23 May 2016 |volume=13 |issue=10 |pages=3021–3034 |doi=10.5194/bg-13-3021-2016 |bibcode=2016BGeo...13.3021B |doi-access=free }}</ref>
* During the 20th century, large amounts of DDT, petroleum products, radioactive materials, sulphuric acid, and other toxins [[Chemical dumps in ocean off Southern California|were dumped in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Southern California]].
