{{short description|City that has no carbon footprint}}
A '''zero-carbon city''' is a goal of city planners<ref name="Fuller-Wright"/> that describes a significant reduction in carbon use by a city. The term describes a range of carbon reduction, ranging from a city that generates as much or more carbon-free [[Sustainable Energy for All|sustainable energy]] as it uses,<ref>{{cite web |title=DOCSOC/1508196v1/022283-0050 Memorandum of Understanding |url=https://www.cityoflancasterca.org/Home/ShowDocument?id=14808 |website=City of Lancaster |date=2011 |access-date=27 September 2022}}</ref> to a city that manages [[greenhouse gas emissions]] and reduces its [[carbon footprint]] to a minimum (ideally 0 or negative) by using [[renewable energy]] sources, by reducing [[carbon emissions]] through efficient urban design, technology use and lifestyle changes, and balancing any remaining emissions through [[carbon sequestration]].<ref name="Padmanaban"/><ref name="HSBC">{{cite book |title=Towards the Zero-Carbon City |date=July 2019 |publisher=HSBC Centre of Sustainable Finance |url=https://www.sustainablefinance.hsbc.com/-/media/gbm/sustainable/attachments/towards-the-zero-carbon-city.pdf |archive-date=2022-09-01 |access-date=2022-09-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220901004145/https://www.sustainablefinance.hsbc.com/-/media/gbm/sustainable/attachments/towards-the-zero-carbon-city.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="Allen">{{cite journal |last1=Allen |first1=Myles R. |last2=Friedlingstein |first2=Pierre |last3=Girardin |first3=Cécile A.J. |last4=Jenkins |first4=Stuart |last5=Malhi |first5=Yadvinder |last6=Mitchell-Larson |first6=Eli |last7=Peters |first7=Glen P. |last8=Rajamani |first8=Lavanya |title=Net Zero: Science, Origins, and Implications |journal=Annual Review of Environment and Resources |date=17 October 2022 |volume=47 |issue=1 |pages=annurev–environ–112320-105050 |doi=10.1146/annurev-environ-112320-105050 |doi-access=free |hdl=11250/3118584 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Since the supply chains of a city stretch far beyond its borders, Princeton University's High Meadows Environmental Institute suggests using a  transboundary definition of a '''net-zero carbon city''' as "one that has net-zero carbon infrastructure and food provisioning systems".<ref name="Kelly"/>

Most cities throughout the world burn coal, oil or gas as a source of energy, resulting in the release of [[Carbon dioxide in Earth's atmosphere|carbon dioxide into the atmosphere]], a key greenhouse gas. The development of [[Climate change and cities|cities is therefore intimately linked to the causes and impacts of climate change]].<ref name="Padmanaban"/><ref name="Seto">{{cite journal |last1=Seto |first1=Karen C. |last2=Churkina |first2=Galina |last3=Hsu |first3=Angel |last4=Keller |first4=Meredith |last5=Newman |first5=Peter W.G. |last6=Qin |first6=Bo |last7=Ramaswami |first7=Anu |title=From Low- to Net-Zero Carbon Cities: The Next Global Agenda |journal=Annual Review of Environment and Resources |date=18 October 2021 |volume=46 |issue=1 |pages=377–415 |doi=10.1146/annurev-environ-050120-113117 |doi-access=free }}</ref>  {{As of|2019}}, cities accounted for two thirds of all energy consumption and generated 70% of energy-related greenhouse gas emissions.<ref name="Owen-Burge">{{cite news |last1=Owen-Burge |first1=Charlotte |title=Carbon neutral cities: Can we fight climate change without them? |url=https://climatechampions.unfccc.int/carbon-neutral-cities-can-we-fight-climate-change-without-them/ |access-date=31 August 2022 |work=Climate Champions |date=6 May 2021 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="UN2019">{{cite web |title=Cities: a "cause of and solution to" climate change |url=https://news.un.org/en/story/2019/09/1046662 |website=UN News |access-date=31 August 2022 |date=18 September 2019 |language=en |archive-date=4 March 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210304125023/https://news.un.org/en/story/2019/09/1046662 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="IEA2021"/> Over 50% of the people in the world currently live in cities, a proportion that is projected to rise to 70% by 2050, and almost 80% by 2080.<ref name="HSBC"/>

[[File:Electrical and Mechanical Services Department Headquarters Photovoltaics.jpg|thumb|right|210px|Rooftop solar [[photovoltaic system]] array in [[Hong Kong]]]]
[[Urban development]] focused on lowering carbon is seen as an inevitable trend for [[Sustainable urbanism|sustainability in urban spaces]].<ref name="Seto"/><ref name="Peng 201–212"/><ref name="Morris">{{cite book |last1=Morris |first1=Langdon |last2=Naz |first2=Farah |title=Net Zero City: The Ten-year Transformation Plan : how to Overcome the Climate Crisis by 2032 |date=2021 |publisher=Langdon Morris |isbn=979-8-4653-6115-6 }}{{pn|date=September 2025}}</ref> Underlying goals include avoiding harm to the planet and countering the impacts of [[climate change]].<ref name="HSBC"/>  {{As of|2022}}, over 1000 cities worldwide have undertaken steps to transition in response to [[climate change]] as part of the Cities Race to Zero campaign,<ref name="Wray"/> one part of a larger United Nations Race to Zero campaign.<ref name="Bindman"/>   Among them are cities including Rio de Janeiro, New York, Paris, Oslo, Mexico City, Melbourne, London, Milan, Cape Town, Buenos Aires, Caracas, Copenhagen, Vancouver<ref name="Brown"/> and [[Hong Kong]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Who's in Race to Zero? |url=https://unfccc.int/climate-action/race-to-zero/who-s-in-race-to-zero |website=United Nations Climate Change |access-date=20 September 2022}}</ref>  In the United States, more than 100 cities have pledged to become [[carbon neutral]].<ref name="C40-USA"/> 

An established modern city attempting to achieve net-zero status needs to assess seven key provisioning systems, for energy, transportation-communications, food, construction materials, water, green infrastructure, and waste-management.<ref name="Kelly">{{cite news |last1=Kelly |first1=Morgan |title=What is a net-zero city? Depends on how you count urban carbon emissions |url=https://environment.princeton.edu/news/what-is-a-net-zero-city-depends-on-how-you-count-urban-carbon-emissions/ |access-date=31 August 2022 |work=High Meadows Environmental Institute |publisher=Princeton University |date=May 13, 2021}}</ref><ref name="Ramaswami"/><ref name="Fuller-Wright">{{cite news |last1=Fuller-Wright |first1=Liz |title=What climate choices should cities make? A Princeton data tool helps planners set priorities. |url=https://www.princeton.edu/news/2022/03/30/city-planners-can-make-smarter-climate-choices-using-new-princeton-data-tool |access-date=31 August 2022 |work=Princeton University |date=March 30, 2022 |language=en}}</ref>  Strategies for reaching net zero include developing renewable energy supplies, reducing energy and resource use through better urban design and lifestyle changes, reducing waste, and creating green spaces and carbon sinks to remove carbon from the atmosphere.<ref name="Padmanaban">{{cite journal |last1=Padmanaban |first1=Deepa |title=How cities can fight climate change |journal=Knowable Magazine |date=2022 |doi=10.1146/knowable-060922-1 }}</ref><ref name="Seto"/> Approaches to sustainable urban planning of zero carbon cities increasingly emphasize the use of locally sourced food, energy, and renewable resources.<ref name="Dabaieh"/> 

Some city planners have designed zero-carbon cities from scratch, instead of using and adapting established cities. This gives city planners greater control over all aspects of city design and how each city can contribute to being without carbon emissions. Such design enables the city to benefit from [[economies of scale]] and from construction options that might not be feasible in a city with existing structures. Such zero-carbon cities maintain optimal living conditions and economic development while eliminating [[environmental impact]].<ref name="Peng 201–212">{{cite journal |last1=Peng |first1=Yuan |last2=Bai |first2=Xuemei |title=Experimenting towards a low-carbon city: Policy evolution and nested structure of innovation |journal=Journal of Cleaner Production |date=February 2018 |volume=174 |pages=201–212 |doi=10.1016/j.jclepro.2017.10.116 |bibcode=2018JCPro.174..201P |hdl=1885/139438 |hdl-access=free}}</ref> 

==Guiding principles==
Net zero is a scientific concept that can be defined in terms of measurable targets. It can provide a frame of reference for understanding and assessing the impact of actions to address climate change. To be used as a framework for climate action, it must be operationalised and measured as part of the ongoing activities of social, political and economic systems.<ref name="Fankhauser">{{cite journal |last1=Fankhauser |first1=Sam |last2=Smith |first2=Stephen M. |last3=Allen |first3=Myles |last4=Axelsson |first4=Kaya |last5=Hale |first5=Thomas |last6=Hepburn |first6=Cameron |last7=Kendall |first7=J. Michael |last8=Khosla |first8=Radhika |last9=Lezaun |first9=Javier |last10=Mitchell-Larson |first10=Eli |last11=Obersteiner |first11=Michael |last12=Rajamani |first12=Lavanya |last13=Rickaby |first13=Rosalind |last14=Seddon |first14=Nathalie |last15=Wetzer |first15=Thom |title=The meaning of net zero and how to get it right |journal=Nature Climate Change |date=January 2022 |volume=12 |issue=1 |pages=15–21 |doi=10.1038/s41558-021-01245-w |bibcode=2022NatCC..12...15F |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Allen"/><ref name="Charlotte"/>

Time scale is an essential factor driving the urgency of net zero interventions. The impact of carbon emissions on surface warming of the planet is [[monotonic]], [[linear equation|near-linear]] (as of 2021) and long term. Attempts to achieve net zero must therefore be long term plans, maintained over multiple decades. The goal of net zero is to achieve a state of balance that can be maintained over multiple decades to centuries.<ref name="Fankhauser"/>

Scientists can measure ongoing changes in the global atmosphere and estimate carbon budgets, but identifying and operationalising interventions occurs at multiple levels worldwide. As a frame of reference for decision-makers, global impact must be translated into definable targets for entities at national, subnational, corporate, organizational and individual levels.<ref name="Fankhauser"/>

In practice, determination of net-zero targets has been self-regulated and voluntary. Entitles set and achieve goals, some participating in voluntary campaigns and initiatives such as the [[Paris Agreement]], the United Nations Race to Zero campaign, [[Cities Race to Zero]], the [[Net-Zero Asset Owner Alliance|Net Zero Asset Owners Alliance]], and the [[Science Based Targets initiative]]. Regular global progress assessments, including those of independent global initiatives such as [[Carbon Disclosure Project|CDP]] and the Transition Pathway Initiative (TPI), provide a form of feedback.<ref name="Fankhauser"/>   {{As of|2022}}, over 1000 cities,<ref name="Wray"/><ref name="C40"/> including 25 megacities worldwide<ref name="Brown">{{cite news |last1=Brown |first1=Jessica |title=How cities are going carbon neutral |url=https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20211115-how-cities-are-going-carbon-neutral |access-date=15 September 2022 |work=www.bbc.com |date=16 November 2021 |language=en}}</ref> and 100 cities in the United States, are part of Cities Race to Zero.<ref name="C40-USA"/> 

While the setting of targets is key, it must be followed up through effective mechanisms for governance, monitoring, accountability and reporting. Long-term goals must be translated into practical near-term actions, with detailed plans and methods for establishing [[Shifting baseline|baselines]], measuring outcomes and assessing impacts.<ref name="Fankhauser"/><ref name="Charlotte"/>
In many ways, cities are in a critical position to address climate issues effectively: they are large enough to benefit from economies of scale, and close enough to actual problems to focus on developing real implementable strategies. As demands on their infrastructures increase, they have a strong incentive to address issues and find and share solutions.<ref name="IEA2021">{{cite web |title=Empowering Cities for a Net Zero Future: Unlocking resilient, smart, sustainable urban energy systems |url=https://iea.blob.core.windows.net/assets/4d5c939d-9c37-490b-bb53-2c0d23f2cf3d/G20EmpoweringCitiesforaNetZeroFuture.pdf |website=International Energy Agency|date=2021 |access-date=12 September 2022}}</ref> 

Seven aspects of net zero have been identified as highly important to its successful use as a framework for climate action. These have relevance to the development of net zero cities.<ref name="Fankhauser"/>
* Sooner is better. Front-loading climate action, combined with long-term planning over years or decades, is the most cost-effective way to reach temperature targets, as well as the most flexible in the face of new information.<ref name="Fankhauser"/>
* Be comprehensive.  Plans that tackle comprehensive rather than partial emissions reductions are becoming necessary as carbon levels reach critical tipping points.  Harder-to-treat problem areas must be addressed as well as easier ones.<ref name="Fankhauser"/>
* Beware of over-reliance on early-stage [[carbon removal]] strategies. These are not yet well understood and may enable a "business as usual" attitude to climate change.<ref name="Fankhauser"/>
* Reassess and improve systems for [[carbon offsets]]. Such systems have been questioned in terms of their scientific and technical capabilities; environmental integrity; monitoring, reporting and verification structures; and social and environmental impact.<ref name="Fankhauser"/>
* Apply principles of [[sustainable development]].  Achieving net zero globally requires implementation of equitable and just transitions that balance social, economic and environmental objectives in areas with very different conditions.<ref name="Fankhauser"/>
* Focus on broad strategies for [[sustainability]]. Cities can potentially address multiple problems at once, through solutions that are nature-based, biodiversity-based and people-led.<ref name="Fankhauser"/> It is important to consider that parents with small children, the poor, the elderly and the disabled may experience a city differently from those who are affluent and more easily mobile.<ref name="Larose">{{cite news |last1=Larose |first1=Lysanne |title=Most climate policies worldwide do not consider the rights of people with disabilities |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/science/what-on-earth-climate-action-people-with-disabilities-1.6576205 |access-date=12 September 2022 |work=CBC News |date=September 9, 2022}}</ref>
* See opportunities. New net-zero solutions and innovation will drive economic shifts which will include opportunities for investment, renewal and growth.<ref name="Fankhauser"/><ref name="Charlotte">{{cite book |title=Circular Charlotte: Towards a zero waste and inclusive city |date=2018 |publisher=City of Charlotte |location=Charlotte, North Carolina |url=https://charlottenc.gov/SWS/CircularCharlotte/Documents/Circular%20Charlotte_Towards%20a%20zero%20waste%20and%20inclusive%20city%20-%20full%20report.pdf |access-date=27 September 2022 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Burg">{{cite news |last1=Burg |first1=Natalie |title=Who Funds the Fight Against Climate Change? |url=https://meansandmatters.bankofthewest.com/article/sustainable-living/taking-action/who-funds-the-fight-against-climate-change/ |access-date=27 September 2022 |work=Means and Matters |date=April 20, 2022}}</ref>

There are strong similarities between zero carbon cities and [[eco-cities]]. Discussions of eco-cities tend to focus more broadly on social and environmental issues, with less emphasis on [[carbon monitoring]] and the necessity of reaching [[Carbon neutrality|net zero energy balance]].<ref name="Dabaieh">{{cite book |last1=Dabaieh |first1=Marwa |last2=Maguid |first2=Dalya |last3=El Mahdy |first3=Deena |title=Sustainable Cities - Authenticity, Ambition and Dream |chapter=Towards Adaptive Design Strategies for Zero-Carbon Eco-Cities in Egypt |date=2019 |doi=10.5772/intechopen.80725 |isbn=978-1-78985-523-4 }}{{predatory}}</ref>
Many of the principles proposed for developing [[eco-cities]] are also relevant to net zero cities, including revising [[land use]] priorities to create [[Sustainable community|sustainable]] [[Mixed-use development|mixed-use]] communities;  revising transportation priorities to favor [[walking|foot]], [[bicycle]], cart and [[public transit]] over [[automobile]]s; increasing [[environmental awareness]]; supporting local agriculture and [[community garden]]s; and promoting [[recycling]] and [[resource conservation]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Roseland |first1=Mark |title=Dimensions of the eco-city |journal=Cities |date=August 1997 |volume=14 |issue=4 |pages=197–202 |doi=10.1016/s0264-2751(97)00003-6 }}</ref>

==City infrastructure==
[[File:Green roof bike rack.jpg|thumb |right | 210px | Green roof bicycle rack for greener transportation, shade and carbon storage]] 
{{external media | width = 210px | float = right | headerimage= [[File:Four-solaire-global-sun-oven.jpg|210px|Solar oven]] | video1 = [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WeNaMlibiak&ab_channel=HappenFilms "Sustainable City Living on 1/10th of an Acre - ''Degrowth in the Suburbs''], October 21, 2018 }}

Urban areas involve essential infrastructure for energy, transport, water, food, shelter, construction, public spaces, and waste management. Transforming cities to achieve net zero sustainability means rethinking both [[Supply (economics)|supply-side]] issues (power supplies and transportation) and [[Demand|demand-side]] issues (reducing use through better urban design and policy.)<ref name="Padmanaban"/><ref name="Seto"/> Key factors in [[city planning]] include [[Urban density|density]], [[Mixed-use development|land use mix]], connectivity, and [[accessibility]].<ref name="Seto"/>

To achieve net zero, a city must collectively reduce emissions of [[greenhouse gases]] to zero and cease all practices that [[Greenhouse gas#Direct greenhouse gas emissions|emit]] greenhouse gases.  Achieving net zero sustainability also means considering sources and production of materials, and ensuring that what comes into the city travels via [[zero-emission transport]].<ref name="Peng 201–212"/><ref name="Dabaieh"/> Appearing to reduce emissions in one location by shifting emissions-causing activities to a different location will not contribute to the global goal of a sustainable net zero environment.<ref name="Reeves">{{cite news |last1=Reeves |first1=Martin |last2=Young |first2=David |last3=Dhar |first3=Julia |last4=O'Dea |first4=Annelies |title=The risks and benefits for companies going net zero |url=https://www.weforum.org/agenda/2022/02/net-zero-risks-benefits-climate/ |access-date=19 September 2022 |work=World Economic Forum |date=February 28, 2022 |language=en}}</ref>

===Energy===
To become a zero-carbon city,  renewable energy must supersede other [[non-renewable energy]] sources and become the sole source of energy, so a zero-carbon city is a renewable-energy-economy city. Transitioning to a zero carbon city means examining the generation of power sources, such as [[Renewable Electricity and the Grid|renewable electricity]] and decarbonising electricity production.<ref name="Peng 201–212"/><ref name="Dabaieh"/>

Electricity needs are increasingly being met through the development of solar and wind power as energy sources, which are becoming the cheapest forms of power. The shift to solar power, in particular, means that energy can be produced close to its intended use.  This is suited to a distributed energy infrastructure in which local areas are connected into a city-wide or region-wide [[electrical grid]]. The ability to provide a steady supply of electricity is also being supported by the development of more efficient and cost-effective battery storage technology.<ref name="Seto"/> 

[[File:Electricity Grid Schematic English.svg|thumb|right|upright=1.4| General layout of electricity networks. Voltages and depictions of electrical lines are typical for Germany and other European systems.]]
Issues of equity, balance, and efficiency are all relevant to energy distribution and use.  A net-zero carbon electricity grid is a necessary foundation for supply side strategies that aim to shift provisioning systems for buildings, energy use, mobility, and light industrial energy use to electric power. The development of a net-zero carbon electric grid can become the basis for transitioning key urban activities such as transportation, heating, and cooking from fossil fuels to zero-carbon electricity.<ref name="Seto"/>

===Transport===
[[File:Elements of Low-Carbon Urban Development.png|thumb|alt=Elements of Low-Carbon Urban Development|Elements of Low-Carbon Urban Development: less cars, better public transit, mixed use development]]

Transportation of people and goods is estimated to contribute 20% of global greenhouse gas emissions.<ref name="Seto"/>
In terms of transport, approaches to low-carbon urban development often focus on reducing fossil-fuel based transportation, improving public transit, and creating areas of mixed use development so that people are more likely to work and shop near their homes, reducing transportation needs.<ref name="Padmanaban"/>  A study of 274 cities worldwide suggests that compact urban development is important in both affluent mature cities and developing-country cities with emerging infrastructures, reducing urban emissions by up to 25%.<ref name="Creutzig">{{cite journal |last1=Creutzig |first1=Felix |author1-link=Felix Creutzig |last2=Baiocchi |first2=Giovanni |last3=Bierkandt |first3=Robert |last4=Pichler |first4=Peter-Paul |last5=Seto |first5=Karen C. |title=Global typology of urban energy use and potentials for an urbanization mitigation wedge |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |date=19 May 2015 |volume=112 |issue=20 |pages=6283–6288 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1315545112 |pmid=25583508 |pmc=4443311 |bibcode=2015PNAS..112.6283C |doi-access=free }}</ref>

The transition from fossil-fuel-based cars and trucks to [[electric vehicles]] (EVs) is occurring globally.  China has been a major center of technology growth for EVs.  Vehicle-fuel technologies that can contribute to reductions in energy use include [[Hybrid electric vehicle|hybrid electric]], [[Plug-in electric vehicle|plug-in electric]], [[Natural gas vehicle|natural gas]], and [[Ethanol fuel|bioethanol-powered]] vehicles. The last diesel and gasoline cars are expected to be produced in the 2020s, with 25% or more of all vehicles worldwide being electric by 2040 as [[fossil fuel]] prices rise.<ref name="Seto"/>

[[File:Clean mobility instead of dirty traffic.jpg|thumb|Possible scenario of smart and [[sustainable mobility]]]]
A narrow focus on electrifying vehicles can lead planners to overlook opportunities for increasing efficiency within existing systems.<ref name="Padmanaban"/> Good urban planning can develop an infrastructure that combines and supports initiatives in multiple areas. For example, the generation of solar power and the provision of recharge hubs near public transit can support the use of electric vehicles for both private and public transit.<ref name="Seto"/> Another way to support use of electric vehicles might be to integrate EV charging points into lampposts.<ref name="IEA2021"/>

Increasingly, city planners are looking to the use of digital technologies to create [[Smart city|smarter and more sustainable cities]].<ref name="Michie">{{cite news |last1=Michie |first1=Craig |last2=Cohen |first2=Ronald |title=How measuring emissions in real time can help cities achieve net zero |url=https://theconversation.com/how-measuring-emissions-in-real-time-can-help-cities-achieve-net-zero-172651 |access-date=13 September 2022 |work=The Conversation |date=December 17, 2021 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="C40Map">{{cite web |title=How to determine your city's net zero carbon buildings strategy |url=https://www.c40knowledgehub.org/s/article/How-to-determine-your-city-s-net-zero-carbon-buildings-strategy?language=en_US |website=C40 Knowledge Community|date=2022 |access-date=13 September 2022}}</ref>  By gathering large diverse datasets and modelling the impact of possible interventions, planners hope to identify and target key aspects of energy use, air quality, and traffic for improvement. By incorporating smart measurement technology into buildings, lighting, appliances and transportation, systems can better adapt to changing conditions, reduce energy consumption, and improve city services.<ref name="empowering">{{cite web |title=Empowering "Smart Cities" toward net zero emissions - News |url=https://www.iea.org/news/empowering-smart-cities-toward-net-zero-emissions |website=IEA|date=22 July 2021 |access-date=13 September 2022}}</ref><ref name="IEA2021"/>

=== Heating, cooling and cooking ===
[[File:Induktionshäll.JPG|thumb | right | 210px | [[Induction cooking]]]]
Heating, cooling and cooking are also targets for improved energy efficiency and reduction of carbon emissions. Increasingly following Europe and Asia, North Americans are switching from [[Gas stove|gas]] or [[Electric stove|electrical resistance stoves]] to [[induction cooking]].<ref name="Sederman">{{cite web |last1=Sederman |first1=Adelina |title=The Clean Energy Home Series (Part 3): What are Electric and Induction Cooktops? |url=https://environmentamerica.org/center/articles/the-clean-energy-home-series-part-3-what-are-electric-and-induction-cooktops/ |website=Environment America Research & Policy Center |date=18 March 2022 |access-date=12 September 2022}}</ref><ref name="McKivigan">{{cite news |last1=McKivigan |first1=Meg St-Esprit |title=How electric stoves are poised to dethrone the mighty gas range |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/home/2022/02/17/induction-cooktops-healthier-alternative-to-gas-stove/ |access-date=12 September 2022 |newspaper=Washington Post |date=February 17, 2022}}</ref> Consumers are also switching heating systems from coal, [[fuel oil]], or natural gas to electricity-driven steam or hot water; and to [[Air source heat pump|air-source]] or [[Ground source heat pump|ground-source heat pumps]] for both heating and cooling.<ref name="Seto"/>

=== Food ===
Food production tends to be heavily dependent on fossil fuels,  in the production of [[nitrogen fertilizer]] and to power [[agricultural machinery]] used in the planting, tending and harvesting of crops.<ref name="Woods">{{cite journal |last1=Woods |first1=Jeremy |last2=Williams |first2=Adrian |last3=Hughes |first3=John K. |last4=Black |first4=Mairi |last5=Murphy |first5=Richard |title=Energy and the food system |journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences |date=27 September 2010 |volume=365 |issue=1554 |pages=2991–3006 |doi=10.1098/rstb.2010.0172 |pmid=20713398 |pmc=2935130 }}</ref><ref name="Selvanandan">{{cite news |last1=Selvanandan |first1=Vamini |title=COMMENTARY: Food for a healthy planet and healthy people |url=https://www.rmotoday.com/opinion/commentary-food-for-a-healthy-planet-and-healthy-people-5807684 |access-date=19 September 2022 |work=RMOToday.com |date=19 September 2022 |language=en}}</ref>  The movement of food from producers to consumers also tends to involve major fossil-fuel costs, since many crops are grown far from their potential market and have a short shelf life.<ref name="Norton">{{cite web |last1=Norton |first1=Daphne |title= Energy Expenditures Related to Food Production |url=https://sustainability.emory.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/InfoSheet-Energy26FoodProduction.pdf |website=Emory University |access-date=13 September 2022}}</ref>  Many countries depend on international markets to obtain critical food supplies. Food production and [[supply chain]]s are being increasingly destabilized by the [[effects of climate change on agriculture]], the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], and the [[Russian invasion of Ukraine]].<ref name="McClements"/><ref name="Baylis">{{cite journal |last1=Baylis |first1=Kathy |last2=Heckelei |first2=Thomas |last3=Hertel |first3=Thomas W. |title=Agricultural Trade and Environmental Sustainability |journal=Annual Review of Resource Economics |date=5 October 2021 |volume=13 |issue=1 |pages=379–401 |doi=10.1146/annurev-resource-101420-090453 }}</ref><ref name="Bankova">{{cite news |last1=Bankova |first1=Dea |last2=Dutta |first2=Prasanta Kumar |last3=Ovaska |first3=Michael |title=The war in Ukraine is fuelling a global food crisis |url=https://graphics.reuters.com/UKRAINE-CRISIS/FOOD/zjvqkgomjvx/ |access-date=13 September 2022 |work=Reuters |date=May 30, 2022 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Climate Change |url=http://www.ers.usda.gov/topics/natural-resources-environment/climate-change |website=USDA ERS |access-date=13 September 2022}}</ref> In the United States, at the same time that millions of Americans experience [[food insecurity]], as much as 40 percent of [[Food loss and waste|food is wasted]].<ref name="Mugica"/>

[[File:Farmer's Market Peppers.jpg|thumb | right | 210px | To eat locally, shop at a neighborhood farmer's market]]
[[File:Food rescued from going to the garbage.jpg|thumb | right | 210px | Usable retail food past its "best by" date, for redistribution to those in need]]
At the consumer level, steps towards achieving net zero include eating more local and plant-based foods, minimizing food waste, and composting remaining plant-based wastes. Consumers and investors may also choose to support companies based on their carbon footprint and transparency.<ref name="WEF-food">{{cite news |title=Food systems can lead the way to net zero, if we act now |url=https://www.weforum.org/agenda/2022/03/food-systems-net-zero/ |access-date=13 September 2022 |work=World Economic Forum |date=March 16, 2022 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Mugica"/><ref name="Selvanandan"/>

In terms of city infrastructure, initiatives to identify and redirect usable food ("[[food rescue]]"),<ref name="harvest">{{cite web |title=How to Start a Food Rescue Program in Your Community |url=https://www.cityharvest.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/StartaFoodRescueOrg.pdf |website=City Harvest |access-date=19 September 2022}}</ref> to separate waste streams, and to improve handling of food waste are all important.<ref name="Povich">{{cite news |last1=Povich |first1=Elaine S. |title=Waste Not? Some States Are Sending Less Food to Landfills |url=https://www.pewtrusts.org/en/research-and-analysis/blogs/stateline/2021/07/08/waste-not-some-states-are-sending-less-food-to-landfills |access-date=13 September 2022 |work=pew.org |date=July 9, 2021 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Mugica">{{cite book |last1=Mugica |first1=Yerina |last2=Rose |first2=Terra |title=Tackling Food Waste in Cities - A Policy and Program Toolkit |date=2019 |publisher=Natural Resources Defense Council |url=https://www.nrdc.org/sites/default/files/food-waste-cities-policy-toolkit-report.pdf |access-date=13 September 2022}}</ref><ref name="Selvanandan"/>
In low-income countries, small-scale and household-level [[biogas]] systems are being used to convert wastes into energy. [[Composting]] and [[anaerobic digestion]] (AD) are increasingly being used in countries at all income levels.<ref name="Spang">{{cite journal |last1=Spang |first1=Edward S. |last2=Moreno |first2=Laura C. |last3=Pace |first3=Sara A. |last4=Achmon |first4=Yigal |last5=Donis-Gonzalez |first5=Irwin |last6=Gosliner |first6=Wendi A. |last7=Jablonski-Sheffield |first7=Madison P. |last8=Momin |first8=Md Abdul |last9=Quested |first9=Tom E. |last10=Winans |first10=Kiara S. |last11=Tomich |first11=Thomas P. |title=Food Loss and Waste: Measurement, Drivers, and Solutions |journal=Annual Review of Environment and Resources |date=17 October 2019 |volume=44 |issue=1 |pages=117–156 |doi=10.1146/annurev-environ-101718-033228 }}</ref><ref name="Kaza">{{cite book |last1=Kaza |first1=Silpa |last2=Yao |first2=Lisa C. |last3=Bhada-Tata |first3=Perinaz |last4=Van Woerden |first4=Frank |title=What a Waste 2.0 |date=20 September 2018 |publisher=World Bank |location=Washington, DC |doi=10.1596/978-1-4648-1329-0 |isbn=978-1-4648-1329-0 }}</ref>

Farmers and farming communities need scientific, technical, and financial support to move to more climate-friendly farming practices and to support initiatives for [[climate change adaptation]], [[regenerative agriculture]] and [[biosequestration]].<ref name="WEF-food"/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Niles |first1=Meredith T.|author1-link=Meredith Niles |last2=Ahuja |first2=Richie |last3=Barker |first3=Todd |last4=Esquivel |first4=Jimena |last5=Gutterman |first5=Sophie |last6=Heller |first6=Martin C. |last7=Mango |first7=Nelson |last8=Portner |first8=Diana |last9=Raimond |first9=Rex |last10=Tirado |first10=Cristina |last11=Vermeulen |first11=Sonja |title=Climate change mitigation beyond agriculture: a review of food system opportunities and implications |journal=Renewable Agriculture and Food Systems |date=June 2018 |volume=33 |issue=3 |pages=297–308 |doi=10.1017/S1742170518000029 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Anyiam |first1=P. N. |last2=Adimuko |first2=G. C. |last3=Nwamadi |first3=C. P. |last4=Guibunda |first4=F. A. |last5=Kamale |first5=Y. J. |title=Sustainable Food System Transformation in a Changing Climate |journal=Nigeria Agricultural Journal |date=31 December 2021 |volume=52 |issue=3 |pages=105–115 |url=https://www.ajol.info/index.php/naj/article/view/223414 }}</ref><ref name="Miao">{{cite journal |last1=Miao |first1=Ruiqing |last2=Khanna |first2=Madhu |title=Harnessing Advances in Agricultural Technologies to Optimize Resource Utilization in the Food-Energy-Water Nexus |journal=Annual Review of Resource Economics |date=6 October 2020 |volume=12 |issue=1 |pages=65–85 |doi=10.1146/annurev-resource-110319-115428 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Collaboration between stakeholders at all levels of the private, public and civil sectors is needed to improve food sector infrastructure.<ref name="WEF-food"/><ref name="McClements">{{cite journal |last1=McClements |first1=David Julian |last2=Barrangou |first2=Rodolphe |last3=Hill |first3=Colin |last4=Kokini |first4=Jozef L. |last5=Lila |first5=Mary Ann |last6=Meyer |first6=Anne S. |last7=Yu |first7=Liangli |title=Building a Resilient, Sustainable, and Healthier Food Supply Through Innovation and Technology |journal=Annual Review of Food Science and Technology |date=25 March 2021 |volume=12 |issue=1 |pages=1–28 |doi=10.1146/annurev-food-092220-030824 |pmid=33348992 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

=== Construction ===
[[File:House Energy Efficiency Features.png|thumb | right | 210px | Common residential energy efficiency features: tight construction, insulation, energy efficient windows, heating and cooling]]
[[File:Nullenergiehaus ArM.jpg|thumb | right | 210px | Zero energy house built in Germany, 1992, with photovoltaic and thermal-solar systems]]

The [[building energy efficiency|energy efficiency of buildings]] can be assessed and improved in multiple ways that help to reduce carbon emissions.<ref>{{cite web |title=Net Zero: what to measure and where to begin. |url=https://hoarelea.com/2020/04/07/net-zero-what-to-measure-and-where-to-begin/ |website=Hoare Lea |access-date=13 September 2022 |date=7 April 2020 |archive-date=13 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220913133520/https://hoarelea.com/2020/04/07/net-zero-what-to-measure-and-where-to-begin/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> 
Insulation and energy-efficient windows are commonly used in colder cities.  Incorporation of features such as solar panels, green roofs and walls, and heat pumps into new or existing buildings can significantly reduce energy use.<ref name="Pell">{{cite web |last1=Pell |first1=Billy |title=Energy Efficient Building Design: 23 Key Features To Consider |url=https://aeroseal.com/air-duct-sealing-blog/energy-efficient-building-design/ |website=Aeroseal |access-date=12 September 2022 |date=9 May 2019}}</ref> 
New types of materials such as [[smart glass]] are being developed to improve the energy efficiency of buildings.<ref name="Miller">{{cite journal |last1=Miller |first1=Brittney J. |title=How smart windows save energy |journal=Knowable Magazine |date=2022 |doi=10.1146/knowable-060822-3 }}</ref> 

Energy efficiency is not the only factor to consider.  Types of materials used can vary widely in both their up-front and over-time carbon costs. It is important to carefully consider the up-front embodied emissions of existing materials.<ref name="Jungclaus">{{cite book |last1=Jungclaus |first1=Matt |last2=Esau |first2=Rebecca |last3=Olgyay |first3=Victor |last4=Rempher |first4=Audrey |title=Reducing Embodied Carbon in Buildings Low-Cost, High-Value Opportunities |date=2021 |publisher=RMI |url=https://rmi.org/wp-content/uploads/dlm_uploads/2021/08/Embodied_Carbon_full_report.pdf}}</ref><ref name="King">{{cite book |last1=King |first1=Bruce |first2=Chris |last2=Magwood |title=Build beyond zero : new ideas for carbon-smart architecture |date=2022 |publisher=Island Press |location=Washington D.C. |isbn=9781642832112}}</ref><ref name="Magwood">{{cite report |last1=Magwood |first1=Chris |last2=Bowden |first2=Erik |last3=Trottier |first3=Melanie |title=Emissions of Materials Benchmark Assessment for Residential Construction (EMBARC) |date=2022 |doi=10.13140/RG.2.2.34242.66243 }}</ref><ref>{{cite thesis |last1=Magwood |first1=Chris |title=Opportunities for CO2 Capture and Storage in Building Materials |date=2019 |doi=10.13140/RG.2.2.32171.39208 }}</ref><ref name="Kreps">{{cite news |last1=Kreps |first1=Bart Hawkins |title='Getting to zero' is a lousy goal |url=https://www.resilience.org/stories/2022-08-09/getting-to-zero-is-a-lousy-goal/ |access-date=27 September 2022 |work=Resilience |date=9 August 2022}}</ref> Researchers are also working to develop construction materials that do not release carbon during manufacturing or that can absorb and store more carbon.<ref name="Padmanaban"/><ref name="Ürge-Vorsatz">{{cite journal |last1=Ürge-Vorsatz |first1=Diana |last2=Khosla |first2=Radhika |last3=Bernhardt |first3=Rob |last4=Chan |first4=Yi Chieh |last5=Vérez |first5=David |last6=Hu |first6=Shan |last7=Cabeza |first7=Luisa F. |title=Advances Toward a Net-Zero Global Building Sector |journal=Annual Review of Environment and Resources |date=17 October 2020 |volume=45 |issue=1 |pages=227–269 |doi=10.1146/annurev-environ-012420-045843 |doi-access=free }}</ref>  [[Steel]] and [[cement]] are heavily used in construction and are very energy intensive to make. Biomass-based materials such as wood and bamboo have lower energy-formation costs. Practices for recycling and reusing construction waste can also save on the amount of energy that has gone into producing and transporting materials.<ref name="Seto"/>

The size of buildings has an impact on their energy costs in terms of both construction and use.<ref name="Seto"/>  Some recommend a four-storey multi-family building built of low-carbon higher density materials such as straw and wood as an ideal.<ref name="Alter">{{cite news |last1=Alter |first1=Lloyd |title=Landmark Study Shows How to Change the Building Sector From a Major Carbon Emitter to a Major Carbon Sink |url=https://www.treehugger.com/green-architecture/landmark-study-shows-how-change-building-sector-major-carbon-emitter-major-carbon-sink.html |access-date=27 September 2022 |work=Treehugger |date=December 10, 2019 |language=en}}</ref>  Mid-size multi-unit buildings can support economies of scale during building and are likely to be more economical in use than single-unit homes. High-rise buildings, particularly in hot climates, are more costly to cool and operate. When planning an area, a mix of mid- and high-rise buildings in a compact urban format is likely to be efficient.<ref name="Seto"/>

=== Green infrastructure ===
[[File:Green infrastructure Directorate-General for Environment.jpg|thumb|right|210px|Potential components of green infrastructure, European Commission]]
[[File:2012-12-04 Stormwater Bio-Treatment along sidewalk.jpg|thumb|right|210px | Stormwater management in green space along sidewalk]] 
[[Green infrastructure]] includes private and public garden areas, parks, trees, and urban agriculture. Green infrastructure mitigates the effects of carbon emissions in multiple ways, by naturally [[Carbon dioxide removal|removing and storing carbon dioxide]], and by shading and cooling surrounding areas which reduces energy needs for cooling. The development of green space in cities, particularly long-lived trees, is a cost-effective method of [[carbon sequestration]].<ref name="Seto"/><ref name="Waldrop">{{cite journal |last1=Waldrop |first1=M. Mitchell |title=What can cities do to survive extreme heat? |journal=Knowable Magazine |date=2022 |doi=10.1146/knowable-101922-2 }}</ref> The inclusion of green space in urban areas can also help with wide variety of other issues, from [[stormwater]]<ref>{{cite book |author=Fourth Economy |title=Green Stormwater Infrastructure (GSI) A Tool for Economic Recovery and Growth in Pennsylvania |date=May 2021 |publisher=Sustainable Business Network of Greater Philadelphia |location=Pittsburgh, PA |url=https://www.sbnphiladelphia.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/GSI_A-Tool-for-Economic-Recovery-and-Growth-in-PA_doubleview.pdf |access-date=12 September 2022}}</ref> to mental health.<ref name="Kruize">{{cite journal |last1=Kruize |first1=Hanneke |last2=van der Vliet |first2=Nina |last3=Staatsen |first3=Brigit |last4=Bell |first4=Ruth |last5=Chiabai |first5=Aline |last6=Muiños |first6=Gabriel |last7=Higgins |first7=Sahran |last8=Quiroga |first8=Sonia |last9=Martinez-Juarez |first9=Pablo |last10=Aberg Yngwe |first10=Monica |last11=Tsichlas |first11=Fotis |last12=Karnaki |first12=Pania |last13=Lima |first13=Maria Luísa |last14=García de Jalón |first14=Silvestre |last15=Khan |first15=Matluba |last16=Morris |first16=George |last17=Stegeman |first17=Ingrid |title=Urban Green Space: Creating a Triple Win for Environmental Sustainability, Health, and Health Equity through Behavior Change |journal=International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health |date=11 November 2019 |volume=16 |issue=22 |pages=4403 |doi=10.3390/ijerph16224403 |pmid=31717956 |pmc=6888177 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

=== Waste and energy exchange ===
[[File:Recycling Containers.jpg|thumb |right| 210px|Separating materials for different recycling streams]]
Wastes can be managed through a variety of ways, including reuse, recycling, storage, treatment, energy recovery, and disposal.<ref name="waste">{{cite web |title=Wastes |url=https://www.epa.gov/report-environment/wastes |website=US EPA |access-date=12 September 2022 |language=en |date=2 November 2017}}</ref> 
In some cases, a by-product of one set of processes can be used to advantage by someone else, sometimes referred to as urban industrial symbiosis.<ref name="Seto"/> For example, waste heat from industries and grocery stores has been used to heat residential and commercial buildings.<ref name="Lund">{{cite journal |last1=Lund |first1=Peter D. |last2=Mikkola |first2=Jani |last3=Ypyä |first3=J. |title=Smart energy system design for large clean power schemes in urban areas |journal=Journal of Cleaner Production |date=15 September 2015 |volume=103 |pages=437–445 |doi=10.1016/j.jclepro.2014.06.005 |bibcode=2015JCPro.103..437L }}</ref>  The city of [[Charlotte, North Carolina]] has identified becoming a zero waste city as one of four key areas of performance for the goal of developing a [[circular economy]].<ref name="Charlotte"/>

[[File:Landfill gas collection system.JPG|thumb |right|210px |Landfill Gas Collection]]
"[[Waste-to-energy]]" describes processes through which useful by-products such as energy can be recovered from otherwise unusable sources.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Murphy |first1=Michael L. |title=Encyclopedia of Energy |chapter=Waste-to-Energy Technology |date=2004 |pages=373–383 |doi=10.1016/B0-12-176480-X/00359-4 |isbn=978-0-12-176480-7 }}</ref>
Technologies for [[carbon capture and storage]] are being developed to mitigate emissions from fossil fuel power plants and industrial sources.<ref name="Abdulla">{{cite journal |last1=Abdulla |first1=Ahmed |last2=Hanna |first2=Ryan |last3=Schell |first3=Kristen R. |last4=Babacan |first4=Oytun |last5=Victor |first5=David G. |display-authors=4 |title=Explaining successful and failed investments in U.S. carbon capture and storage using empirical and expert assessments |journal=Environmental Research Letters |date=29 December 2020 |volume=16 |issue=1 |page=014036 |doi=10.1088/1748-9326/abd19e |doi-access=free }}</ref> 
The collection and disposal of waste can potentially be used for the generation of electricity, steam, or heat, but systems to support this are not yet well developed.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Narayan |first1=Abishek Sankara |last2=Marks |first2=Sara J. |last3=Meierhofer |first3=Regula |last4=Strande |first4=Linda |last5=Tilley |first5=Elizabeth |last6=Zurbrügg |first6=Christian |last7=Lüthi |first7=Christoph |title=Advancements in and Integration of Water, Sanitation, and Solid Waste for Low- and Middle-Income Countries |journal=Annual Review of Environment and Resources |date=18 October 2021 |volume=46 |issue=1 |pages=193–219 |doi=10.1146/annurev-environ-030620-042304 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Huovila">{{cite journal |last1=Huovila |first1=Aapo |last2=Siikavirta |first2=Hanne |last3=Antuña Rozado |first3=Carmen |last4=Rökman |first4=Jyri |last5=Tuominen |first5=Pekka |last6=Paiho |first6=Satu |last7=Hedman |first7=Åsa |last8=Ylén |first8=Peter |title=Carbon-neutral cities: Critical review of theory and practice |journal=Journal of Cleaner Production |date=20 March 2022 |volume=341 |article-number=130912 |doi=10.1016/j.jclepro.2022.130912 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2022JCPro.34130912H }}</ref> 

Reviews of attempts to attain zero-waste note that the term is used widely and not consistently.  Many countries lack an overall zero waste strategy.<ref name="Zaman"/>  In most cases in the United States, waste management is inefficient.<ref name="waste"/> Without clear national zero waste strategy and policies that identify key areas, it is difficult to coordinate and promote zero waste initiatives in communities and industry.<ref name="Zaman">{{cite journal |last1=Zaman |first1=Atiq Uz |title=A comprehensive review of the development of zero waste management: lessons learned and guidelines |journal= Journal of Cleaner Production |date=2015 |volume=91 |pages=12–25 |doi=10.1016/j.jclepro.2014.12.013 |bibcode=2015JCPro..91...12Z }}</ref><ref name="IEA2021"/>

== Measuring net zero ==
Assessing the urban [[carbon footprint]] of cities is a complex issue.<ref name="Kelly"/><ref name="C40Map"/><ref name="Michie"/><ref name="Ramaswami"/><ref name="Huo">{{cite journal |last1=Huo |first1=Da |last2=Huang |first2=Xiaoting |last3=Dou |first3=Xinyu |last4=Ciais |first4=Philippe |last5=Li |first5=Yun |last6=Deng |first6=Zhu |last7=Wang |first7=Yilong |last8=Cui |first8=Duo |last9=Benkhelifa |first9=Fouzi |last10=Sun |first10=Taochun |last11=Zhu |first11=Biqing |last12=Roest |first12=Geoffrey |last13=Gurney |first13=Kevin R. |last14=Ke |first14=Piyu |last15=Guo |first15=Rui |last16=Lu |first16=Chenxi |last17=Lin |first17=Xiaojuan |last18=Lovell |first18=Arminel |last19=Appleby |first19=Kyra |last20=DeCola |first20=Philip L. |last21=Davis |first21=Steven J. |last22=Liu |first22=Zhu |title=Carbon Monitor Cities near-real-time daily estimates of {{CO2}} emissions from 1500 cities worldwide |journal=Scientific Data |date=1 September 2022 |volume=9 |issue=1 |pages=533 |doi=10.1038/s41597-022-01657-z |pmid=36050332 |pmc=9434530 |bibcode=2022NatSD...9..533H }}</ref><ref name="Moran">{{cite journal |last1=Moran |first1=Daniel |last2=Kanemoto |first2=Keiichiro |last3=Jiborn |first3=Magnus |last4=Wood |first4=Richard |last5=Többen |first5=Johannes |last6=Seto |first6=Karen C |title=Carbon footprints of 13 000 cities |journal=Environmental Research Letters |date=1 June 2018 |volume=13 |issue=6 |pages=064041 |doi=10.1088/1748-9326/aac72a |bibcode=2018ERL....13f4041M |doi-access=free |hdl=11250/2504867 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref name="count">{{cite web |title=What is your carbon footprint? |url=https://www.nature.org/en-us/get-involved/how-to-help/carbon-footprint-calculator/ |website=The Nature Conservancy |access-date=27 September 2022}}</ref>  
Four major accounting systems for measuring urban greenhouse gases have been developed, each with a slightly different conceptualization of what it means to be a net-zero carbon city: territorial source-based accounting, community-wide infrastructure supply chain greenhouse gas footprinting, consumption-based GHG accounting, and total community-wide greenhouse gas footprinting.<ref name="Seto"/><ref name="Ramaswami">{{cite journal |last1=Ramaswami |first1=Anu |last2=Tong |first2=Kangkang |last3=Canadell |first3=Josep G. |last4=Jackson |first4=Robert B. |last5=Stokes |first5=Eleanor (Kellie) |last6=Dhakal |first6=Shobhakar |last7=Finch |first7=Mario |last8=Jittrapirom |first8=Peraphan |last9=Singh |first9=Neelam |last10=Yamagata |first10=Yoshiki |last11=Yewdall |first11=Eli |last12=Yona |first12=Leehi |last13=Seto |first13=Karen C. |title=Carbon analytics for net-zero emissions sustainable cities |journal=Nature Sustainability |date=June 2021 |volume=4 |issue=6 |pages=460–463 |doi=10.1038/s41893-021-00715-5 |bibcode=2021NatSu...4..460R }}</ref><ref name="Heinonen">{{cite journal |last1=Heinonen |first1=Jukka |last2=Ottelin |first2=Juudit |last3=Ala-Mantila |first3=Sanna |last4=Wiedmann |first4=Thomas |last5=Clarke |first5=Jack |last6=Junnila |first6=Seppo |title=Spatial consumption-based carbon footprint assessments - A review of recent developments in the field |journal=Journal of Cleaner Production |date=20 May 2020 |volume=256 |article-number=120335 |doi=10.1016/j.jclepro.2020.120335 |bibcode=2020JCPro.25620335H |hdl=1959.4/102091 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Lombardi">{{cite journal |last1=Lombardi |first1=Mariarosaria |last2=Laiola |first2=Elisabetta |last3=Tricase |first3=Caterina |last4=Rana |first4=Roberto |title=Assessing the urban carbon footprint: An overview |journal=Environmental Impact Assessment Review |date=1 September 2017 |volume=66 |pages=43–52 |doi=10.1016/j.eiar.2017.06.005 |bibcode=2017EIARv..66...43L }}</ref><ref name="Chavez">{{cite journal |last1=Chavez |first1=Abel |last2=Ramaswami |first2=Anu |title=Articulating a trans-boundary infrastructure supply chain greenhouse gas emission footprint for cities: Mathematical relationships and policy relevance |journal=Energy Policy |date=1 March 2013 |volume=54 |pages=376–384 |doi=10.1016/j.enpol.2012.10.037 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2013EnPol..54..376C }}</ref>
The [[United Kingdom]] is one example of a country that is measuring greenhouse gas emissions and assessing its progress towards net zero using a variety of different official measures.<ref name="UKStats">{{cite web |title=Net zero and the different official measures of the UK's greenhouse gas emissions - Office for National Statistics |url=https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/environmentalaccounts/articles/netzeroandthedifferentofficialmeasuresoftheuksgreenhousegasemissions/2019-07-24#measuring-the-uks-progress-to-net-zero |website=www.ons.gov.uk|date=24 July 2019 |access-date=13 September 2022}}</ref>

==Examples==
=== Converting existing cities ===
Increasingly, existing cities are planning to become low or zero carbon. {{As of|2022}}, over 1000 cities worldwide have undertaken steps to transition in response to [[climate change]] as part of the [[Cities Race to Zero]] campaign,<ref name="Wray">{{cite news |last1=Wray |first1=Sarah |title='We need to do more': COP26 city highlights – November 2 |url=https://cities-today.com/we-need-to-do-more-cop26-city-highlights-november-2/ |access-date=31 August 2022 |work=Cities Today |date=2 November 2021}}</ref><ref name="C40">{{cite web |title=From LA to Bogotá to London, global mayors unite to deliver critical city momentum to world leaders tasked with keeping 1.5 degree hopes alive at Glasgow's COP26 |url=https://www.c40.org/news/cop-26-cities-race-to-zero/ |website=C40 Cities |access-date=31 August 2022|date=November 2, 2021}}</ref> one part of the larger [[United Nations Race to Zero]] campaign.<ref name="Bindman">{{cite news |last1=Bindman |first1=Polly |title=Which cities are in the race to net zero? |url=https://capitalmonitor.ai/sdgs/sdg-11-sustainable-cities-and-communities/green-cities-race-net-zero/ |access-date=13 September 2022 |work=Capital Monitor |date=22 July 2022}}</ref> In the United States, more than 100 cities have pledged to participate in Cities Race to Zero.<ref name="C40-USA">{{cite news |title=More than 100 American Cities Make Historic Pledge to Accelerate Net-Zero Emissions, Deliver Action Needed to Meet National Climate Goals |url=https://www.c40.org/news/american-cities-net-zero-climate-goals/ |access-date=13 September 2022 |work=C40 Cities |date=October 25, 2021}}</ref>
The following examples illustrate some of the types of initiatives for net zero cities, the extent to which they received multi-level support, and their impact.<ref name="Seto"/>
 
==== Bulawayo, Zimbabwe ====
As the second largest city in [[Zimbabwe]], with an urban population between 680,000 and 1.5 million people, [[Bulawayo]] has gone through a period of rapid growth in the twentieth century;  an economic decline in the first decade of the twenty-first century; and next a return to rapid growth that incorporates the [[United Nations Sustainable Development Goals]] into the city's strategic plan. Bulawayo hopes to "leapfrog" over existing technology and recreate its economy by adopting next generation technology.<ref name="Seto"/>

[[File:Acacia sieberiana 2.jpg|thumb | right | 210px | ''[[Vachellia sieberiana]]'' trees support [[carbon sequestration]]<ref name="Chidumayo">{{cite book |editor-first1=Emmanuel N. |editor-first2=Davison J. |editor-last1=Chidumayo |editor-last2=Gumbo |title=The Dry Forests and Woodlands of Africa |date=2010 |doi=10.4324/9781849776547 |isbn=978-1-136-53138-5 }}{{pn|date=September 2025}}</ref> ]]
Initiatives include replacement of the city's power station with renewable solar power, "Trackless Trams" for transit, smart technologies for electrical grid management, and circular economy technologies to manage and reduce waste.<ref name="Seto"/> Researchers are also examining fuelwood production and the potential for carbon sequestration in Bulawayo's public green spaces.<ref name="Ngulani">{{cite journal |last1=Ngulani |first1=Thembelihle |last2=Shackleton |first2=Charlie M. |title=Fuelwood Production and Carbon Sequestration in Public Urban Green Spaces in Bulawayo, Zimbabwe |journal=Forests |date=May 2022 |volume=13 |issue=5 |pages=741 |doi=10.3390/f13050741 |bibcode=2022Fore...13..741N |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==== Canberra, Australia ====
[[File:Manning Clark North light rail stop, Canberra, looking west, November 2019.jpg|thumb | right | 210px  |[[Manning Clark North light rail station]], Canberra<ref name="Canberra">{{cite web |title=CMET is committed to delivering a safe, efficient rail network that creates environmental, social and economic benefit for Canberra |url=https://cmet.com.au/about/sustainability/ |website=Canberra Metro Operations |date=2 August 2018 |access-date=19 September 2022}}</ref>]]
[[File:Bikeway UC.jpg|thumb | right | 210px  | [[Belconnen Bikeway]] passing the University of Canberra]]

The [[Australian Capital Territory]] (ACT) which contains the capital [[Canberra, Australia]] was the first area in Australia to adopt a net-zero process for an entire urban region. Canberra is known for its strong urban planning and attention to climate change objectives.<ref name="Seto"/><ref name="ACT2019"/>

ACT passed a Climate Change and Greenhouse Gas Reduction Act as of 2010. Its Climate Council set 5-year goals with regular progress reports. As reported in ''Climate Change Strategy 2019–2025'' (2019), Canberra committed to reducing emissions by 40% from 1990 to 2020.  It has achieved that goal by shifting to the purchase of 100% renewable energy sources through the National Electricity Grid. The city has also improved transportation through the use of zero emissions light rail and buses, and added cycling paths.  Through these and other initiatives, Canberra's current goal is to use 100% renewable energy by 2045.<ref name="Seto"/><ref name="ACT2019">{{cite book |last1=Australian Capital Territory. Environment |first1=Planning and Sustainable Development Directorate |title=Canberra's living infrastructure plan : cooling the city. |date=2019 |publisher=Australian Capital Territory, Canberra |location=Canberra City, Australian Capital Territory |isbn=978-1-921117-84-8 |url=https://www.environment.act.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0003/1414641/ACT-Climate-Change-Strategy-2019-2025.pdf |access-date=13 September 2022}}</ref>

==== Chongming, China ====
{{Main|Chongming District}}
[[File:Dongping Na Fo Park 05.jpg|thumb | right | 210px | Dongping Forest Park on Chongming Island provides [[carbon sequestration]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Zhe |last2=Cui |first2=Xuan |last3=Yin |first3=Shan |last4=Shen |first4=GuangRong |last5=Han |first5=YuJie |last6=Liu |first6=ChunJiang |title=Characteristics of carbon storage in Shanghai's urban forest |journal=Chinese Science Bulletin |date=April 2013 |volume=58 |issue=10 |pages=1130–1138 |doi=10.1007/s11434-012-5443-1 |bibcode=2013ChSBu..58.1130W }}</ref>]]

Over the last decade, [[Shanghai]], China has implemented dozens of low carbon policies to reduce energy usage and address the effects of climate change.<ref name="Peng 201–212"/> 
Chongming Island, once a rural area of Shanghai, is one focus for net zero city development. In 2001, the Shanghai Municipal Government (SMG) proposed the creation of a low-carbon eco-island to explore the potential for the development of low-carbon cities. The American firm Skidmore, Owings & Merrill was competitively chosen as the designer of the Chongming Master Plan in 2004.<ref name="Seto"/><ref name="Yi"/><ref name="Zhao"/>

[[File:Dry - solid-state anaerobic digestion AD biogas plant.jpg|thumb | right | 210px | Diagram for dry solid-state anaerobic digestion AD [[biogas]] plant]]
In 2010, SMG developed the Chongming Eco-Island Construction Outline as a framework with indicators for redesigning Chongming. These included using energy-saving materials, recycled materials and solar energy to construct new buildings; upgrading existing buildings to save energy;  closing the existing coal plant; developing renewable energy sources (wind, solar, and [[biogas]]); converting buses to electric vehicles and adding foot and bicycle paths; recycling wastewater with low-carbon techniques; reusing wastes for organic fertilizer and biogas; and the development of forests and wetlands to sequester carbon. Factories were required to meet strict ecological requirements or shut down; economic development has been slow and many residents are unemployed.<ref name="Seto"/><ref name="Yi">{{cite news |last1=Yi |first1=Shi |title=Shanghai leads way in China's carbon transition |url=https://www.eco-business.com/news/shanghai-leads-way-in-chinas-carbon-transition/ |access-date=13 September 2022 |work=Eco-Business |date=June 28, 2021 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Zhao">{{cite journal |last1=Zhao |first1=Changying |last2=Ju |first2=Shenghong |last3=Xue |first3=Yuan |last4=Ren |first4=Tao |last5=Ji |first5=Ya |last6=Chen |first6=Xue |title=China's energy transitions for carbon neutrality: challenges and opportunities |journal=Carbon Neutrality |date=19 April 2022 |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=7 |doi=10.1007/s43979-022-00010-y |doi-access=free |bibcode=2022CarNe...1....7Z |pmc=9015888 }}</ref>

==== Copenhagen, Denmark ====
[[File:Middelgrunden wind farm 2009-07-01 edit filtered.jpg|thumb |right |210px | Middelgrunden offshore wind farm near Copenhagen, Denmark, 2009 ]]
In 2012 [[Copenhagen]], Denmark created the CPH2025 Climate Plan with the target of becoming the first carbon-neutral capital by 2025 and for Denmark to be entirely carbon-neutral by 2050.<ref name="Szumski"/> The city has shifted energy and heating systems to use wind, solar and biomass for heating and sea water for cooling; improved transit by using electric cars and adding bicycle paths, and renovated buildings to be more energy efficient.<ref name="Gerdes">{{cite news |last1=Gerdes |first1=Justin |title=Copenhagen's ambitious push to be carbon-neutral by 2025 |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2013/apr/12/copenhagen-push-carbon-neutral-2025 |access-date=13 September 2022 |work=the Guardian |date=12 April 2013 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Carbon neutral capital |url=https://international.kk.dk/carbon-neutral-capital |website=international.kk.dk |access-date=13 September 2022 |language=en}}</ref> From 2009-2022, Copenhagen reduced {{CO2}} emissions by 80%.<ref name="Szumski"/>

To achieve the remaining 20% reduction, the city hoped to use [[carbon capture and storage]] (CCS).  In 2022, the state indicated that the proposed Amager Resource Centre (ARC) incinerator would not qualify for state financial aid under equity capital requirements of the state's CCS funding program.  Copenhagen has stated that it still hopes to achieve a 100% reduction in carbon emissions, but will not be able to do so by 2025.<ref name="Szumski">{{cite news |last1=Szumski |first1=Charles |title=Copenhagen's dream of being carbon neutral by 2025 goes up in smoke |url=https://www.euractiv.com/section/energy-environment/news/copenhagens-dream-of-being-carbon-neutral-by-2025-go-up-in-smoke/ |access-date=13 September 2022 |work=www.euractiv.com |date=23 August 2022}}</ref>

==== Denver, USA ====
[[File:SD2017 Gallery of Houses (37471239722).jpg|thumb | right | 210px | CRETE house, collecting rainwater and creating shade with green walls, 2017 [[Solar Decathlon]] (Denver)<ref name="Caulfield">{{cite news |last1=Caulfield |first1=John |title=Takeaways for Builders From the Solar Decathlon |url=https://www.probuilder.com/takeaways-builders-solar-decathlon |access-date=19 September 2022 |work=Professional Builder |date=6 February 2018 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Xie"/><ref>{{cite web |title=Solar Decathlon 2017: Washington University – St. Louis |url=https://www.solardecathlon.gov/2017/where-is-wash-u-now.html |website=www.solardecathlon.gov |access-date=19 September 2022}}</ref>]]
[[File:2017 Solar Decathlon (37471746702).jpg|thumb | right | 210px | Reconstructed BEACH House, 2017 [[Solar Decathlon]] (Denver)<ref name="Xie">{{cite news |last1=Xie |first1=Jenny |title=Tour 11 solar-powered homes that push the limits of sustainable living |url=https://archive.curbed.com/2017/10/17/16455382/solar-decathlon-2017-teams-houses-winner |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201020131342/https://archive.curbed.com/2017/10/17/16455382/solar-decathlon-2017-teams-houses-winner |url-status=dead |archive-date=October 20, 2020 |access-date=19 September 2022 |work=Curbed |date=17 October 2017 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Solar Decathlon 2017: Team Daytona Beach: Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University and Daytona State College |url=https://www.solardecathlon.gov/2017/where-is-daytona-beach-now.html |website=www.solardecathlon.gov |access-date=19 September 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Solar Decathlon: High-Resolution Event Photos |url=https://www.solardecathlon.gov/2017/photos-event.html |website=www.solardecathlon.gov |access-date=19 September 2022}}</ref>]]

[[Denver, Colorado]] is an established city with aging building stock.  It signed its first Climate Action Plan in 2007 with the initial low-carbon goal of reducing emissions per capita by 10% by 2012. Denver achieved this goal as a result of the passage of renewable portfolio standards by the State of Colorado and climate actions on the part of the city.<ref name="Seto"/> 

The city carefully tracked the progress of its climate action plans in detail and modelled the effects of its programs.  They determined that low-carbon actions focusing on efficiency and conservation would be insufficient to reduce GHG emissions at the levels desired.  In 2018, Denver changed its strategy to deep decarbonization. Denver is now proposing to make broad systemic changes with the goal of reducing emissions by 80% by 2050.<ref name="Seto"/>

=== Constructing new cities ===
The following examples were prototyped to be newly built zero-carbon cities: [[Dongtan, Shanghai|Dongtan]],<ref name="Chang">{{cite journal |last1=Chang |first1=I-Chun Catherine |title=Failure matters: Reassembling eco-urbanism in a globalizing China |journal=Environment and Planning A: Economy and Space |date=August 2017 |volume=49 |issue=8 |pages=1719–1742 |doi=10.1177/0308518X16685092 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2017EnPlA..49.1719C }}</ref> China and [[Masdar City]], United Arab Emirates.

====Dongtan, Shanghai====
{{Main|Dongtan, Shanghai}}
[[Dongtan, Shanghai|Dongtan]], China was a sustainable eco-city project planned in the 2000s that was never built.  Dongtan was to be located at the east end of Chongming Island, adjacent to the Chongming Dongtan National Nature Reserve.<ref name="Hart">{{cite news |last1=Hart |first1=Sara |title=Zero-Carbon Cities |url=https://www.architecturalrecord.com/articles/6699-zero-carbon-cities |access-date=14 September 2022 |work=Architectural Record |date=March 19, 2007 |language=en}}</ref> The developers planned on a fully built city, with 80,000 residents by 2020.<ref name="Planning for sustainability">{{cite journal |last1=Cheng |first1=Hefa |last2=Hu |first2=Yuanan |title=Planning for sustainability in China's urban development: Status and challenges for Dongtan eco-city project |journal=J. Environ. Monit. |date=2010 |volume=12 |issue=1 |pages=119–126 |doi=10.1039/b911473d |pmid=20082005 }}</ref>

The planned city's urban design addressed issues of sustainable energy management, waste management, renewable energy process implementation, architecture, infrastructure, and even the planning of communities and social structures.  It proposed to use renewable energy, electric battery or hydrogen-fuel cell transportation, recycled water, hydroponic farming, organic waste recycling and waste-generation of clean energy.<ref name="Hart"/>

However, by 2008, support for the project had disappeared.
Reasons for the project's closure include its proposed location in a highly-valued wetlands area, tensions between its development partners (Arup, a British engineering company, and Shanghai Industrial Investment, a state-owned developer), and loss of political support (due to the jailing of Dongtan's top political backer, former Shanghai Communist Party chief Chen Liangyu, on corruption charges in 2008).<ref name="Brenhouse">{{cite news |last1=Brenhouse |first1=Hillary |title=Plans Shrivel for Chinese Eco-City |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/06/25/business/energy-environment/25iht-rbogdong.html |access-date=14 September 2022 |work=The New York Times |date=24 June 2010}}</ref><ref name="McGirk">{{cite news |last1=McGirk |first1=Jan |title=Why eco-cities fail |url=https://chinadialogue.net/en/cities/7934-why-eco-cities-fail/ |access-date=14 September 2022 |work=China Dialogue |date=May 27, 2015 |language=en}}</ref>

Although the project was not implemented, as an example of urban design it has inspired and informed [[Eco-Cities in China|other cities in China]] and worldwide.<ref name="Chang"/> Ideas from Dongtan were incorporated into the renovation of the [[Chongming District]]. Dongtan became a model for a subsequently [[Sino-Singapore Tianjin Eco-city|planned eco-city]] outside [[Tianjin]].<ref name="Chun">{{cite journal |last1=Chang |first1=I-Chun Catherine |last2=Sheppard |first2=Eric |title=China's Eco-Cities as Variegated 1 Urban Sustainability: Dongtan Eco-City and Chongming Eco-Island |journal=Journal of Urban Technology |date=January 2013 |volume=20 |issue=1 |pages=57–75 |doi=10.1080/10630732.2012.735104 }}</ref>

==== Masdar City, United Arab Emirates ====
{{Main|Masdar City}}
{{external media | width = 210px | float = right | headerimage=  | video1 = [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w2pRGuY0WxE&ab_channel=CBCNews%3ATheNational "Is this the greenest city in the world?"], [[CBC News]],  June 26, 2014.}}

For the Masdar Initiative, [[Foster + Partners]] designed a 2.5-square-mile sustainable carbon and [[waste]]-free city combining the principles of an ancient walled city with modern alternative energy technologies. One of the city's goals was to be self-sufficient in energy by using about 80% solar energy, along with wind and biomass sources. Solar energy was to be generated through [[photovoltaic panels]], [[concentrated solar power|concentrated solar collectors]], and solar thermal tubes.<ref name="Mckenna">{{cite news |last1=Mckenna |first1=Phil |title=First zero-carbon city to rise out of the desert |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn13838-first-zerocarbon-city-to-rise-out-of-the-desert.html |access-date=14 September 2022 |work=New Scientist |date=6 May 2008}}</ref> The city was designed with wind cooling towers and narrow streets to maximize shaded areas and keep cooling costs down. Buildings incorporate solar and geo-thermal cooling as well as using high-tech construction materials and siting.<ref name="Lee">{{cite news |last1=Lee |first1=Susan |title=Masdar City: The ultimate experiment in sustainable urban living? |url=https://www.cnn.com/style/article/conversation-masdar-city-lee/index.html |access-date=14 September 2022 |work=CNN |date=30 September 2016 |language=en}}</ref>

Economically, the city was planned to become a center for alternative energy and technology development as well as an example of their use. The site was located close to Abu Dhabi and an international airport, connecting to surrounding communities through a transportation infrastructure of rail, road and public transit. Transportation within the city was to use battery-powered and auto piloted [[personal rapid transit]] systems (PRT) as well as walking and cycling. Visitors to the city must park their cars outside and use public transit.<ref name="Planning for sustainability"/> 

[[File:Shams solar power plant.jpg|thumb | right | 210px | Solar collectors at Shams 1 solar power plant]]
Construction was planned to occur in phases and began in February 2008. As of 2010, the first buildings went into use in the first section to be completed, a {{frac|3|1|2}}-acre zone that included the [[Masdar Institute of Science and Technology]].<ref name="Ouroussoff">{{cite news |last1=Ouroussoff |first1=Nicolai |title=In Arabian Desert, a Sustainable City Rises |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/09/26/arts/design/26masdar.html |access-date=15 September 2022 |work=The New York Times |date=25 September 2010}}</ref> 
[[Shams Solar Power Station]] (SHAMS 1), Masdar City's main source of power, became operational in 2013, with a capacity of 100 megawatts.<ref name="NREL">{{cite web |title=Shams 1 {{!}} Concentrating Solar Power Projects |url=https://solarpaces.nrel.gov/project/shams-1 |website=National Renewable Energy Laboratory |access-date=15 September 2022}}</ref> It was the largest [[concentrated solar power]] (CSP) facility in the world at that time.<ref name="Quick">{{cite news |last1=Quick |first1=Darren |title=World's largest concentrated solar power plant opens in the UAE |url=https://newatlas.com/shams-1-worlds-largest-concentrated-solar-power-plant/26707/ |access-date=15 September 2022 |work=New Atlas |date=19 March 2013}}</ref><ref name="Dennehy">{{cite news |last1=Dennehy |first1=John |title=From the deserts of Abu Dhabi to the world, how Masdar is building a greener tomorrow |url=https://www.thenationalnews.com/uae/2022/08/18/from-the-deserts-of-abu-dhabi-to-the-world-how-masdar-is-building-a-greener-tomorrow/ |access-date=15 September 2022 |work=The National |date=18 August 2022 |language=en}}</ref>

Originally projected to be completed by 2015, the city's construction was significantly delayed due to the [[2008 financial crisis]].<ref name="Time012011">{{cite magazine |url=http://content.time.com/time/health/article/0,8599,2043934,00.html |title=Masdar City: The World's Greenest City? |magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]] |first=Bryan |last=Walsh |date=25 January 2011 |access-date=8 September 2013 |archive-date=22 April 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210422122307/http://content.time.com/time/health/article/0,8599,2043934,00.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> 
In 2017, Masdar City completed a pilot project for an Eco-Villa, a 405 square-metre four-bedroom property<ref name="Eco-Villa">{{cite news |title=Eco-Villa prototype opens its doors at Masdar City - News - Emirates |url=https://www.emirates247.com/news/emirates/eco-villa-prototype-opens-its-doors-at-masdar-city-2017-01-20-1.646752 |access-date=15 September 2022 |work=Emirates247 |date=January 20, 2017 |language=en}}</ref> presented as an affordable net zero energy family home.<ref name="Gibbon">{{cite news |last1=Gibbon |first1=Gavin |title=Masdar's eco-villas to be designed for Emirati households |url=https://www.arabianbusiness.com/gcc/uae/436155-masdars-eco-villas-to-be-designed-for-emirati-households |access-date=15 September 2022 |work=Arabian Business |date=26 Dec 2019}}</ref><ref name="gate">{{cite news |title=Masdar City Unveils Eco-Villa, the First Net-Zero Energy House - INVEST-GATE |url=https://invest-gate.me/news/masdar-city-unveils-eco-villa-the-first-net-zero-energy-house/ |access-date=15 September 2022 |work=invest-gate.me |date=22 January 2017}}</ref> 
{{As of|2020}}, only a small part of the city had been finished.  Many of those who work there are commuters, not residents. Completion of the city was projected to occur in 2030.<ref name="Flint">{{cite news |last1=Flint |first1=Anthony |title=What Abu Dhabi's City of the Future Looks Like Now |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2020-02-14/the-reality-of-abu-dhabi-s-unfinished-utopia |access-date=29 August 2022 |work=Bloomberg |date=14 February 2020 |language=en}}</ref> In 2022, the city announced its next expansion, Masdar City Square (MC2), to be completed by 2024. It will add seven new office buildings including the city's first net-zero energy office building.<ref>{{cite news |title=Abu Dhabi smart city breaks ground on new development |url=https://www.smartcitiesworld.net/commercial-buildings/commercial-buildings/abu-dhabi-smart-city-breaks-ground-on-new-development-7865 |access-date=15 September 2022 |work=Smart Cities World |date=6 July 2022 |language=En}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Masdar City announces new project as it advances contribution to UAE Net-Zero by 2050 Strategy |url=https://livingbusiness.com/masdar-city-announces-new-project-as-it-advances-contribution-to-uae-net-zero-by-2050-strategy/ |access-date=15 September 2022 |work=Living Business |date=5 July 2022}}</ref>

Masdar City has experienced setbacks, and has not yet reached its goals.  It can be viewed as a lesson in the importance of balancing social, environmental and economic factors in city design.  Nonetheless, Masdar City is credited with developing and implementing important technologies for resilient [[Sustainable city|sustainable cities]], and with inspiring others worldwide.<ref name="Lee"/><ref name="Randeree">{{cite journal |last1=Randeree |first1=Kasim |last2=Ahmed |first2=Nadeem |title=The social imperative in sustainable urban development: The case of Masdar City in the United Arab Emirates |journal=Smart and Sustainable Built Environment |date=1 January 2018 |volume=8 |issue=2 |pages=138–149 |doi=10.1108/SASBE-11-2017-0064 }}</ref>
